q.s: Antonella, a native of the Caribbean, learns that a family member died suddenly. She begins to cry uncontrollably, loses control as she yells aggressively, and faints. Which of the following conditions best describes the symptoms Antonella experienced?
q.ex: Ataque de nervios is a culture-bound syndrome recognized in the DSM-5 that is commonly observed in Latino and Caribbean populations. The condition typically occurs in response to acute stressors such as the death of a family member or other traumatic events. Characteristic symptoms include uncontrollable crying, aggressive outbursts, trembling, fainting or loss of consciousness, and a sense of being out of control. Antonella's presentation—uncontrollable crying, aggressive yelling, and fainting following news of a sudden death—matches the classic symptom pattern of ataque de nervios. Option A is correct because it accurately identifies this culturally specific

q.s: Which of the following best represents the description of an independent variable in this study?

o.l: The number of people at the location when the confederate fell
The level of experience of the scooter rider
The location on the campus where the confederate fell
The students on campus who watched the confederate fall off the scooter

f.c: Students enrolled in an introductory psychology course want to examine the bystander effect on their campus. The students devise a study in which one of them will pretend to fall while riding a scooter. The students choose a confederate from among the group to ride the scooter. The confederate will fall at the same location when many students are present. Then, the next day, the confederate will fall at the same location when fewer students are present. After each fall, the confederate will record whether they are helped.

q.ex: An independent variable is the factor that researchers deliberately manipulate or control in an experiment to observe its effect on the dependent variable. In this study, the researchers are examining helping behavior in response to someone falling, and they are systematically varying the number of bystanders present at each location. The number of people present when the confederate fell is the condition being manipulated by the experimenters to test how group size affects helping behavior, which is a classic investigation of the bystander effect. Option A is correct because it identifies the variable that the researchers are controlling and changing across different trials to measure its impact on whether people help the fallen confederate.

q.s: Which of the following concepts best applies to what Aidan is experiencing as he begins his new job?

f.c: Aidan, a recent college graduate, has just started an exciting new job. He has been hired by a large company that he has long admired. He feels stress because he worries that he lacks the necessary skills to perform well in this job, but is excited to learn.

q.ex: Eustress refers to positive or beneficial stress that motivates and energizes an individual, typically associated with exciting life changes or challenges. Starting a new job is a classic example of eustress because while it involves stress and adjustment, it is generally viewed as a positive opportunity that can enhance performance and personal growth. Unlike distress, which is harmful and overwhelming, eustress helps people rise to meet new challenges with enthusiasm and focus. The other options do not fit this scenario: diathesis-stress relates to mental illness development, superordinate goals involve cooperation between groups, and drive-reduction theory concerns physiological needs and homeostasis. Eustress is correct because beginning

q.s: Which of the following examples best illustrates Piaget’s concept of conservation?

o.l: Seven-year-old William understands that when water is poured from a short, wide glass into a taller, thinner glass, the amount of water is the same.
Six-month-old Aubrey cries when her toy is covered by a blanket.
Three-year-old Wen says “No” when asked if her sister has a sister.
Seven-year-old Patrice sorts trading cards into groups by the type of superhero power the character possesses.

q.ex: Conservation is Piaget's concept referring to the understanding that certain properties of objects remain the same even when their appearance changes. This cognitive ability typically develops during the concrete operational stage, around age seven. The water-pouring example directly demonstrates conservation of liquid quantity, as William recognizes that changing the shape of the container does not alter the actual amount of water present. The other options illustrate different developmental concepts: object permanence (crying when toy is hidden), egocentrism (not understanding reciprocal relationships), and classification skills (sorting by categories). Option A is correct because it specifically shows a child understanding that quantity is conserved despite a perceptual transformation in appearance.

q.s: Which of the following is a primary function of the nervous system depicted in the figure?

o.l: Breaking down food to process into energy
Sending and receiving sensory and motor signals
Receiving chemical signals from the outside world
Secreting hormones that regulate body temperature

q.ex: The nervous system's primary function is to transmit information throughout the body via electrical and chemical signals. This system consists of neurons that send sensory information from receptors to the brain and spinal cord, and motor signals from the central nervous system to muscles and glands. Breaking down food is a function of the digestive system, while hormone secretion is primarily handled by the endocrine system. Although the nervous system does receive some chemical signals, its defining characteristic is the comprehensive sending and receiving of both sensory and motor signals throughout the body. Option B is correct because it accurately describes the fundamental communication role of the nervous system in coordinating bodily functions through signal transmission.

q.s: Which of the following examples best illustrates sensory adaptation?

o.l: Sam adds salt to the soup he is cooking until he can just taste the salt.
After Joel jumped into a swimming pool, the water felt uncomfortably cold, but after a while the water felt mildly cool.
After taking her medication for years, Avery must increase her dose to get the same effect.
Watching billboard lights flash on and off causes Remi to perceive motion where none exists.

q.ex: Sensory adaptation refers to the decreased sensitivity to a constant or unchanging stimulus over time. When sensory receptors are continuously exposed to the same stimulus, they become less responsive, causing the perception of that stimulus to diminish. Joel's experience in the swimming pool demonstrates this phenomenon perfectly: initially, the cold water triggers a strong sensory response, but as his temperature receptors adapt to the constant cold stimulus, his perception changes and the water feels only mildly cool. The other options describe different concepts: Sam's experience relates to absolute threshold, Avery's situation describes drug tolerance, and Remi's perception involves apparent motion or the phi phenomenon. Option B is correct because

q.s: Which of the following research methods was used in this study?

f.c: In a recent study, researchers examined the impact of wearing face masks on speech perception. Participants were screened for normal hearing, then randomly assigned to one of two groups. Both groups listened to the same series of phrases spoken by a research assistant. In the first group, the research assistant wore a face mask, while in the second group, he did not. The researchers measured the amplitude at which the participants could hear the phrases with and without the face mask. The study’s findings indicated that wearing face masks impaired the participants’ ability to perceive speech.

q.ex: An experiment is a research method in which the researcher manipulates one or more independent variables and measures their effect on dependent variables while controlling for extraneous factors. This method allows researchers to establish cause-and-effect relationships between variables. The key distinguishing feature of an experiment is the deliberate manipulation of variables by the researcher, along with random assignment of participants to conditions when possible. In contrast, naturalistic observation involves watching behavior in natural settings without intervention, meta-analysis combines results from multiple studies statistically, and case studies involve in-depth examination of a single individual or small group. The correct answer is an experiment because this research method involves systematic manipulation of variables to determine causal relationships.

q.s: Which of the following is the dependent variable in this study?

o.l: Whether the research assistant wore a face mask or not
Whether the participants were assigned to an experimental or control group
The amplitude at which the participants could perceive the spoken phrases

f.c: In a recent study, researchers examined the impact of wearing face masks on speech perception. Participants were screened for normal hearing, then randomly assigned to one of two groups. Both groups listened to the same series of phrases spoken by a research assistant. In the first group, the research assistant wore a face mask, while in the second group, he did not. The researchers measured the amplitude at which the participants could hear the phrases with and without the face mask. The study’s findings indicated that wearing face masks impaired the participants’ ability to perceive speech.

q.ex:
The dependent variable is the outcome or response that researchers measure to assess the effect of manipulating the independent variable. In an experiment, it is what is being observed or tested, not what is being manipulated by the researchers. The amplitude at which participants could perceive spoken phrases represents the measured outcome that would change based on experimental conditions. Whether the research assistant wore a mask and whether participants were in experimental or control groups are independent variables that researchers manipulate. The screening test is a procedural element used to select participants, not a measured outcome.

The correct answer is C because the amplitude at which participants could perceive spoken phrases is the measured outcome that depends on the experimental manipulation.

q.s: Which of the following concepts best explains the point at which the participants were first able to detect the sound of the research assistant’s voice?

f.c: In a recent study, researchers examined the impact of wearing face masks on speech perception. Participants were screened for normal hearing, then randomly assigned to one of two groups. Both groups listened to the same series of phrases spoken by a research assistant. In the first group, the research assistant wore a face mask, while in the second group, he did not. The researchers measured the amplitude at which the participants could hear the phrases with and without the face mask. The study’s findings indicated that wearing face masks impaired the participants’ ability to perceive speech.

q.ex: The absolute threshold is the minimum amount of stimulus energy needed to detect a stimulus 50 percent of the time. When participants first become able to detect the sound of the research assistant's voice, they are experiencing this minimum level of detection. This differs from the just-noticeable difference, which measures the smallest change in an existing stimulus that can be detected, not the initial detection itself. Place theory relates to how we perceive pitch through location on the basilar membrane, and gate control theory explains pain perception, neither of which addresses basic sound detection. The correct answer is the absolute threshold because it specifically defines the point at which a stimulus first becomes detectable to our senses.

q.s: Which of the following fields of psychology is best reflected in Kori’s work practices?

f.c: Kori is a psychologist who works at a care center for older residents. She teaches classes on managing chronic pain using mindfulness and meditation. Kori also evaluates the eating habits, emotions, and relationships of residents to improve their quality of life and reduce their discomfort.

q.ex: Health psychology focuses on how biological, psychological, and social factors influence health and illness, including the promotion of healthy behaviors and prevention of disease. Since the question asks which field is best reflected in Kori's work practices and the correct answer is health psychology, Kori's work must involve applying psychological principles to health-related issues such as stress management, lifestyle changes, disease prevention, or helping patients cope with medical conditions. This distinguishes her work from industrial-organizational psychology (which focuses on workplace behavior), experimental psychology (which emphasizes research methodology), and evolutionary psychology (which examines psychological traits through evolutionary theory). Health psychology is correct because Kori's practices involve the intersection of psychology

q.s: Marcus is typing his notes from class. Which of the following is primarily helping Marcus move his fingers as he types?
q.ex: The peripheral nervous system consists of all nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, including motor neurons that control voluntary muscle movements. When Marcus types, his brain sends signals through the spinal cord to peripheral motor nerves, which then activate the muscles in his fingers to execute the precise movements required for typing. The temporal lobe processes auditory information and memory, the autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions like heart rate and digestion, and the hippocampus is involved in forming new memories. The peripheral nervous system is correct because it directly transmits motor commands from the central nervous system to the skeletal muscles that move the fingers during voluntary actions like typing.

q.s: Which of the following is the operational definition of the dependent variable?

o.l: Test scores on the class material

f.c: Dr. Keith conducted a study to investigate whether caffeine improves focus and attention. He selected a random sample of students from his college class and then randomly assigned each of them to drink a cup of coffee or a cup of water before class. At the end of class, he administered a test on their knowledge of class material presented that day.

q.ex: An operational definition specifies how a variable will be measured or manipulated in concrete, observable terms. The dependent variable is what researchers measure to assess the effect of the independent variable. "Test scores on the class material" is the only option that provides a specific, measurable outcome that can be quantified and recorded. "Focus and attention" is too vague and abstract without specifying how it would be measured, while "a cup of coffee" and "a cup of water" appear to be treatments or conditions (independent variables) rather than measured outcomes. Option C is correct because it clearly defines what will be measured in concrete, operational terms.

q.s: Which of the following elements of Dr. Keith’s research would most strengthen Dr. Keith’s ability to infer a causal relationship between caffeine intake and improved focus and attention?

o.l: Dr. Keith selects a random sample of students in the class.
Dr. Keith gains approval from an Institutional Review Board.
Dr. Keith keeps conditions the same between the two groups except for the independent variable.
Dr. Keith debriefs the students at the end of the study.

f.c: Dr. Keith conducted a study to investigate whether caffeine improves focus and attention. He selected a random sample of students from his college class and then randomly assigned each of them to drink a cup of coffee or a cup of water before class. At the end of class, he administered a test on their knowledge of class material presented that day.

q.ex: To establish a causal relationship in an experiment, a researcher must demonstrate that changes in the independent variable directly cause changes in the dependent variable, while ruling out alternative explanations. The key to achieving this is experimental control, which means keeping all conditions identical between groups except for the independent variable being tested. In Dr. Keith's study, if caffeine intake is the only difference between the experimental and control groups, any observed differences in focus and attention can be confidently attributed to the caffeine rather than to other factors. q.s: Dr. Keith found that students who drink coffee demonstrate less focus and attention, as evidenced by lower test scores, and then claimed that he expected that result all along. Based on this description, which of the following is Dr. Keith displaying?

f.c: Dr. Keith conducted a study to investigate whether caffeine improves focus and attention. He selected a random sample of students from his college class and then randomly assigned each of them to drink a cup of coffee or a cup of water before class. At the end of class, he administered a test on their knowledge of class material presented that day.

q.ex: Hindsight bias occurs when someone claims they "knew it all along" after learning the outcome of an event, even though they likely did not predict it beforehand. Dr. Keith demonstrated this bias by claiming he expected the results about coffee and focus after already observing the data. This is a classic example of retrospectively believing one predicted an outcome that was not actually predicted in advance. The availability heuristic involves making judgments based on readily available examples, actor/observer bias concerns how we explain our own versus others' behavior, and fundamental attribution error involves overemphasizing personality factors when explaining others' actions. q.s: Three-year-old Antra avoids eye contact, lacks facial expressions, and struggles to show empathy for others who are upset. Which of the following disorders is most consistent with these symptoms?
q.ex: Autism spectrum disorder is characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts. The core symptoms include difficulties with social-emotional reciprocity, nonverbal communicative behaviors like eye contact and facial expressions, and developing and maintaining relationships. Antra's avoidance of eye contact, lack of facial expressions, and difficulty showing empathy are hallmark features of autism spectrum disorder, particularly when these symptoms appear in early childhood. Major depressive disorder typically involves mood disturbances rather than fundamental social communication deficits, ADHD primarily affects attention and impulse control, and antisocial personality disorder is not diagnosed in young children and involves violation of others'

q.s: To meet ethical guidelines, what must Dr. Yang include in this study?

o.l: A debriefing session to explain the study purpose to the participants
A thorough breakdown of the study costs
A meta-analysis of all relevant literature on the topic
A higher level of participant compensation

f.c: Dr. Yang is conducting a study in which the researcher instructs participants to act cruelly or dishonestly toward another study participant. She hopes that the study will help her to understand better how different factors affect whether people obey a person who has authority.

q.ex: Ethical guidelines in psychological research require that participants be fully informed about the nature and purpose of a study after their participation is complete. This process, called debriefing, is especially important when deception is used or when participants might have questions about the study's aims. Debriefing allows researchers to explain the true purpose of the study, address any concerns, and ensure participants leave without misconceptions or distress. While informed consent occurs before participation, debriefing occurs after and serves to maintain transparency and respect for participants. Option A is correct because debriefing sessions are a fundamental ethical requirement in psychological research to protect participant welfare and maintain scientific integrity.

q.s: Which of the following concepts best explains Alice’s final attitude about the camp?

f.c: Alice saved money from her job to attend a sports camp that she was really excited to attend. At the camp, she endured challenging morning runs and grueling physical activity that she disliked. She thought that the food was terrible and that her bed was uncomfortable. After she returned home, she was asked if she enjoyed the camp. She replied, "It was the best experience of my life.”

q.ex: Cognitive dissonance occurs when a person holds conflicting beliefs, attitudes, or behaviors, creating psychological discomfort that motivates them to resolve the inconsistency. When individuals cannot change their behavior or circumstances, they often change their attitudes to align with their actions. In Alice's case, after committing to attend the camp despite initial reluctance or negative expectations, she likely experienced dissonance between her behavior (attending) and her original attitude (not wanting to go). To reduce this uncomfortable tension, she adjusted her final attitude to be more positive about the camp, making it consistent with her decision to participate. The correct answer is cognitive dissonance because it best explains how Alice's

q.s: Which of the following research methods is Dr. Hart using?

f.c:
Dr. Hart is a cognitive neuroscientist studying how sleep deprivation affects memory consolidation. Participants are given 5 minutes to memorize 30 unrelated words. Then Dr. Hart randomly assigns the participants to one of two groups. In Group 1, participants are not allowed to sleep uninterrupted. Instead, they are awakened each time their EEG shows they are in the REM sleep phase. In Group 2, participants are allowed to sleep for up to 8 uninterrupted hours. The next day, the participants are asked to recall as many unrelated words as possible. 

The mean score for Group 1 is 7 words. The mean score for Group 2 is 12 words. Dr. Hart finds that the differences are statistically significant.

This method allows researchers to establish cause-and-effect relationships between variables. The key distinguishing features of an experiment are random assignment of participants to conditions, manipulation of variables by the researcher, and control over extraneous variables. q.s: How is Dr. Hart operationally defining sleep deprivation?

o.l: Monitoring participants each time their EEG indicates they are in NREM sleep
Awakening participants each time their EEG indicates REM sleep
The number of unrelated words remembered after the observed night of sleep

f.c:
Dr. Hart is a cognitive neuroscientist studying how sleep deprivation affects memory consolidation. Participants are given 5 minutes to memorize 30 unrelated words. Then Dr. Hart randomly assigns the participants to one of two groups. In Group 1, participants are not allowed to sleep uninterrupted. Instead, they are awakened each time their EEG shows they are in the REM sleep phase. In Group 2, participants are allowed to sleep for up to 8 uninterrupted hours. The next day, the participants are asked to recall as many unrelated words as possible. 

The mean score for Group 1 is 7 words. The mean score for Group 2 is 12 words. Dr. Hart finds that the differences are statistically significant.

q.ex: An operational definition specifies the precise procedures or measurements used to identify or produce a concept in a research study. In this case, Dr. Hart is defining sleep deprivation through a specific experimental manipulation: awakening participants whenever their EEG readings show they have entered REM sleep. This creates a form of selective sleep deprivation by preventing participants from completing REM sleep cycles while still allowing other sleep stages to occur. The operational definition is not about measuring outcomes like word recall or simply monitoring sleep stages, but rather about the specific method used to create the sleep deprivation condition. Option C is correct because it describes the concrete procedure Dr. Hart uses to operationally define and produce

q.s: Which of the following theories does this research support regarding the importance of uninterrupted sleep?

o.l: Eight hours of uninterrupted sleep is the best way for the body to conserve resources.
REM sleep typically occurs more frequently as the sleep cycle progresses.

Dr. Hart is a cognitive neuroscientist studying how sleep deprivation affects memory consolidation. Participants are given 5 minutes to memorize 30 unrelated words. Then Dr. Hart randomly assigns the participants to one of two groups. In Group 1, participants are not allowed to sleep uninterrupted. Instead, they are awakened each time their EEG shows they are in the REM sleep phase. In Group 2, participants are allowed to sleep for up to 8 uninterrupted hours. The next day, the participants are asked to recall as many unrelated words as possible. 

The mean score for Group 1 is 7 words. The mean score for Group 2 is 12 words. Dr. Hart finds that the differences are statistically significant.

q.ex:
Uninterrupted sleep is crucial for memory consolidation, which is the process by which the brain transfers information from short-term to long-term memory storage. During sleep, particularly during REM and slow-wave sleep stages, the brain actively processes and strengthens neural connections formed during waking hours. When sleep is fragmented or interrupted, these consolidation processes are disrupted, leading to impaired memory formation and retention. Research consistently demonstrates that continuous, uninterrupted sleep cycles allow the brain to complete these essential memory-related functions more effectively than fragmented sleep patterns.

The correct answer is B because it directly addresses the specific cognitive mechanism—memory consolidation—that requires

q.s: Which of the following statements is most likely true of Demyana?

o.l: She has experienced immune suppression due to the prolonged high level of distress.
She has been using emotion-focused coping to successfully relieve her distress.
She has experienced fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression.
She has experienced instinctive drift through these many challenges.

f.c: For more than a year, Demyana has experienced consistently high levels of distress. She has experienced distress in her school life, work life, and relationships with her peers.

q.ex:
Chronic or prolonged stress leads to sustained activation of the body's stress response system, particularly elevated cortisol levels. When stress hormones remain elevated over extended periods, they suppress immune system functioning by reducing the production and effectiveness of white blood cells and other immune components. This immune suppression makes individuals more vulnerable to illness and infection. Since the question indicates Demyana has experienced prolonged high levels of distress, the most likely physiological consequence is immune system suppression. This is a well-documented effect in psychoneuroimmunology research showing the direct connection between psychological stress and physical health outcomes.

The correct choice A is correct because prolonged distress consistently produces immune supp

q.s: An online advertisement uses data and logical arguments to convince consumers to try a new skincare product. Which of the following methods best represents this persuasive approach?
q.ex: The central route to persuasion involves careful, thoughtful consideration of the actual content of a persuasive message, focusing on facts, logic, and substantive arguments. When an advertisement uses data and logical arguments, it is appealing to the audience's rational thinking and encouraging them to process information systematically. This contrasts with the peripheral route, which relies on superficial cues like celebrity endorsements or attractive packaging rather than substantive content. The door-in-the-face and foot-in-the-door techniques are compliance strategies involving sequential requests, not methods of processing persuasive information. Option C is correct because using data and logical arguments directly engages the audience's

q.s: When teaching an introductory Spanish class, Jermaine first introduces students to individual words and then helps students string the words together into sentences. This is an example of which of the following?
q.ex: Scaffolding is a teaching method based on Vygotsky's sociocultural theory where an instructor provides structured support to help learners progress from their current ability level to a higher level of understanding. The teacher breaks down complex tasks into manageable steps and gradually builds upon simpler skills to achieve more sophisticated ones. In this scenario, Jermaine uses scaffolding by first teaching individual Spanish words as foundational building blocks, then guiding students to combine these words into complete sentences, which represents a more advanced linguistic skill. This systematic progression from simple to complex exemplifies the core principle of scaffolding in education. The correct answer is D because scaffolding specifically describes

q.s: In which lobes of the brain should Dr. Cruickshank expect to see activity when subjects process the sounds of the vocabulary words?

f.c: Dr. Cruickshank conducted a study to examine whether cerebral cortex activity in the brain would be higher during memory retrieval for a test or during the initial learning process. She conducted brain scans on 10 volunteers while they were learning a new set of vocabulary words and while they were given a test on the same vocabulary words.

q.ex:
The temporal lobes contain the primary auditory cortex, which is responsible for processing auditory information including sounds and spoken language. When subjects hear vocabulary words, the sound waves are converted to neural signals that are processed in the auditory cortex located in the temporal lobes. Additionally, Wernicke's area, which is crucial for language comprehension, is also located in the temporal lobe (typically the left hemisphere). Therefore, Dr. Cruickshank should expect to see activity in the temporal lobes when subjects process the sounds of vocabulary words because this is where auditory processing and language comprehension occur.

The correct answer is B (Temporal lobes) because

q.s: Which of the following research questions is this study most likely trying to answer?

o.l: What type of audience is most receptive to an advertisement?
How does psychological state affect physical health?
How does the source of information affect how persuasive the information is?

f.c: Participants in a study are randomly shown one of two advertisements for a new dessert brand. In each advertisement, the participants are told about how delicious, satisfying, and healthy the dessert is. In one advertisement, this information is presented by a doctor wearing a lab coat. In the other advertisement, the information is presented by a popular movie actor.

q.ex:
The correct answer examines source credibility and persuasion, which is a fundamental concept in social psychology research. Studies investigating how the source of information affects persuasiveness typically manipulate who delivers a message (expert versus non-expert, attractive versus unattractive source, etc.) and measure the resulting attitude change or behavioral compliance. This research question directly addresses the relationship between message source characteristics and the effectiveness of persuasive communication. The study design would involve comparing how the same information is received differently based on who presents it, making this the research question the study is most likely addressing.

The correct choice is C because it specifically focuses on the relationship between information source and persuasiveness,

q.s: Dr. Reinhardt is interested in how to build resiliency among employees who work in large manufacturing plants so that they are less likely to miss work because of illness. Dr. Reinhardt’s research could best be classified as which of the following areas of psychology?
q.ex: Positive psychology is the scientific study of human strengths, well-being, and optimal functioning, focusing on factors that enable individuals and communities to thrive. Dr. Reinhardt's research on building resiliency among employees directly aligns with positive psychology's core emphasis on developing psychological strengths and protective factors that promote health and well-being. Resiliency, the ability to adapt and bounce back from adversity, is a central construct in positive psychology research. While behavioral psychology focuses on observable behaviors and their modification, social psychology examines interpersonal influences, and evolutionary psychology studies adaptive mechanisms, none of these specifically emphasizes building human strengths and thriving as their primary focus

q.s: Which of the following concepts best explains Leo’s interpretation of his physical responses in this scenario?

f.c:
While walking home, Leo saw his girlfriend hugging someone. His heart began to race, he began to sweat, and he felt tears in his eyes beginning to form. In response to those physical reactions, Leo thought, “I am feeling sad.” 

As he got closer to them, Leo recognized the person his girlfriend had been hugging as her brother. As his heart continued to pound, Leo felt happiness and he thought, “She still loves me.”

q.ex: Cognitive appraisal refers to the process by which an individual evaluates and interprets a situation or stimulus to determine its emotional significance. This concept, central to appraisal theories of emotion, explains how people assess their physical responses and environmental circumstances to understand what emotion they are experiencing. When Leo interprets his physical responses in the scenario, he is engaging in cognitive appraisal by mentally evaluating what his bodily sensations mean in context. This differs from the facial-feedback hypothesis, which focuses specifically on how facial expressions influence emotions, or display rules, which concern cultural norms for expressing emotions. Cognitive appraisal is correct because it directly addresses the interpretation

q.s: Which of the following examples best illustrates latent learning?

o.l: Every time a rat presses a lever it receives food, which increases its lever-pressing behavior.
After imitating how his father shaves for many years, Simon can hold the razor correctly.
A rat allowed to wander a maze for a few days can run it more quickly after a reward is later introduced.
Every time Raysa ties her shoes correctly, her mother gives her a sticker, so Raysa improves at tying her shoes.

q.ex:
Latent learning refers to knowledge that is acquired without reinforcement and remains hidden until there is an incentive to demonstrate it. The key characteristic is that learning occurs during exploration without any obvious reward, but the learned information becomes apparent only when motivation is introduced later. In option C, the rat explores and learns the maze layout without reinforcement, but this learning only becomes evident in performance when a reward is subsequently offered. This demonstrates the classic latent learning paradigm originally studied by Edward Tolman, where cognitive maps are formed during unrewarded exploration but only expressed behaviorally when reinforcement makes the knowledge useful.

Option C is correct because it shows learning occurring without immediate reinforcement that

There is a positive correlation between artists’ ages and the production of their most well-known work.
The number of top artists producing their most well-known work peaks at an age in the late thirties and then gradually declines.
Artists are more likely to generate their most well-known work after the age of 65.

f.c: The data in the graph display the ages at which top artists, including painters, writers, and composers, produce what is generally agreed upon to be their most well-known work.

q.ex: The graph shows a distribution where the frequency of artists producing their most well-known work increases through their twenties and thirties, reaches a maximum point in the late thirties age range, and then decreases as age increases beyond that point. q.s: During puberty, Ellis experienced many physical changes, including a significant broadening of his shoulders and a deepening of his voice. Which of the following concepts best describes these physical changes?

o.l: The development of secondary sex characteristics

q.ex: Secondary sex characteristics are physical features that emerge during puberty but are not directly involved in reproduction. These characteristics distinguish males from females and include features such as broadened shoulders, deepened voice, facial hair growth in males, and breast development and widened hips in females. Ellis's physical changes of broader shoulders and a deeper voice are classic examples of male secondary sex characteristics that develop during puberty due to increased testosterone production. The correct answer is C because these specific physical changes are the defining examples of secondary sex characteristics, which is the precise psychological and biological term for such pubertal body changes.

q.s: What is the operational definition of the dependent variable in this study?

o.l: The exposure to 15 highly emotional video clips
The group that categorized the list of words without watching any video clips
The score given for accurately categorizing words under the concepts
The 100 participants being randomly assigned to two groups of 50

f.c:
Dr. Robles conducted a study to investigate the influence of emotion on problem-solving ability. She randomly assigned 100 participants to two groups of 50. 

One group was shown a series of 15 highly emotional video clips and then categorized a list of 60 words using 10 different concepts. The other group categorized the list of words using the 10 concepts without watching any video clips. 

Dr. Robles calculated each participant’s score based on categorizing words under the correct concepts. The more words participants categorized correctly, the higher their score.

q.ex: The dependent variable is what researchers measure as the outcome in an experiment. An operational definition specifies exactly how that variable will be measured or quantified. In this study, the dependent variable is the participants' ability to categorize words, and the operational definition is the specific measurement method used: the score given for accurately categorizing words under the concepts. Option A describes the independent variable (what is manipulated), Option B describes the control group, and Option D describes the random assignment procedure. Option C is correct because it defines precisely how the outcome variable will be measured numerically.

Introduction

Pain-related concerns are a primary reason people seek medical care. Most pain-related concerns are addressed using biological therapies such as psychoactive drugs. A growing interest in finding non-biological approaches to pain management led researchers to explore studies that used group therapy as an alternative approach for people experiencing chronic pain.

Participants

The researchers combined and analyzed findings from 29 peer-reviewed articles that presented studies on the use of group therapy to treat pain. Collectively, the studies included approximately 4,571 participants with an average age of 53.1 years old. Seventy-eight percent of participants were women, and 22% were men.1

Most of the studies did not include other demographic information about the participants, but all of the studies were conducted in English-speaking nations. All of the studies included were approved by a committee of professionals to ensure the appropriateness of the study, and participants agreed to be in the study and knew they could withdraw from participation at any time. The researchers maintained the data in a way that would prevent participant information from being known.

Method

The researchers included studies that examined group therapy as an effective approach to pain management if those studies met the following conditions: 

  • Used random assignment to groups with a manipulated independent variable 

  • Were published between 1990 and 2020

  • Involved participants who were diagnosed with or treated for fibromyalgia2, chronic pain, and/or specific pain 

  • Measured changes in pain intensity before and after group therapy that used a variety of psychotherapeutic approaches 

  • Used a “treatment-as-usual” or wait-listed control group 

  • Included at least 20 participants who completed the group therapy and related assessments 

  • Included groups that met at least three times face-to-face for group therapy 

Most of the studies focused on fibromyalgia or other, nonspecific musculoskeletal pain. Other types of pain reported by participants included chronic back pain, arthritis, combined back and neck pain, cancer-related pain, and headaches or migraines. 

All of the studies examined the effectiveness of group therapy on pain management. Twelve of the groups had one person lead the sessions, and ten of the groups had more than one person lead the sessions. The most common treatment approach was cognitive-behavioral therapy (17 out of 29 studies). Sessions lasted an average of 120 minutes, with an average of 9 sessions offered per study. Most groups consisted of between 5 and 10 people (reported by 18 of the 29 studies).

Results and Discussion

The overall effect size of group therapy on reducing pain intensity was small. However, the researchers found significant improvements in patients’ outcomes aside from a reduction in pain intensity, patients reporting decreases in pain interference with their lives, patients thinking their pain is not the worst possible outcome (catastrophizing), and patients’ improved perceptions of pain, anxiety, depression, and barriers to physical functioning. The patients’ improvements remained consistent in long-term follow-ups lasting up to a year. These findings suggest that group therapy helps people who experience chronic pain by lessening their perception of pain intensity rather than alleviating their pain intensity.

Researchers also found that group therapy was more effective for women who participated in women-only groups than for women who participated in mixed-gendered groups. According to the researchers, groups that used cognitive-behavioral therapy appeared to be less effective at addressing pain management than groups that used other approaches to therapy (e.g., behavioral therapy). The researchers speculated that since cognitive-behavioral therapy is less focused on building group cohesion, it may not be the best approach for group therapy that addresses pain management.

Based on their findings, the researchers concluded that group therapy may be more effective than biological therapies in treating some pain-related concerns.

q.s: Which of the following approaches to alleviating a stressful situation is most consistent with Ken’s strategy?

f.c: Ken had a very challenging interaction with one of his closest friends in which hurtful words were exchanged. After considering possible solutions, Ken decided that while it might be uncomfortable at first, the best solution was to confront his friend directly to discuss what happened and work toward a solution.

q.ex: Problem-focused coping involves directly addressing the source of stress by taking action to change or eliminate the stressful situation itself. This approach contrasts with emotion-focused coping, which aims to manage the emotional response to stress rather than the stressor. Ken's strategy must involve actively working to solve or modify the problem causing his stress, such as creating a plan, seeking resources, or taking concrete steps to change his circumstances. This direct, action-oriented approach to managing stress by tackling its root cause defines problem-focused coping. The correct answer is problem-focused coping because Ken is addressing the stressor directly rather than just managing his emotional reaction to it.

q.s: Which of the following explanations would a developmental psychologist generally offer to Sarah?

o.l: Positive punishment can encourage Connor to sit up.

It is likely that Connor has a genetic disorder that needs to be treated immediately.

f.c: Sarah is the mother of an eight-month-old boy named Connor. Connor has been struggling to sit up on his own without assistance. While visiting a friend, Sarah noticed that her friend’s five-month-old daughter was sitting up with ease.

q.ex: A developmental psychologist studies typical patterns of human growth and development across the lifespan. When addressing concerns about infant milestones like sitting upright, a developmental psychologist would emphasize that developmental milestones occur within normal age ranges rather than at fixed points. Individual variation is expected and normal, with some babies achieving milestones earlier or later than others while still falling within typical development. This perspective focuses on understanding normative developmental patterns and recognizing that a range of ages for milestone achievement is developmentally appropriate. Option B is correct because it reflects the developmental psychology principle that milestones occur within a range of ages and acknowledges normal variation in child development.

q.s: Which memory system is most useful for Robyn in this scenario?

Introduction

In this study, the researchers compared the effectiveness of two different types of exposure therapy for treating post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Participants

Participants were male active duty soldiers who had experienced a trauma during a prior deployment1and had symptoms that met the DSM criteria for PTSD. Participants were restricted both from engaging in other forms of therapy to treat PTSD and from starting any new medicine for PTSD during the study. 

The final sample included 162 soldiers who agreed to be in the study and knew they could withdraw from participation at any time. The average age of the participants was 30.26 years. All the participants were men. Race and ethnicity demographics are provided in Table 1.

Table 1: Race/Ethnicity2Data for Participants

The study was approved by a committee of professionals to ensure the appropriateness of the study, and all treatments considered factors that might impose a difficulty for participants when using exposure therapies in treating PTSD.

Method

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups:

  • a waitlisted group that was eligible to begin therapy but did not receive therapy during the study;
  • an imaginal exposure therapy group in which participants verbally recalled their trauma with their therapist and then practiced controlled breathing techniques and engaged in cognitive and emotional processing of the trauma; and,
  • a virtual reality exposure therapy group in which participants verbally recalled their trauma while wearing a virtual reality headset. As the participants in this group described the trauma they experienced, the therapist customized the virtual reality to mirror their descriptions. Along with the headset, participants wore headphones that introduced sounds associated with the traumas the soldiers described (e.g., gunfire). Special speakers also produced vibrations under the soldiers’ feet. Finally, smells associated with traumas were introduced into the environment. As they experienced the virtual reality simulation, the participants practiced controlled breathing techniques and engaged in cognitive and emotional processing of the experience with their therapist. 

The study lasted for five weeks. Participants in the two exposure groups received 10 therapy sessions that lasted 1.5 to 2 hours each. After the five-week study concluded, soldiers in the waitlisted group were provided with therapy. 

Study data were collected by clinicians who were blind to the participants’ treatment groups. The researchers collected data on the following study measures:

  • PTSD symptoms, using a structured interview that measured the number and severity of PTSD symptoms and a PTSD symptom severity survey with a 17-item checklist that used 5-point Likert scales
  • Levels of depression, using a 21-item depression inventory that used 4-point Likert scales
  • Levels of anxiety, using a 21-item anxiety inventory that also used 4-point Likert scales 

Higher scores on these scales indicated more, or more severe, PTSD symptoms and higher levels of depression and anxiety, respectively. Measures were taken before treatment, at the midpoint of the treatment (2.5 weeks), and at the end of treatment (5 weeks).

Results and Discussion

At the beginning of the study, the three groups of participants did not differ significantly from each other in terms of PTSD symptoms and severity, levels of depression, or levels of anxiety. q.s: A survey question asks respondents to rate, on a scale of 1 to 10, how much their actions correspond with their attitudes. How might the language of this survey question influence the outcomes of a correlational study on cognitive dissonance?

o.l: Language emphasizing the link between actions and attitudes may introduce self-report bias.
Emotionally charged language may enhance response authenticity.
Language focusing on participants' dissonance may reduce social desirability bias.
Ambiguous language increases the likelihood of accurate self-reporting.

q.ex: When a survey question explicitly asks respondents to rate how much their actions correspond with their attitudes, it directly draws attention to potential inconsistencies between what people believe and what they do. This awareness can trigger self-report bias, where participants may consciously or unconsciously adjust their responses to appear more consistent than they actually are, since most people prefer to view themselves as internally coherent. In cognitive dissonance research, this type of leading language undermines the validity of the study because participants become aware of what is being measured and may modify their responses accordingly. The question essentially primes respondents to think about attitude-behavior consistency, making them more likely to report higher correspondence than truly exists.

Researchers like Dr. Lanier are using which of the following methods as described in the scenario to explore damaged brain areas with specific behaviors?

f.c: Dr. Lanier studies brain structures associated with sight in mice. She removes parts of the mice’s occipital lobes at birth to determine what features of the environment they cannot see based on which part of the lobe was removed. Her research was approved by the Animal Care Committee at her institution.

q.ex: Lesioning is a research method in which specific areas of the brain are deliberately damaged or destroyed to observe the resulting effects on behavior and cognitive function. By creating controlled damage to particular brain regions, researchers can establish causal relationships between those areas and specific behaviors or abilities. This method allows scientists to determine what functions are controlled by different parts of the brain by observing what capabilities are lost when those areas are damaged. The correct answer is lesioning because this technique directly involves studying damaged brain areas to understand their relationship with specific behaviors.

q.s: Which of the following statements best explains why this is a false claim?

o.l: Dr. Sanjay did not obtain informed consent from the parents or guardians of the students.
Dr. Sanjay needed to confirm that the students told the truth about what they ate.
Dr. Sanjay cannot make cause-and-effect claims from correlational data.
Dr. Sanjay needed to wait more than three days to measure word recall.

f.c: Dr. Sanjay conducted a study to determine whether eating breakfast affects academic performance. At the beginning of the week, he gathered survey data from students in his third-grade class about whether they ate breakfast. The next day, Dr. Sanjay showed the students ten new vocabulary words. Three days later, he administered a test to the students to measure their word recall. After analyzing the data, he claimed that eating breakfast improves the ability to recall new words.

q.ex: Dr. Sanjay's study appears to have measured naturally occurring relationships between dietary habits and memory performance without manipulating variables or using random assignment. Correlational research can only identify associations between variables, not causal relationships. To establish causation, a researcher must conduct a controlled experiment where participants are randomly assigned to conditions and the independent variable is directly manipulated. Since Dr. Sanjay collected correlational data by observing existing patterns rather than experimentally controlling diet, any claim that one variable causes changes in another would be invalid. Option C is correct because researchers cannot make cause-and-effect claims from correlational data.

Without seeing the specific details of Myketa's behavior in the stimulus, rationalization would be the correct answer if Myketa is providing seemingly logical reasons or excuses for actions that stem from other motivations. A company tests applicants for a personality trait that is linked to better job performance.
A teenager must earn a passing score on a written test to get their driver’s license.

q.ex: An aptitude test measures a person's potential ability or capacity to perform well in a specific area or job, rather than measuring what they have already learned or achieved. Options A, C, and D are achievement tests that measure acquired knowledge or skills, or they measure physical changes from training. Option B is correct because it evaluates inherent characteristics that predict future performance rather than testing current knowledge or past learning.

q.s: Maksym’s parents set moderate expectations about discipline, exhibit high levels of warmth, and have open lines of communication. Which of the following best describes the parenting style of Maksym’s parents?
q.ex: The authoritative parenting style is characterized by three key features: moderate to high expectations for behavior, high warmth and responsiveness, and open communication between parent and child. This style balances demandingness with responsiveness, creating a supportive environment where rules exist but are explained and discussed. Authoritarian parenting involves high control with low warmth, while permissive parenting involves high warmth with low control. Scaffolding is not a parenting style but rather an instructional technique. The correct answer is authoritative because Maksym's parents demonstrate all three defining characteristics of this parenting approach.

This response required no conditioning or previous experience to occur—it was a reflexive reaction to a naturally aversive event. q.s: Which strategy should Cesar use?

f.c: Cesar is participating in a memory competition. He must memorize a long, novel string of numbers in 60 seconds, then try to recall them immediately without missing or misplacing any numbers.

q.ex: Chunking is a memory strategy that involves organizing information into smaller, manageable groups or "chunks" to enhance retention and recall. This technique works by grouping related items together, making it easier for the brain to process and store information in working memory. For example, breaking a long phone number into segments (like 555-123-4567 instead of 5551234567) demonstrates chunking. The strategy is particularly effective because it reduces cognitive load and allows individuals to remember more information by organizing it into meaningful patterns. Chunking is the correct answer because it is an active, evidence-based learning strategy that improves memory performance.

q.s: Which of the following psychological disorders would Jaymes most likely be diagnosed with?

f.c: Two weeks ago, Jaymes was full of energy, talking quickly, and staying up all night creating art. Now, Jaymes has no appetite, feels sad, and has difficulty concentrating.

q.ex: Without the specific case details about Jaymes, I can explain the distinguishing features of bipolar disorder that would lead to this diagnosis. Bipolar disorder is characterized by alternating episodes of mania (elevated mood, increased energy, impulsivity, decreased need for sleep) and depression (low mood, loss of interest, fatigue). This cycling between extreme mood states distinguishes it from dissociative identity disorder (which involves distinct personality states), schizophrenia (which involves psychotic symptoms like hallucinations and delusions), and PTSD (which involves trauma-related symptoms like flashbacks and hypervigilance). The correct answer is bipolar disorder because

q.s: Pierce had surgery and was prescribed a painkiller that mimicked endorphins in his body. He experienced some intense, uncomfortable pain for a day or two after he was finished taking his medicine as prescribed. Pierce's painful experience associated with termination of the use of an addictive substance is known as which of the following?
q.ex: Withdrawal refers to the physical and psychological symptoms that occur when a person stops using a substance their body has become dependent on. When Pierce took the painkiller that mimicked endorphins, his body adapted to the presence of this external substance and reduced its own natural endorphin production. Once he stopped taking the medication, his body experienced a deficit until it could restore normal endorphin levels, resulting in the intense pain he felt. This uncomfortable experience following the cessation of an addictive substance is the defining characteristic of withdrawal, making option i2 correct.

q.s: When parents refuse to accept several psychologists' diagnosis of a child's mental illness, they are using which of the following defense mechanisms?
q.ex: Denial is a defense mechanism in which an individual refuses to accept reality or facts that are too uncomfortable or threatening to acknowledge. When parents reject multiple professional diagnoses of their child's mental illness, they are actively refusing to accept an anxiety-provoking truth about their child's condition. This differs from rationalization, which involves creating logical excuses for behavior, or displacement, which redirects emotions to a safer target. Projection involves attributing one's own unacceptable thoughts to others, which does not apply here. The correct answer is denial because the parents are directly refusing to acknowledge the diagnosed reality of their child's mental illness despite expert confirmation.

q.s: After several trials during which a dog is given a certain kind of food at the same time that a specific tone is sounded, there is evidence of conditioning if the dog salivates when

o.l: the food and tone are presented together
a different tone is presented with the food

q.ex: Classical conditioning occurs when a neutral stimulus becomes associated with an unconditioned stimulus through repeated pairings, eventually eliciting a conditioned response on its own. In this scenario, the tone begins as a neutral stimulus while the food naturally causes salivation as an unconditioned response. After repeated pairings of the tone with food, the tone becomes a conditioned stimulus. Evidence of successful conditioning is demonstrated when the previously neutral tone alone can trigger salivation without the food being present. Therefore, the correct answer is when the tone only is presented, as this shows the dog has learned the association between the tone and food.

q.s: Male birds from a species called bird of paradise use a complex set of behaviors to convince the female members of the species that they are suitable mates. This type of behavior is a complex pattern of organized, unlearned behavior that is species-specific. Which of the following best identifies this type of behavior?
q.ex: An instinct is defined as a complex pattern of unlearned, biologically determined behavior that is characteristic of a species. The bird of paradise mating display described in the stimulus fits this definition precisely because it is organized, unlearned (innate rather than acquired through experience), and species-specific. Drives are internal states that motivate behavior toward satisfying basic needs, motives are broader reasons for behavior that can be learned, and emotions are affective states with physiological and cognitive components. The correct answer is an instinct because the mating display is an innate, complex behavioral pattern that all male birds of paradise perform without needing to learn it.

q.s: Distrust of others is symptomatic of
q.ex: Paranoia is characterized by persistent, irrational distrust and suspicion of others, often involving beliefs that others intend harm or deception. This distrust is the defining feature that distinguishes paranoia from other psychological conditions. While mania involves elevated mood and increased energy, dementia involves cognitive decline and memory loss, and catatonia involves motor disturbances and unresponsiveness, none of these conditions have distrust as a primary symptom. Paranoia is correct because excessive distrust of others is its central and most recognizable characteristic.

q.s: The psychodynamic perspective proposes that dream analysis is a useful device for which of the following?
q.ex: The psychodynamic perspective, developed primarily by Sigmund Freud, views dreams as the "royal road to the unconscious." According to this theory, dreams contain both manifest content (what we remember) and latent content (hidden unconscious meanings). Dream analysis serves as a therapeutic technique to uncover and understand the unconscious wishes, conflicts, and motives that are disguised in dream symbolism. The goal is not to decrease repression or strengthen defense mechanisms, but rather to bring unconscious material into conscious awareness, thereby providing insight into the patient's hidden psychological processes. Option i4 is correct because gaining insight into unconscious motives is the fundamental purpose of dream analysis

q.s: When rehearsal of incoming information is prevented, which of the following will most likely occur?

o.l: The information will remain indefinitely in short-term memory.
There will be no transfer of the information to long-term memory.
The sensory register will stop processing the information.
Retrieval of the information from long-term memory will be easier.

q.ex: Rehearsal is the process of actively repeating or mentally reviewing information to maintain it in short-term memory and facilitate its transfer to long-term memory. According to the multi-store model of memory, information must be rehearsed in short-term memory to be encoded into long-term memory. When rehearsal is prevented, information typically decays from short-term memory within 15-30 seconds and is not consolidated into long-term storage. Without rehearsal serving as the mechanism for encoding, the information cannot make the transition from temporary to permanent storage. Therefore, preventing rehearsal will most likely result in no transfer of information to long-term memory, making option i1

q.s: Which of the following behavior-therapy techniques is typically used to reduce fear of heights?
q.ex: Systematic desensitization is a behavioral therapy technique specifically designed to reduce phobias and anxiety responses through gradual exposure paired with relaxation. The procedure involves creating a hierarchy of fear-inducing situations, teaching relaxation techniques, and then systematically exposing the client to progressively more anxiety-provoking scenarios while maintaining a relaxed state. For fear of heights, a client would start with minimal exposure (such as imagining standing on a low step) and gradually progress to more challenging situations (like standing on a high balcony). This technique works by counter-conditioning the fear response with relaxation, making it the standard behavioral treatment for specific phobias like ac

q.s: Jeremy stubbed his toe when he was getting some water in the middle of the night. Within a few minutes, the pain in his toe began to ease. The painkilling substances produced by the brain are known as which of the following?
q.ex: Endorphins are the body's natural painkilling substances produced by the brain and nervous system. These neurotransmitters bind to opioid receptors in the brain, blocking pain signals and producing feelings of pleasure or well-being. When Jeremy stubbed his toe, his body released endorphins in response to the pain, which is why the discomfort began to ease within minutes. Acetylcholine is involved in muscle activation and memory, leptin regulates appetite and metabolism, and adrenaline is a stress hormone that prepares the body for fight-or-flight responses. Endorphins are correct because they are specifically the brain's natural

q.s: In terms of the effect on the central nervous system, alcohol is most accurately classified as which of the following types of drug?
q.ex: Alcohol is classified as a depressant because it slows down the activity of the central nervous system by enhancing the effects of GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter, and reducing the activity of glutamate, an excitatory neurotransmitter. This results in decreased neural activity, leading to effects such as slowed reaction times, impaired coordination, reduced inhibitions, and sedation. While alcohol is technically psychoactive (any substance that affects mental processes), the most accurate and specific classification based on its primary mechanism of action is as a depressant. Stimulants have the opposite effect by increasing CNS activity, and narco

q.s: On a fishing trip, Ed realizes that he has mistakenly packed the sewing box instead of the tackle box. He wants to fish but returns home because he does not have any line or hooks. Ed's failure to realize that sewing thread can be used as fishing line and that a bent needle can be used as a hook is an example of
q.ex: Functional fixedness is a cognitive bias that limits a person to using an object only in the way it is traditionally used, preventing them from recognizing alternative functions. In this scenario, Ed cannot see beyond the conventional uses of sewing thread and needles, failing to recognize that thread could serve as fishing line and a bent needle could function as a hook. This mental block prevents him from solving his problem creatively, even though the necessary materials are available in a different form. The correct answer is functional fixedness because Ed's inability to repurpose the sewing materials for fishing demonstrates this specific type of cognitive limitation where objects are viewed as having only their standard functions.

q.s: Which of the following responses was most likely acquired through classical conditioning?

o.l: The startle response of a baby the first time the baby hears thunder
A child's fear of dogs after the child has been bitten by a dog
The uncontrollable blinking of a woman who has just gotten dust in her eye
The salivation of a dog that is halfway through a bowl of its favorite food

q.ex: Classical conditioning involves learning to associate a previously neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus that naturally produces a response. In option i1, the child initially had no inherent fear of dogs (neutral stimulus), but after being bitten (unconditioned stimulus that naturally causes pain and fear), the child learned to associate dogs with that negative experience. The startle response to thunder, uncontrollable blinking from dust, and salivation while eating are all unconditioned reflexes that occur naturally without learning. Option i1 is correct because it demonstrates acquired learning through the pairing of a neutral stimulus with an aversive experience, which is the defining characteristic of classical conditioning.

q.s: The failure of bystanders to give victims of automobile accidents needed assistance is sometimes explained as an instance of
q.ex: Diffusion of responsibility occurs when individuals in a group are less likely to take action or feel accountable because they assume others will intervene. In bystander situations like automobile accidents, the presence of multiple witnesses leads each person to feel less personal responsibility to help, as they believe someone else will step in. This phenomenon explains why victims sometimes receive no assistance despite many people being present. Group polarization involves attitude strengthening in groups, deindividuation refers to loss of self-awareness in crowds, and situational attribution is about explaining behavior through external factors rather than describing the bystander effect itself. Diffusion of responsibility is correct because it directly explains the psychological mechanism causing byst

q.s: The control group in the experiment is the group that

o.l: the researchers thought would be most aggressive
performed the larger number of aggressive acts

f.c:
The next questions refer to the situation described below.

In an experiment designed to determine whether watching violent scenes on television increases the frequency of aggressive behavior in children, one group of subjects saw a nonviolent cartoon and another group saw a violent cartoon. In the play period that followed the viewing of the cartoons, researchers observed the two groups of children together and counted instances of aggressive behavior.

q.ex: A control group in an experiment is the group that does not receive the experimental treatment or intervention being tested. In this experiment, the independent variable being manipulated is exposure to violent content. The experimental group would be exposed to the violent cartoon (the treatment condition), while the control group would be exposed to the nonviolent cartoon (the baseline or comparison condition). This allows researchers to compare outcomes between groups and determine whether the violent content specifically caused any differences in behavior. The correct answer is the group that watched the nonviolent cartoon because they serve as the baseline comparison group that did not receive the experimental treatment of violent content exposure.

q.s: The dependent variable in the experiment is the

o.l: amount of aggressive behavior exhibited by the children
amount of time that each child spent interacting with the other children
group in which each child was originally placed

f.c:
The next questions refer to the situation described below.

In an experiment designed to determine whether watching violent scenes on television increases the frequency of aggressive behavior in children, one group of subjects saw a nonviolent cartoon and another group saw a violent cartoon. In the play period that followed the viewing of the cartoons, researchers observed the two groups of children together and counted instances of aggressive behavior.

q.ex: The dependent variable is what researchers measure to assess the effect of their manipulation. It is the outcome that depends on changes in the independent variable. In this experiment, the researchers are measuring the amount of aggressive behavior exhibited by the children as their outcome of interest. The group placement and violent cartoon are independent variables that the experimenters control or manipulate, while time spent interacting with other children would be an alternative dependent variable that is not the focus here. The amount of aggressive behavior is what the experimenters are observing and quantifying as a result of their experimental conditions, making it the dependent variable.

q.s: Which of the following is most characteristic of individuals with chronic schizophrenia?
q.ex: Schizophrenia is a severe mental disorder primarily characterized by disruptions in thought processes, perceptions, and emotional responsiveness. The hallmark symptoms include positive symptoms like hallucinations and delusions, negative symptoms like flat affect and social withdrawal, and cognitive symptoms, with disordered thinking being central to the diagnosis. Disordered thinking manifests as disorganized speech, loose associations, and difficulty organizing thoughts coherently. While mood disorders involve extreme mood swings, conversion disorders involve loss of body function, and dementia involves memory loss, these are not the defining features of chronic schizophrenia. Disordered thinking is correct because it represents the core

q.s: Activation of the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system results in
q.ex: The sympathetic nervous system is responsible for the body's "fight or flight" response during stressful or emergency situations. When activated, it prepares the body for action by increasing functions that help with immediate survival while decreasing non-essential functions. This includes increasing heart rate, dilating pupils, and increasing respiratory rate to provide more oxygen to muscles. Conversely, it decreases digestive activity and salivation since these processes are not immediately necessary during emergencies. An increase in respiratory rate is correct because faster breathing delivers more oxygen to support the heightened physical demands of the fight or flight response.

q.s: The terms "modeling" and "imitation" are most closely associated with which of the following?
q.ex: Social learning theory, developed primarily by Albert Bandura, centers on the idea that people learn by observing others' behaviors and the consequences of those behaviors. Modeling refers to the process where an individual demonstrates a behavior for others to observe, while imitation is when the observer reproduces that observed behavior. These concepts are fundamental to social learning theory, which emphasizes that learning occurs in a social context through observation rather than solely through direct reinforcement or conditioning. The famous Bobo doll experiments demonstrated how children learned aggressive behaviors simply by watching adults model those behaviors, establishing modeling and imitation as core mechanisms of social learning.

q.s: In a famous series of experiments conducted by Harry Harlow, infant monkeys were separated from their mothers at birth. The infants were then given two surrogate mothers (a terry-cloth "mother" and a wire "mother"), each of which alternately had a nursing bottle that provided food to the infants. The experimental results showed that in frightening situations the infant monkeys

o.l: failed to seek out either of the mothers because of their lack of experience in seeking contact comfort
preferred the wire mother, even when the terry-cloth mother had the nursing bottle
preferred the terry-cloth mother, even when the wire mother had the nursing bottle
would run and cling to whichever mother had the nursing bottle

q.ex: Harlow's experiments demonstrated that attachment in infant monkeys is based primarily on contact comfort rather than feeding. The infant monkeys consistently sought out and clung to the soft terry-cloth mother when frightened, regardless of which surrogate provided food. This finding challenged the prevailing behaviorist theory that attachment forms solely through association with food reinforcement. The research showed that tactile comfort and the need for a secure base are fundamental to attachment bonds, even overriding the basic need for nourishment in stressful situations. Therefore, option i3 is correct because the infant monkeys preferred the terry-cloth mother for comfort and security even when the wire mother was the source

q.s: People who believe that their efforts will be successful and that they are in control of events have a high level of which of the following?
q.ex: Self-efficacy refers to an individual's belief in their capacity to execute behaviors necessary to produce specific performance attainments. It represents confidence in the ability to exert control over one's own motivation, behavior, and social environment. People with high self-efficacy believe their efforts will lead to successful outcomes and that they can influence events in their lives. While self-esteem relates to overall self-worth, self-efficacy specifically concerns beliefs about personal capability and control over outcomes. The correct answer is self-efficacy because it directly defines the belief that one's efforts will succeed and that one controls events.

q.s: A teenager would most probably draw on which of the following to recall her tenth birthday party?
q.ex: Episodic memory is the type of long-term memory that stores personally experienced events along with their contextual details, including time and place. A tenth birthday party represents a specific autobiographical event from a particular time in the teenager's life, complete with personal experiences and contextual information about when and where it occurred. Semantic memory stores general facts and knowledge without personal context, while echoic memory is a brief sensory memory for sounds lasting only seconds. Eidetic imagery refers to the rare ability to retain detailed visual images for a short time after viewing them. Episodic memory is correct because recalling a personal birthday party requires accessing autobiographical memories of specific life events

q.s: Leadership, job satisfaction, and employee motivation are all studied in which of the following psychological disciplines?
q.ex: Industrial-organizational psychology is the branch of psychology that applies psychological principles and research methods to the workplace. This field specifically focuses on topics related to worker behavior, organizational dynamics, and workplace effectiveness, including leadership styles, employee job satisfaction, and factors that influence worker motivation. Human factors psychology deals with human-machine interaction and ergonomics, community psychology focuses on social systems and community well-being, and counseling psychology addresses personal and interpersonal functioning. Industrial-organizational psychology is correct because it is explicitly defined as the study of behavior in work settings and organizational contexts.

q.s: Researchers at a local university conduct research to find the biological bases for Alzheimer's disease. According to the ethical guidelines set by the American Psychological Association (APA), which of the following is true of psychological research in which animals are used as subjects?

o.l: It must not involve the use of surgical procedures.
It is no longer permitted by the APA without special authorization.
