Food outranked all other factors in the development of the infant monkeys’ attachment to the mother.
Infant monkeys mimic the surrogate mothers' behavior.

q.ex: Harry Harlow's famous surrogate mother experiments demonstrated that infant monkeys spent significantly more time clinging to the cloth-covered surrogate mother, even when only the wire mother provided food. The infant monkeys would only briefly visit the wire mother to feed, then return to the cloth mother for comfort and security, especially when frightened. This research proved that tactile comfort and physical contact were more important than food in forming attachment bonds. The findings challenged the prevailing behaviorist theory that attachment was based solely on feeding and reinforcement, showing instead that contact comfort was the primary basis of attachment for the infant monkeys.

q.s: Devi spent time developing a set of note cards for an upcoming test that used word associations based on what the words meant in relation to each other. Which of the following did Devi use with this study method?
q.ex: Effortful processing refers to encoding information into memory through conscious, deliberate effort and attention, often using strategies like rehearsal, organization, or elaboration. When Devi created note cards using word associations based on meaningful relationships between concepts, she engaged in intentional, strategic studying that required focused mental work. This active manipulation and organization of information to create meaningful connections represents effortful processing rather than automatic encoding. State-dependent memory involves recall being better when in the same physical or mental state as during encoding, latent learning is learning that occurs without reinforcement and isn't immediately demonstrated, and procedural memory involves skills and habits rather than conscious study strategies. Effortful processing

q.s: Matt finds that when he is doing chores around his home, he can listen to an audiobook and still remember what the story was about. However, when his friends texts him about their plans for the weekend, he realizes that he has to rewind his audiobook because he forgot was the story was about. Which of the following accurately describes the level of processing Matt experiencing for doing chores around his home?
q.ex: When Matt performs chores while listening to an audiobook, he can maintain attention on both tasks because the chores require automatic processing. Automatic processing refers to mental activities that require little to no conscious attention or cognitive resources, typically developed through extensive practice and repetition. Household chores are routine, well-learned tasks that Matt can execute without focused mental effort, leaving cognitive capacity available for the audiobook. However, when his friend texts him, this requires controlled processing that demands conscious attention, which diverts his cognitive resources away from the audiobook and causes him to lose track of the story. The correct answer is automatic because it describes the low-demand, habitual level of processing Matt

q.s: Money most often modifies people’s behavior because it is a powerful
q.ex: Money functions as a secondary reinforcer because it has acquired its reinforcing properties through learned association with primary reinforcers like food, shelter, and other basic needs. Unlike primary reinforcers that satisfy biological needs directly, secondary reinforcers gain their value through conditioning and experience. Money itself has no intrinsic value but becomes powerful because people learn it can be exchanged for things that do satisfy their needs and wants. This learned association makes money one of the most effective secondary reinforcers in modifying human behavior across diverse situations and cultures. The correct answer is secondary reinforcer because money derives its reinforcing power through conditioning rather than having inherent biological value.

q.s: Jalil goes to a party where he meets several new people. When he tells his brother about it the next day, he can only remember the names of the last 3 people that he met. Which of the following memory concepts best describes Jalil's memory for the names of the people at the party?
q.ex: The recency effect describes the tendency to better remember items or information encountered at the end of a sequence or list. In this scenario, Jalil can only recall the names of the last three people he met at the party, demonstrating superior memory for the most recently presented information. This occurs because recent information is still active in short-term memory and has not yet been displaced by subsequent information. The primacy effect would involve remembering the first people he met, the spacing effect relates to distributed practice improving retention, and the law of effect concerns reinforcement of behaviors. The correct answer is the recency effect because Jalil specifically remembers the final names from his sequence of introductions.

q.s: Which of the following statements best describes the placebo effect?

o.l: Dr. Kennedy observed that if people expected a treatment to work, it would, even if the patient received a fake treatment.
Dr. Tyler observed that people taking antipsychotic medication improved their quality of life more than those who did not take medication.
Dr. Adams helped his clients uncover unconscious feelings about their childhood trauma, which helped them become better adjusted to stress.
Dr. Lincoln used active listening to help clients sense and perceive the world better.

q.ex: The placebo effect occurs when a person experiences a real change in their condition after receiving an inactive or fake treatment, simply because they believe the treatment will work. This psychological phenomenon demonstrates that expectations and beliefs about treatment can produce measurable physiological or psychological effects, even when no active therapeutic ingredient is present. Option i0 correctly describes this concept by noting that people improved when they expected treatment to work, despite receiving a fake treatment. The other options describe legitimate therapeutic interventions or medication effects rather than the placebo effect. Option i0 is correct because it accurately captures the essential element of the placebo effect: improvement resulting from expectation rather than from any active treatment component.

q.s: Researchers at a local hospital are interested in whether teenagers who use internet-connected devices are more depressed than those who do not. In developmental psychology, one advantage of doing this research as a cross-sectional study over using longitudinal methods is that cross-sectional research does which of the following?

o.l: Involves subjects of the same age.

q.ex: A cross-sectional study examines different groups of participants at a single point in time, while a longitudinal study follows the same participants over an extended period. The primary practical advantage of cross-sectional research is efficiency: data can be collected from all participants simultaneously or within a brief timeframe, allowing researchers to obtain results quickly. In contrast, longitudinal studies require researchers to track participants across months or years, demanding sustained funding, participant retention, and extended commitment from the research team. Cross-sectional studies do not inherently control for cognitive ability or gender any better than longitudinal studies, and they actually compare different age groups rather than subjects of the same age. The correct answer is

q.s: Which of the following is an example of social facilitation?

o.l: A student scores higher on tests taken with classmates than with strangers.
A child smiles more often in the presence of family members than in the presence of strangers.
An elementary school student reads more books when promised free pizza for reading a greater number.
An athlete performs better in games before a large crowd than she does in practice.

q.ex: Social facilitation refers to the phenomenon where an individual's performance on a task improves when in the presence of others compared to when alone. This effect is most pronounced for well-learned or simple tasks, where the presence of an audience or co-actors enhances performance. The athlete performing better in games before a large crowd than in practice demonstrates this concept because the presence of spectators improves her performance on a well-practiced skill compared to practicing alone. Option i3 is correct because it shows improved performance on a familiar task due to the mere presence of others, which is the defining characteristic of social facilitation.

q.s: Mr. and Ms. Jones-Smith have five children who range in age from 12 to 2. Their children all follow a tight schedule for meals, studying, chores, and sleep. They are allowed to spend one hour each night playing a complex board game or putting together puzzles. They go on one vacation each year as a family, and the vacation always involves some type of learning experience the children must recall to their parents after the vacation. Which parenting style is characterized by high demands for obedience and low warmth?
q.ex: The authoritarian parenting style is defined by high demands and expectations for obedience combined with low warmth and responsiveness to children's emotional needs. In this scenario, the Jones-Smith family demonstrates classic authoritarian characteristics: rigid schedules for all activities, structured and educational play rather than free play, and even vacations that require performance and recall rather than simple enjoyment. The emphasis is entirely on control, structure, and compliance with parental rules, with no mention of emotional warmth, flexibility, or consideration of the children's preferences. This contrasts with authoritative parenting, which also has high demands but includes high warmth and two-way communication. The correct answer is

q.s: Which of the following disorders would a doctor prescribe lithium to treat?
q.ex: Lithium is a mood-stabilizing medication primarily prescribed to treat bipolar disorder, a condition characterized by alternating episodes of mania (elevated mood, increased energy) and depression. The drug works by regulating neurotransmitter activity in the brain to reduce the severity and frequency of these mood swings. While the other conditions listed are legitimate psychological disorders, they are not typically treated with lithium: agoraphobia responds to anti-anxiety medications and therapy, anorexia nervosa requires nutritional rehabilitation and psychotherapy, and dissociative fugue is treated with psychotherapy. Bipolar disorder is correct because lithium has been the gold-standard pharmacological

q.s: If students get approximately the same score on the second administration of a test as they did on the first, then the test is
q.ex: Reliability refers to the consistency of a test's measurements across multiple administrations. When students receive approximately the same scores on repeated testing, the test demonstrates test-retest reliability, which is a key indicator that the assessment produces stable and dependable results. This consistency shows the test is measuring something in a reproducible way rather than producing random or fluctuating scores. The correct answer is reliable because consistent scores across administrations are the defining characteristic of a reliable test.

q.s: Although people can acquire phobias to almost any object or situation, certain phobias (e.g., those to snakes, spiders, heights) are much more common than others. This finding can best be explained by which of the following concepts?
q.ex: Biological preparedness refers to the evolutionary predisposition humans have to more easily develop fears of objects or situations that posed survival threats to our ancestors. Snakes, spiders, and heights were genuine dangers throughout human evolutionary history, so individuals who quickly learned to fear and avoid these threats had better survival rates. This evolutionary advantage made humans biologically "prepared" to acquire these specific phobias more readily than fears of modern dangers like electrical outlets or cars. The concept explains why certain phobias are disproportionately common across cultures despite varying individual experiences. Biological preparedness is correct because it directly accounts for why some phobias occur more frequently than others based on evolutionary significance

q.s: Tremaine believes kids who go to his school's rival high school are arrogant and entitled since they live in a community that has a slightly higher socioeconomic status than his own community. At a birthday party one night at a friend's house, Tremaine meets Reynard and they find they have a lot in common. Tremaine is dismayed when he finds out the next day that Reynard goes to the rival high school. Tremaine holding a predetermined belief about a group of people, regardless of the personal qualities of the individual members, is referred to as which of the following?
q.ex: Stereotyping is the process of holding oversimplified, generalized beliefs about a group of people without regard to individual differences among group members. In this scenario, Tremaine has a predetermined belief that all students at the rival high school are arrogant and entitled based solely on their community's socioeconomic status. When he meets Reynard and discovers they have much in common, this challenges his stereotype, yet he had already formed this generalized belief before knowing Reynard as an individual. Discrimination refers to behavioral actions against a group, dissonance refers to conflicting beliefs or attitudes, and polarization refers to the strengthening of group attitudes. The correct

q.s: In an experiment to test the effects of hunger on aggressive behavior, aggressive behavior would be the
q.ex: In experimental research, the dependent variable is the outcome or behavior being measured to determine if it changes in response to manipulation of another variable. The independent variable is what the researcher manipulates or controls. In this experiment, hunger is being manipulated by the researcher to observe its effects, making hunger the independent variable. Aggressive behavior is what is being measured as the outcome, making it the dependent variable because it depends on the level of hunger. The dependent variable is always what you measure or observe for changes, while the independent variable is what you deliberately vary or control.

q.s: The Gestalt principle that refers to an individual’s tendency to perceive an incomplete figure as whole is called
q.ex: Closure is the Gestalt principle that describes the perceptual tendency to complete incomplete figures or fill in gaps to perceive a whole, unified object. When viewing a circle with a small segment missing, for example, people typically perceive a complete circle rather than an arc. This principle reflects the mind's automatic drive to create meaningful, complete patterns from fragmentary visual information. Figure-ground relates to distinguishing objects from backgrounds, proximity involves grouping nearby elements, and shape constancy refers to recognizing objects despite viewing angle changes. The correct answer is closure because it specifically addresses perceiving incomplete figures as complete wholes.

q.s: Mrs. Downing is 80 years old and lives in an assisted living facility. She often stops speaking in the middle of sentences because she can't remember the topic being discussed. She also tries on most days to leave the facility so she can get home to cook dinner for her family. The depletion of which of the following neurotransmitters is most closely associated with the symptoms of Alzheimer’s disease that Mrs. Downing is likely experiencing?
q.ex: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by progressive cognitive decline, including memory loss and confusion, which are evident in Mrs. Downing's inability to remember conversation topics and her disorientation about time and place. The primary neurological feature of Alzheimer's disease is the significant depletion of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter crucial for memory formation and learning processes. Acetylcholine-producing neurons in the brain, particularly in the hippocampus and cortex, deteriorate in Alzheimer's patients, leading to the characteristic memory deficits and cognitive impairments. While dopamine is associated with Parkinson's disease and movement disorders

q.s: Research indicates that a toddler with a secure attachment style is most likely to do which of the following when left with a caregiver, such as a babysitter, for the first time?

o.l: Show distress when left, calm down and play, and run to the mother when she returns
Cry when left and continue to cry until the mother returns
Not notice when the mother leaves and not seek attention from the mother when she returns
Show distress when the mother leaves and not seek attention when the mother returns

q.ex: A securely attached toddler has developed a healthy emotional bond with their primary caregiver, characterized by using the caregiver as a secure base for exploration and seeking comfort when distressed. When separated from the mother, a securely attached child will show initial distress because they prefer their caregiver's presence, but they can be soothed by the substitute caregiver and will engage in play or exploration. Upon the mother's return, the securely attached child actively seeks reunion and contact, showing happiness at being reunited. This pattern demonstrates the child's confidence that the caregiver will return and their ability to regulate emotions with support, which are hallmarks of secure

q.s: The claim by behaviorists that the environment alone determines an individual’s behavior was criticized for which of the following?

o.l: failing to explain how personality can change over time
failing to acknowledge cognitive influences on behavior

q.ex: Behaviorism, particularly radical behaviorism, focused exclusively on observable behaviors and environmental stimuli, treating the mind as a "black box" that need not be examined. Critics argued this approach was incomplete because it ignored internal mental processes such as thoughts, beliefs, expectations, and decision-making that influence how people respond to environmental stimuli. The cognitive revolution in psychology emerged partly as a response to this limitation, emphasizing that behavior results from an interaction between environmental factors and cognitive processes. This criticism does not relate to personality change over time, genetics, or unconscious influences, which are concerns of other psychological perspectives. Option i1 is correct because the primary criticism of strict behaviorism

q.s: John is generally pleasant, but during final exams he experiences more intense stress than other students experience. He is irritable and easily frustrated. According to the Big Five model of personality, John would be
q.ex: The Big Five model of personality includes five major dimensions: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. Neuroticism refers to emotional instability and the tendency to experience negative emotions such as anxiety, anger, and vulnerability, particularly in response to stress. John's pattern of experiencing more intense stress than others and becoming irritable and easily frustrated during challenging situations like final exams is characteristic of high neuroticism. While he may be generally pleasant (suggesting baseline agreeableness), his heightened stress reactivity and emotional volatility under pressure specifically indicate elevated neuroticism. Therefore, high neuroticism is the correct answer because it directly

q.s: An individual uses a paper clip to unlock the door to her house because she has misplaced her key. This individual’s approach to solving the problem avoids
q.ex:
Functional fixedness is a cognitive bias that limits a person to using an object only in the way it is traditionally used. In this scenario, the individual recognizes that a paper clip can serve a purpose beyond its typical function of holding papers together and uses it as a tool to unlock a door. By seeing the paper clip as a potential lock-picking tool rather than just a fastener, the person has overcome functional fixedness. The other options relate to forms of logical reasoning that do not directly address the ability to see alternative uses for common objects.

The correct answer is functional fixedness because the individual avoided being mentally constrained by the paper clip's conventional purpose.

q.s: Dr. Guarini is interested in conducting research that examines how much information people can hold in their working memory. She is unsure whether she needs to conduct an experiment or correlational research. Experimental research differs from correlational research in that experimental research can do which of the following?
q.ex:
Experimental research differs from correlational research primarily in its ability to establish causation. In an experiment, researchers manipulate an independent variable while controlling other factors, then measure the effect on a dependent variable. This manipulation and control allows researchers to determine whether changes in one variable actually cause changes in another. Correlational research, by contrast, only measures the relationship between variables as they naturally occur without manipulation, which means it can show associations but cannot establish that one variable causes another. While both methods allow for prediction and both can use dependent variables, only experimental research can reveal causal relations through its use of manipulation and control.

The correct choice is "may reveal a causal relation" because the

q.s:
According to research on interpersonal perception, the formation of friendships is associated with which of the following?

  1. Physical attractiveness

  2. Physical proximity

  3. Attributions of similarity
q.ex: Research on interpersonal perception has consistently identified three key factors that influence friendship formation. Physical attractiveness creates positive first impressions and increases the likelihood of initial interaction. Physical proximity, known as the propinquity effect, increases opportunities for repeated contact and familiarity, which breeds liking. Attributions of similarity, whether in attitudes, values, or interests, enhance attraction because people are drawn to those they perceive as like themselves. All three factors—physical attractiveness, physical proximity, and attributions of similarity—have been empirically demonstrated to facilitate friendship development. Therefore, the correct answer is I, II, and III because each factor independently contributes to interpersonal attraction

q.s: Which of the following is a type of therapy for alcoholism that involves the administration of a drug that will induce nausea after a person consumes alcohol?
q.ex: Aversion therapy is a behavioral treatment technique that pairs an undesirable behavior with an unpleasant stimulus to reduce or eliminate that behavior. In the treatment of alcoholism, aversion therapy involves administering a drug like disulfiram (Antabuse) that causes severe nausea and vomiting when combined with alcohol consumption. This creates a negative association between drinking alcohol and feeling sick, thereby discouraging future alcohol use. The other options represent different therapeutic approaches: implosive therapy and flooding both involve exposure to feared stimuli, while rational-emotive behavior therapy focuses on changing irrational thoughts. Aversion therapy is correct because it specifically describes the

q.s: Richard is in a substance abuse treatment center because of his addiction to stimulants. He is experiencing withdrawal symptoms, so he drinks several large caffeinated sodas throughout the day to curb his symptoms. Caffeine is in the same class as which of the following drugs?
q.ex: Caffeine is classified as a stimulant drug, which means it increases activity in the central nervous system, leading to heightened alertness, increased heart rate, and elevated energy levels. Cocaine is also a stimulant that produces similar effects by increasing neurotransmitter activity in the brain, particularly dopamine. Both caffeine and cocaine belong to the stimulant class of drugs, which is why Richard's use of caffeinated sodas temporarily alleviates his withdrawal symptoms from stimulant addiction. In contrast, marijuana is a hallucinogen/depressant, heroin is an opioid depressant, and alcohol is a depressant

q.s: When ten-month-old Frances throws her toy out of sight, she looks to see where it falls. Developmental psychologists would say that Frances’ behavior indicates that she has developed
q.ex: Object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist even when they cannot be seen, heard, or otherwise sensed. This cognitive milestone typically develops during the sensorimotor stage of development, around 8 to 12 months of age, according to Jean Piaget's theory of cognitive development. When Frances looks to see where her toy falls after throwing it out of sight, she demonstrates that she understands the toy still exists even though she cannot currently see it. This behavior is a clear indicator of object permanence, as she actively searches for the object rather than acting as if it has ceased to exist. The correct answer is object permanence because Frances' searching behavior shows

q.s: After having a stroke resulting from a blockage of blood to the medial temporal lobe, Gerald could not remember new information, such as the books he had just read, new songs he had just heard, or the faces of new people he had just met. Gerald was experiencing
q.ex: Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after a brain injury or neurological event, while previously stored memories remain intact. Gerald's stroke damaged his medial temporal lobe, which includes the hippocampus, a structure critical for encoding new memories. His symptoms—inability to remember books just read, new songs, or new faces—demonstrate he cannot form new long-term memories following his stroke. This pattern of memory impairment, where new information cannot be retained while old memories persist, is the defining characteristic of anterograde amnesia. Option i3 is correct because Gerald's condition specifically involves the loss of ability to create new memories after the stroke,

q.s: Which of the following kinds of learning is involved when a person displays a new behavior after watching someone else perform it?
q.ex: Observational learning occurs when an individual acquires new behaviors by watching and imitating others, a process also known as modeling or social learning. This type of learning was extensively studied by Albert Bandura, who demonstrated through his famous Bobo doll experiments that children could learn aggressive behaviors simply by observing adults perform them. The key feature is that the learner does not need direct reinforcement or personal trial-and-error experience to acquire the behavior. Generalization involves applying learned responses to similar stimuli, latent learning refers to knowledge acquired without immediate demonstration, and insight learning involves sudden problem-solving realizations. Observational learning is correct because it specifically describes the

q.s: Information is relayed to the spinal cord or the brain by which of the following?
q.ex: Sensory neurons, also called afferent neurons, are specialized nerve cells that transmit information from sensory receptors throughout the body to the central nervous system (the spinal cord and brain). These neurons detect stimuli such as touch, temperature, pain, and other sensory inputs and convert them into electrical signals that travel toward the brain for processing. Motor neurons, in contrast, carry signals away from the central nervous system to muscles and glands. Dopamine neurons are a specific type that releases the neurotransmitter dopamine, and "refractory neurons" refers to a temporary state during neural firing rather than a neuron type. The correct answer is sensory

q.s: A person displays behaviors of a psychological disorder that psychologists in the United States have not seen before. The best strategy to investigate the nature of those behaviors is to conduct which of the following?
q.ex: A case study is the most appropriate research method when investigating a novel or rare psychological phenomenon that has not been previously documented. This method involves an in-depth, detailed examination of a single individual or small group, allowing researchers to gather comprehensive qualitative and quantitative data about unique behaviors, symptoms, and circumstances. When psychologists encounter an unfamiliar disorder, they need to thoroughly document and analyze all aspects of the case before broader research methods can be applied. Experiments, cross-sectional studies, and correlational research require larger sample sizes and are better suited for testing hypotheses about already-identified phenomena rather than exploring completely new conditions. A case study is correct because it provides the detailed,

q.s: Which of the following is an explanation of why travelers suffer from jet lag?

o.l: They experience an increase in REM rebound.
There is a decrease in the duration of brain waves in sleep.
They experience excess amounts of NREM sleep.
There is a disruption in their circadian rhythm.

q.ex: Jet lag occurs when travelers cross multiple time zones rapidly, causing their internal biological clock to be out of sync with the external environment. The circadian rhythm is the body's natural 24-hour cycle that regulates sleep-wake patterns, hormone release, and other physiological processes based on environmental cues like light and darkness. When someone travels across time zones, their circadian rhythm remains aligned with their origin location while the destination operates on a different schedule. This mismatch between the internal clock and external time cues results in the fatigue, sleep disturbances, and other symptoms characteristic of jet lag. The correct answer is that there is a disruption in their circadian rhythm

q.s: A student has just failed a psychology exam. Which of the following explanations is LEAST likely to be evidence of the self-serving bias?

o.l: “That material was so hard that no one could have passed that class.”
“The room was too hot for me to be able to concentrate.”

q.ex: The self-serving bias is the tendency to attribute successes to internal factors (personal abilities or effort) while attributing failures to external factors (circumstances beyond one's control). When examining the student's explanations for failing the exam, options i0, i1, and i4 all blame external factors: the teacher's attitude, the material's difficulty, and the room temperature. Option i2, "I didn't study hard enough," attributes the failure to an internal factor—the student's own lack of effort. This internal attribution for failure contradicts the self-serving bias pattern, making it the least likely to be evidence of this bias. The correct choice is i2 because

q.s: Dr. McKeller is replicating the original studies examining classical conditioning that taught dogs to salivate to a tone. When a conditioned stimulus is presented without the unconditioned stimulus, a resulting decrease in the conditioned response is called which of the following?
q.ex: In classical conditioning, extinction occurs when the conditioned stimulus (CS) is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus (UCS), leading to a gradual weakening and eventual disappearance of the conditioned response (CR). In Pavlov's original experiments, if the tone (CS) was presented multiple times without the food (UCS), the dogs would eventually stop salivating to the tone alone. This process demonstrates that the learned association between the CS and UCS can be weakened when the predictive relationship is broken. Extinction is the correct answer because it specifically describes the decrease in conditioned response that results from presenting the CS without the UCS.

q.s: A researcher wants to examine how gender identity relates to how happy people are. Which of the following best describes the reasons why operational definitions are used for research?

o.l: They enable researchers to replicate studies by precisely describing the variables and how they are used.
They exclude mental processes from being studied, as they are no longer considered part of the scientific study of psychology.
They determine which test of statistical significance will be used to analyze the results of the experiment.
They keep the participants in the control group from knowing they have received the placebo.

q.ex: Operational definitions specify exactly how variables will be measured or manipulated in a study, translating abstract concepts into concrete, observable terms. In this research example, the researcher would need to operationally define both "gender identity" and "happiness" by specifying the exact measures or scales used to assess them. This precision allows other researchers to understand exactly what was measured and how, making it possible to repeat the study using the same procedures. Without operational definitions, terms like "happiness" could be interpreted differently by different researchers, preventing accurate replication and comparison of results. Option i0 is correct because operational definitions serve the essential purpose of enabling replication through precise description of variables and procedures.

q.s: Burat enters a cooking competition that requires him to use ingredients and cooking tools that he has never used before. He is able to develop and cook a meal that the judges find tasty. Burat is demonstrating which of the following types of learning, which is the kind that is not demonstrated until the time it is needed?
q.ex:
Latent learning refers to knowledge or skills that are acquired without immediate reinforcement or demonstration, remaining dormant until there is an incentive or need to use them. In this scenario, Burat had previously acquired cooking knowledge and skills that were not actively demonstrated until he entered the competition and faced the challenge of using unfamiliar ingredients and tools. The key characteristic that identifies this as latent learning is that the learning existed before but was not expressed or observable until the specific situation required it. This differs from insight learning, which involves sudden problem-solving realizations, or social and observational learning, which require watching and imitating others.

Latent learning is correct because it

q.s: Pam works hard in school because her parents give her ten dollars for every A she receives. Pam’s parents are attempting to influence her academic efforts by capitalizing on which of the following?
q.ex: Pam's parents are using extrinsic motivation, which refers to behavior driven by external rewards or consequences rather than internal satisfaction. In this case, Pam is working hard specifically to earn the ten-dollar reward her parents offer for each A grade. This external incentive (money) is separate from any inherent enjoyment or personal satisfaction she might derive from learning or achieving good grades. Extrinsic motivation contrasts with intrinsic motivation, where behavior is driven by internal factors like personal interest or the joy of accomplishment itself. The correct answer is extrinsic motivation because the monetary reward represents an external factor designed to influence Pam's academic behavior

q.s: A disadvantage of using the concept of mental age in assessing intelligence because of which of the following?

o.l: It is based on a negatively skewed distribution.
Its norms are no longer appropriate.
It produces unreliable test results among rural children.

q.ex: Mental age represents the level of intellectual functioning typical for a child of a specific chronological age. This concept works well for children because their cognitive abilities develop predictably with age, allowing meaningful comparisons between mental and chronological age. However, intellectual development plateaus in adulthood, meaning cognitive abilities do not continue to increase uniformly with age after maturity. Therefore, calculating a mental age for adults becomes meaningless and inappropriate since a 30-year-old and 50-year-old with similar cognitive abilities would have vastly different IQ scores if mental age were used. The correct answer is that mental age is inappropriate for adults because the concept loses its validity when applied to populations

q.s: A therapist using systematic desensitization to help a client overcome a fear of big dogs would probably begin treatment by asking the client to

o.l: walk into a room where there is a small dog

q.ex: Systematic desensitization is a behavioral therapy technique that treats phobias by pairing relaxation with gradual exposure to the feared stimulus. The treatment follows a specific three-step process: first teaching relaxation skills, then creating an anxiety hierarchy, and finally pairing relaxation with imagined or real exposure to feared situations. Before any exposure to dogs can occur, the client must learn and master relaxation techniques such as deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation. These relaxation skills serve as the foundation for the entire treatment, as they provide the incompatible response to anxiety that makes desensitization effective. Option i4 is correct because mastering relaxation techniques is the

q.s: Which developmental milestone must be reached before an infant experiences separation anxiety?
q.ex: Separation anxiety occurs when an infant becomes distressed upon being separated from their primary caregiver, typically emerging around 8-12 months of age. For an infant to experience separation anxiety, they must first understand that their caregiver continues to exist even when out of sight. Object permanence is the cognitive understanding that objects and people continue to exist even when they cannot be directly perceived. Without object permanence, an infant would not realize their caregiver still exists when absent, and therefore could not experience anxiety about the separation. Object permanence is correct because it is the prerequisite cognitive ability that allows infants to recognize and become distressed by a caregiver's absence.

q.s: Darien’s father dictated who Darien’s friends should be and what classes he should take, and he set an extremely early curfew. If Darien went against his father’s wishes, the repercussions were harsh and swift. What type of parenting did Darien experience?
q.ex: Authoritarian parenting is characterized by high demands and low responsiveness, with parents who enforce strict rules and expect obedience without explanation. In this parenting style, parents exert strong control over their children's lives, make decisions unilaterally, and impose harsh punishments for noncompliance. Darien's father exemplifies this style by dictating his son's friendships and academic choices, setting rigid rules like an extremely early curfew, and responding with harsh and swift consequences when Darien disobeys. This contrasts with authoritative parenting, which combines high expectations with warmth and explanation, and permissive parenting, which involves few

q.s: In a classic study that simulated a prison in the basement of a building on a college campus, young men were assigned roles as either guards or prisoners. The results of the study showed which of the following?

o.l: Leadership styles can differentially influence behavior.
Groups that are hostile toward each other may be united by a common goal.
Situations can exert powerful effects behavior.

q.ex: The Stanford Prison Experiment, conducted by Philip Zimbardo in 1971, demonstrated how situational forces can powerfully shape human behavior. In this study, psychologically healthy college students were randomly assigned to play either guards or prisoners in a simulated prison environment. Within days, the guards became increasingly authoritarian and abusive, while prisoners became passive and distressed, leading to the early termination of the study. The dramatic behavioral changes observed were not due to the participants' personalities or pre-existing traits, but rather to the powerful influence of the social roles and situational context they were placed in. This study became a landmark demonstration of situational determinism, showing that ordinary people can

q.s: Which of the following explanations most clearly demonstrates a dispositional attribution for the reason a student fell asleep in class?

o.l: The student does not care about the class.
The warm temperature of the room put the student to sleep.
The student’s roommates are too noisy at night.

q.ex: A dispositional attribution explains behavior by referring to internal characteristics, personality traits, or attitudes of the person rather than external situational factors. When we say the student does not care about the class, we are attributing the behavior of falling asleep to an internal quality or attitude of the student themselves. The other options all point to external situational factors: the class being boring, the room temperature, and noisy roommates are all circumstances outside the student's personal characteristics. Option i0 is correct because it attributes the sleeping behavior to the student's internal disposition or attitude rather than to external circumstances.

q.s: A researcher interested in finding a simple way to estimate intelligence decides to evaluate skull circumference as a possible indicator of intelligence. He finds that the size of an adult’s skull remains the same from one measurementto the next, but he finds that skull circumference is not a very good predictor of intelligence. In this example, skull circumference as a measure of intelligence is
q.ex: Reliability refers to the consistency of a measurement across repeated administrations, while validity refers to whether a measure actually assesses what it claims to measure. In this example, skull circumference produces consistent results when measured repeatedly on the same person, demonstrating high reliability. However, skull circumference fails to predict intelligence accurately, meaning it does not validly measure the construct it is intended to assess. A measure can be reliable without being valid, as consistency does not guarantee that you are measuring the right thing. Therefore, skull circumference is reliable but not valid as a measure of intelligence.

q.s: Dr. Wundt gave his students an exam on the functions of different parts of the brain, and the average score was an 85. However, when Dr. Wundt calculated the standard deviation, it was a value of 35.2. This concerns Dr. Wundt because he knows that standard deviation is a measure of how much

o.l: difference there is between the highest and the lowest score in a sample
scores in a group differ from the mean of that group
scores from a sample differ from that of the population

q.ex: Standard deviation is a statistical measure that quantifies the amount of variation or dispersion in a set of data values from the mean of that set. A standard deviation of 35.2 with a mean of 85 indicates that student scores are widely spread out from the average, meaning some students scored much higher or lower than 85. This large standard deviation concerns Dr. Wundt because it suggests inconsistent understanding of the material across students, with scores potentially ranging from very low to very high. Option i3 is correct because standard deviation specifically measures how much individual scores in a group differ from the mean of that group.

q.s: Cognitive psychologists are most likely to study which of the following?

o.l: the acquisition of knowledge, planning, and problem solving
how infants move from basic trust to autonomy
the conflicts of the conscious and the unconscious
how survival processes vary across cultures

q.ex: Cognitive psychology is the scientific study of mental processes including attention, memory, perception, language, problem-solving, and decision-making. The field focuses on how people acquire, process, store, and retrieve information, essentially examining the internal workings of the mind. Option i0 directly addresses these core concerns by mentioning knowledge acquisition, planning, and problem-solving, which are fundamental cognitive processes. The other options relate to developmental psychology (i1), psychoanalytic psychology (i2), and cross-cultural psychology (i4), which are distinct subfields with different primary focuses. Option i0 is correct because it accurately identifies the central subject matter of cognitive psychology: the

q.s: A person with damage to Broca's area would most likely demonstrate which of the following symptoms?
q.ex: Broca's area is a region in the frontal lobe of the brain, typically located in the left hemisphere, that is specifically responsible for speech production and language expression. When this area is damaged, individuals develop what is known as Broca's aphasia, characterized by halting, effortful speech and difficulty forming complete sentences, though comprehension generally remains intact. The person knows what they want to say but struggles to physically produce the words. Other options like forgetfulness, hearing difficulties, and balance problems are associated with different brain regions such as the hippocampus, auditory cortex, and cerebellum respectively. Therefore, difficulty with speech production is correct because

q.s: The ability to see a cube in the diagram above is best explained by which of the following?

o.l: The inverted and reversed image that a visual stimulus produces on the retina

q.ex: The ability to perceive a complete three-dimensional cube from a simple line drawing demonstrates the Gestalt principle of closure, which describes how our minds automatically fill in missing information to create complete, meaningful forms. When viewing the cube diagram, our visual system doesn't see just disconnected lines; instead, it organizes these elements into a coherent whole by mentally completing the implied edges and surfaces. This perceptual organization occurs even though the drawing is incomplete and lacks many actual lines that would exist on a real cube. The other options relate to different aspects of vision: retinal image formation deals with how light projects onto the eye, while opponent process and trichromatic theories explain color perception

q.s: Jim decides to seek treatment for his alcoholism that involves taking a medication that causes nausea when paired with alcohol. What type of treatment has Jim chosen?
q.ex:
This treatment represents a behavioral approach because it uses classical conditioning principles to modify Jim's drinking behavior. The medication creates an association between alcohol consumption (the conditioned stimulus) and nausea (an unconditioned response), making alcohol aversive. This technique, known as aversion therapy, is a direct application of behavioral psychology that focuses on changing observable behaviors through learned associations rather than addressing thoughts, unconscious conflicts, or self-actualization. Behavioral treatments work by manipulating environmental consequences and stimulus-response relationships to eliminate unwanted behaviors.

The correct answer is behavioral because the treatment directly conditions a negative physical response to alcohol consumption through pairing, which is a fundamental behavioral modification technique.

q.s: The ratio of mental age to chronological age for a child of average intelligence is
q.ex: Mental age and chronological age are concepts used in calculating intelligence quotient (IQ). Mental age represents a child's intellectual development level based on test performance, while chronological age is the child's actual age in years. For a child of average intelligence, mental age matches chronological age exactly, meaning if a 10-year-old performs at the level typical of 10-year-olds, the ratio is 10:10, which simplifies to 1:1. This 1:1 ratio produces an IQ of 100, which is defined as average intelligence. Option i0 (1:1) is correct because average intelligence means a child's

q.s: People were asked to sign a petition in support of a political candidate. Later, those who signed the petition were asked to donate money to the candidate, and many of them did. This phenomenon is best characterized as
q.ex: The foot-in-the-door technique is a persuasion strategy where compliance with a small initial request increases the likelihood of agreeing to a larger subsequent request. In this scenario, people first agreed to the small request of signing a petition, which made them more likely to comply with the larger request of donating money later. This occurs because the initial compliance creates psychological consistency, as people want their actions to align with their self-perception as supporters of the candidate. The correct answer is the foot-in-the-door technique because it demonstrates the sequential pattern of small-to-large requests that characterizes this compliance strategy.

q.s: On his first day of work at the bakery, Brad was nearly overwhelmed by the sweet odor of the baked goods. However, by lunchtime, he did not even notice the smell. This is an example of
q.ex: Sensory adaptation is the process by which sensory receptors become less sensitive to constant or unchanging stimuli over time. When Brad first arrived at the bakery, his olfactory receptors were actively responding to the sweet odor, making it very noticeable. As he continued to be exposed to the same smell throughout the morning, his sensory receptors gradually decreased their response to this constant stimulus. By lunchtime, his nervous system had adapted to the persistent odor, causing him to no longer consciously notice it even though the smell remained present. This demonstrates sensory adaptation because Brad's sensory system adjusted to the continuous stimulus, reducing his awareness of it.

q.s: A tumor that destroys the ventromedial hypothalamus is likely to produce which of the following?

o.l: Changes in the taste of food, but no change in the amount eaten
Changes in stomach volume and less-frequent eating

q.ex: The ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) functions as a satiety center in the brain, signaling when to stop eating. When the VMH is damaged or destroyed, this satiety signal is lost, removing the mechanism that tells an organism it has had enough food. Without this "stop eating" signal, the individual continues to eat beyond normal caloric needs. This results in hyperphagia (excessive eating) and subsequent weight gain leading to obesity. Therefore, a tumor destroying the VMH produces frequent eating and obesity because the brain can no longer register fullness or satisfaction from food intake.

q.s: Which of the following elements constitutes the independent variable in the study?

o.l: The number of coins the participants tossed
The feedback about relative performance in coin tossing

f.c:
The next questions refer to the following.

A psychological researcher designs a study to determine whether positive feedback affects self-esteem. The researcher requires each participant to toss twenty coins into a coffee can that is three feet away. Half of the participants are told that their performance is superior, and the other half are told that their performance is well below average. Although some of the participants want to quit tossing coins after a few attempts, they are told that once they begin the study they have to complete it. After the coin toss, participants take a test measuring self-esteem. Following the test, all participants are debriefed and told that information about their performance was false. Results of the study indicate that participants who are told their performance is well below average report lower levels of self-esteem than do those who are told their performance is superior.

q.ex: The independent variable is the factor that researchers deliberately manipulate or control in an experiment to observe its effect on the dependent variable. In this study, the researchers are manipulating what feedback participants receive about their coin-tossing performance relative to others. This feedback is what the experimenters are systematically varying across different conditions to measure its impact on another variable, likely self-esteem. The other options represent either dependent variables being measured (self-esteem, number of successful tosses) or procedural elements (number of coins tossed) rather than the manipulated experimental condition. The feedback about relative performance is correct because it is the variable the researchers control and change to test its effects

q.s: Which of the following violations of ethical guidelines occurs in the study?

f.c:
The next questions refer to the following.

A psychological researcher designs a study to determine whether positive feedback affects self-esteem. The researcher requires each participant to toss twenty coins into a coffee can that is three feet away. Half of the participants are told that their performance is superior, and the other half are told that their performance is well below average. Although some of the participants want to quit tossing coins after a few attempts, they are told that once they begin the study they have to complete it. After the coin toss, participants take a test measuring self-esteem. Following the test, all participants are debriefed and told that information about their performance was false. Results of the study indicate that participants who are told their performance is well below average report lower levels of self-esteem than do those who are told their performance is superior.

q.ex: The correct answer involves a violation of the right to withdraw, which is a fundamental ethical principle in psychological research. Participants must be free to discontinue their involvement in a study at any time without penalty or coercion. When researchers prevent, discourage, or fail to honor a participant's decision to withdraw, they violate this essential ethical guideline. This right protects participant autonomy and ensures voluntary participation throughout the entire research process. The correct choice is i1 because the study prevented participants from exercising their right to withdraw from the research when they wished to do so.

q.s: In classical conditioning, stimulus generalization occurs when an organism responds

o.l: to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus
to stimuli that are similar to the unconditioned stimulus
to the conditioned stimulus the same way as to the unconditioned stimulus
with different types of responses to neutral stimuli

q.ex: In classical conditioning, stimulus generalization is the tendency for stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus to elicit the same conditioned response. For example, if a dog is conditioned to salivate to a specific tone, it may also salivate to tones of similar pitch. This occurs because the organism has learned to associate a particular stimulus with a response and extends that association to similar stimuli. The correct answer is that stimulus generalization occurs when an organism responds to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus, as this directly defines the phenomenon of extending a learned response from the original conditioned stimulus to comparable stimuli.

q.s: Tina’s mother often entertains Tina by bouncing a bunny puppet back and forth along the side of Tina’s crib. Initially, Tina pays close attention to the puppet but after a while, she begins to ignore it and continues doing what she was doing before the puppet appeared. Which of the following psychological concepts best explains Tina’s change in behavior?
q.ex: Habituation is a form of learning in which an organism decreases or ceases its response to a stimulus after repeated or prolonged exposure to that stimulus. In this scenario, Tina initially pays close attention to the bunny puppet because it is a novel stimulus. However, after repeated exposure to the same bouncing puppet, Tina learns that it poses no threat and requires no response, so she begins to ignore it. This decrease in response to a repeated, non-threatening stimulus is the defining characteristic of habituation. The correct answer is habituation because it directly explains why Tina's attention to the puppet diminished after continued exposure to the same stimulus.

q.s: Kathy is learning how to cook. She follows every direction on each recipe step by step to make sure her food tastes good. Which of the following describes the problem-solving approach that Kathy is using?
q.ex: An algorithm is a step-by-step problem-solving procedure that guarantees a correct solution if followed precisely. When Kathy follows every direction in a recipe step by step, she is using an algorithmic approach to ensure her food turns out correctly. This methodical, rule-based strategy contrasts with heuristics, which are mental shortcuts that may be faster but don't guarantee success. The representativeness heuristic involves judging probability based on similarity to prototypes, cognitive maps are mental representations of physical spaces, and prototypes are best examples of categories—none of which describe following sequential instructions. Kathy's approach is algorithmic because she systematically executes each

q.s: When a projective technique is used, a person could be asked to

o.l: select statements that she believes best describe her personality
select statements that she believes identify her likes and dislikes
look at some pictures and tell a story about each of them
respond to grade-level questions about math, English, social studies, and science

q.ex: Projective techniques are psychological assessment methods that present ambiguous stimuli to individuals, who then project their unconscious thoughts, feelings, and personality characteristics onto these stimuli through their interpretations. The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) is a classic example where respondents view ambiguous pictures and create stories about them, revealing underlying motivations and conflicts. Options involving selecting pre-written statements about personality or preferences represent structured self-report inventories, not projective techniques. Grade-level academic questions constitute achievement tests rather than personality assessments. Looking at pictures and telling stories about them is correct because it exemplifies the fundamental principle of projective testing: using ambiguous stim

q.s: Which of the following treatments assumes a biological cause for a disorder?
q.ex: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a biomedical treatment that assumes psychological disorders have biological or physiological causes. ECT involves passing electrical currents through the brain to trigger a brief seizure, which alters brain chemistry and can relieve symptoms of severe depression and other mental illnesses. In contrast, systematic desensitization is a behavioral therapy, rational-emotive behavioral therapy addresses thought patterns, and client-centered therapy focuses on psychological growth through empathy and acceptance. Electroconvulsive therapy is correct because it directly treats the biological functioning of the brain rather than addressing thoughts, behaviors, or emotional experiences.

q.s: Because the most popular students in the high school tend to wear a particular brand of athletic shoe, a new student buys a pair of shoes of the same brand. Such behavior demonstrates which of the following social psychological concepts?
q.ex: Conformity refers to changing one's behavior or beliefs to match those of a group or social norm. In this scenario, the new student is adjusting their purchasing decision to align with what popular students are doing, demonstrating a desire to fit in with the social environment. This is distinct from obedience, which involves following direct orders from an authority figure, and from cognitive dissonance, which involves psychological discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs. Groupthink occurs when a cohesive group prioritizes consensus over critical thinking in decision-making processes. The correct answer is conformity because the student is voluntarily adopting the behavior of the popular group to gain social acceptance or

q.s: An individual bystander is most likely to help an injured person under which of the following circumstances?

o.l: When the bystander is the only other person present
When the other people present are not helping the injured person
When a large number of people are present

q.ex: The bystander effect is a well-established psychological phenomenon where individuals are less likely to help someone in need when other people are present. This occurs due to diffusion of responsibility, where each person assumes someone else will take action, and social influence, where people look to others for cues on how to behave. When a bystander is alone with an injured person, there is no one else to share the responsibility, making it clear that they are the only one who can provide help. This eliminates the diffusion of responsibility and significantly increases the likelihood of helping behavior. Therefore, an individual bystander is most likely to help when they are the only other person present because the

q.s: In the Strange Situation experiment, infants who were classified as securely attached were more likely to do which of the following?

o.l: Have a tantrum when the mother left the room
Express happiness when the mother returned to the room
Prevent the mother from leaving the room
Try to play with the stranger when the mother left the room

q.ex: In the Strange Situation experiment developed by Mary Ainsworth, securely attached infants demonstrate a healthy attachment pattern characterized by using their caregiver as a secure base for exploration. When the mother leaves, these infants may show some distress, but the key distinguishing feature is their positive response upon reunion. Securely attached infants actively seek contact with the mother when she returns and are easily comforted by her presence, expressing happiness and relief. This reunion behavior differentiates them from insecurely attached infants who may show avoidance, resistance, or disorganized responses. The correct answer is that securely attached infants express happiness when the mother returns because

q.s: An individual was admitted to the hospital after experiencing a mild tingling on the right side of the face and a sudden inability to speak. Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a doctor would likely find which of the following?

o.l: An abnormality in the brain tissue of the left hemisphere
An increase in brain activity in the left frontal lobe
An abnormal growth in the right frontal lobe
A pattern of red and yellow highlighting activity in Broca’s area

q.ex: The left hemisphere of the brain controls motor functions and sensation for the right side of the body due to the crossing over of neural pathways. Additionally, language production centers, particularly Broca's area, are typically located in the left hemisphere for most individuals. The sudden inability to speak combined with right-sided facial tingling strongly suggests damage or abnormality in the left hemisphere. An MRI would reveal structural abnormalities in brain tissue rather than functional activity patterns, making an abnormality in left hemisphere tissue the most likely finding. The correct answer is i0 because it identifies both the appropriate hemisphere (left, controlling right-sided symptoms and speech) and the appropriate type of M

q.s: Amanda experienced discomfort in class. She put on a sweater when she realized her discomfort was caused by the cold. Her behavior was motivated by which of the following?
q.ex: A drive is an internal state of tension that motivates an organism to reduce or eliminate that tension and return to homeostasis. When Amanda felt cold, this created a physiological imbalance that produced discomfort, generating a drive to restore her body's optimal temperature. Her behavior of putting on a sweater was a direct response to reduce this drive state. The correct answer is a drive because Amanda's motivation stemmed from a basic physiological need (temperature regulation) that created internal tension, which she then acted to reduce through a simple behavioral response.

q.s: Raul wants to teach his daughter Sonia to tie her shoes. First he praises her when she manipulates her shoelaces in any way. Then he praises her when she makes a simple knot. Once she does that consistently, he praises her only when she makes the knot and a loop. He continues the pattern until she can do all the steps required to tie her shoes. Raul’s actions are an example of which of the following techniques?
q.ex: Shaping is a behavioral technique in which successive approximations of a desired behavior are reinforced until the complete target behavior is achieved. Raul systematically reinforces behaviors that progressively come closer to the final goal of shoe-tying, starting with simple lace manipulation and gradually requiring more complex steps before providing praise. This step-by-step reinforcement of increasingly accurate behaviors is the defining characteristic of shaping. The technique differs from modeling (demonstrating the behavior), rehearsal (repeated practice), or negative reinforcement (removing an aversive stimulus to increase behavior). The correct answer is shaping because Raul reinforces successive approximations toward the complete shoe-tying

q.s: Which of the following would hinder a person from reducing the dissonance a person might experience after refusing to contribute money for a gift to a coworker?

o.l: Saying a phrase such as “I am so rude” over and over
Volunteering to buy a gift for another coworker for a different occasion
Repeating the thought that the coworker makes a good salary and does not need a gift
Making a donation to a charity in the coworker’s name

q.ex: Cognitive dissonance occurs when a person experiences psychological discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs or behaviors. To reduce dissonance after refusing to contribute, a person typically rationalizes the decision or changes their attitude to align with their behavior. Saying "I am so rude" over and over reinforces negative self-perception and acknowledges the conflict between the refusal and social norms, which actually increases rather than reduces the dissonance. The other options all provide ways to reduce dissonance through rationalization or compensatory actions that justify the original refusal. Option i0 is correct because it hinders dissonance reduction by maintaining awareness of the inconsistency

q.s:
Which of the following theories most accurately explains pitch perception?

  1. Opponent process

  2. Frequency

  3. Place
q.ex: Pitch perception is explained by two complementary theories that work together across different frequency ranges. The frequency theory states that the basilar membrane vibrates at the same frequency as the sound wave, with neurons firing in synchrony to match lower frequency sounds (up to about 4,000 Hz). Place theory explains that different locations along the basilar membrane respond maximally to different frequencies, with high frequencies stimulating the base and low frequencies stimulating the apex of the cochlea. Opponent process theory relates to color vision, not auditory perception, so it does not explain pitch perception. The correct answer is II and III only because both frequency theory and place theory are necessary to fully account for

q.s: On an intelligence test, the number of questions an individual answers correctly is meaningless without which of the following?
q.ex: A raw score on an intelligence test has no interpretable meaning by itself because there is no frame of reference for understanding what that score represents. Standardization provides the essential context by establishing norms based on a representative sample of the population, allowing an individual's score to be compared against others. Through standardization, raw scores are converted into meaningful metrics like percentiles or standard scores that indicate where someone falls relative to their peers. Without this normative framework, knowing that someone answered 45 questions correctly tells us nothing about whether that performance is average, exceptional, or poor. Standardization is correct because it transforms meaningless raw scores into interpretable, comparable measures of intelligence.

q.s: Specific phobia differs from generalized anxiety disorder in which of the following ways?

o.l: Specific phobia is linked to a particular stimulus, whereas generalized anxiety disorder is not.
Generalized anxiety disorder is linked to a particular stimulus, whereas specific phobia is not.
Specific phobia is not very upsetting for the sufferer, whereas generalized anxiety disorder is.
Generalized anxiety disorder is classified as one of the anxiety disorders, whereas specific phobia is not.

q.ex: Specific phobia is characterized by an intense, irrational fear of a clearly identifiable object or situation, such as heights, spiders, or flying. In contrast, generalized anxiety disorder involves persistent and excessive worry about multiple aspects of daily life without being tied to any specific trigger or stimulus. The key distinction is that specific phobia has a focused, identifiable source of fear, while generalized anxiety disorder features diffuse, free-floating anxiety that pervades various life domains. Both conditions cause significant distress and are classified as anxiety disorders, but they differ fundamentally in whether the anxiety is stimulus-specific or pervasive. Option i0 is correct because it accurately captures

q.s: Significant damage to which of the following parts of the brain will most likely cause a person to fall into a deep coma from which the person will be unable to awaken?
q.ex: The reticular formation is a network of neurons located in the brainstem that plays a crucial role in regulating consciousness, arousal, and sleep-wake cycles. This structure contains the reticular activating system (RAS), which is responsible for maintaining wakefulness and alertness by sending signals to the cerebral cortex. Significant damage to the reticular formation disrupts these essential arousal mechanisms, preventing the brain from maintaining a conscious, wakeful state. While the hypothalamus regulates homeostasis, the frontal lobe controls executive functions, and the thalamus relays sensory information, none of these structures are as directly responsible for maintaining consciousness as the

q.s: A cancer patient becomes nauseated following chemotherapy treatments. After a few treatments, the patient begins having a sick feeling whenever entering the treatment room. The treatment room has become
q.ex: This scenario illustrates classical conditioning, where a previously neutral stimulus becomes associated with an unconditioned response through repeated pairing. Initially, the treatment room was a neutral stimulus that did not cause nausea. However, after being repeatedly paired with chemotherapy (the unconditioned stimulus that naturally causes nausea), the treatment room alone began to elicit the sick feeling. When a previously neutral stimulus acquires the ability to trigger a conditioned response through association with an unconditioned stimulus, it becomes a conditioned stimulus. The treatment room is now a conditioned stimulus because it produces nausea through learned association rather than naturally.

q.s: Melvin, a server at a restaurant, is in the middle of a lunch rush. He is completing orders, serving customers, and seating new guests. He has adapted to this level of stress and is coping. Which of the following terms identifies a stage in the general adaptation syndrome that Melvin is currently experiencing?
q.ex: The general adaptation syndrome, developed by Hans Selye, describes three stages of physiological response to stress: alarm, resistance, and exhaustion. In the alarm stage, the body initially reacts to a stressor with a fight-or-flight response. The resistance stage occurs when the body adapts to continued stress and attempts to cope with it while maintaining normal functioning. Since Melvin has adapted to the stress of the lunch rush and is actively coping while continuing to perform his duties, he is in the resistance stage. The exhaustion stage would occur only if the stress continued beyond his ability to cope, leading to depleted resources and decreased functioning.

q.s: Which of the following is true of a child with high self-efficacy regarding her ability to play soccer?

o.l: She believes she has played poorly if she does not score a goal.
She feels confident that she can play well enough to score a goal.
She wants to score more goals than any other girl on her team.
She plays soccer well only as long as she is interested in soccer.

q.ex: Self-efficacy refers to an individual's belief in their own capability to successfully execute behaviors required to produce specific outcomes. A child with high self-efficacy regarding soccer believes in her ability to perform the necessary skills and actions to achieve success in the sport. This confidence in her capabilities means she feels assured that she can play well enough to accomplish goals like scoring. Self-efficacy is about belief in one's competence and ability to succeed at a task, not about comparing oneself to others, maintaining interest, or setting unrealistic standards for success. Option i1 is correct because it directly reflects the core definition of self-efficacy: confidence in one's ability to perform successfully.

q.s: Morgan made the fundamental attribution error in explaining her students’ poor performance on their geography examination when she said which of the following?

o.l: “I thought it was too cold in the room on test day. Maybe that’s why the students did poorly.”
“The students just do not care enough about their grades.”
“I will have to present the material to them another way and retest.”
“Maybe I am just not a good teacher.”

q.ex: The fundamental attribution error occurs when someone overemphasizes dispositional or personality-based explanations for others' behavior while underestimating the influence of situational factors. In this case, Morgan commits this error by attributing her students' poor test performance to an internal characteristic—their lack of care about grades—rather than considering external factors like teaching methods, test difficulty, or environmental conditions. The other options either acknowledge situational factors (cold room, teaching approach) or focus on Morgan's own role rather than making attributions about the students' character. Option i1 is correct because it demonstrates the classic pattern of the fundamental attribution error: explaining others' negative outcomes through their internal dispos

q.s: Which of the following is the best example of fluid intelligence?

o.l: Reciting the names of all the continents in the world without looking at a map
Using cubes to figure out the solution to a previously unseen puzzle
Giving an adequate definition of a difficult word

q.ex: Fluid intelligence refers to the ability to reason, solve novel problems, and think abstractly without relying on previously acquired knowledge or experience. It involves mental flexibility and the capacity to identify patterns and relationships in unfamiliar situations. Using cubes to solve a previously unseen puzzle directly demonstrates fluid intelligence because it requires reasoning through a new problem without drawing on memorized information. In contrast, reciting continents, defining words, and recognizing music all depend on crystallized intelligence, which involves applying learned knowledge and past experiences. The correct answer is using cubes to figure out the solution to a previously unseen puzzle because it exemplifies the core characteristic of fluid intelligence: solving novel problems through reasoning

q.s: Which of the following treatments would be most effective for someone who experiences a rapid heartbeat, light-headedness, and nausea when speaking in public?
q.ex: The symptoms described—rapid heartbeat, light-headedness, and nausea when speaking in public—indicate a specific phobia or anxiety disorder related to public speaking. Systematic desensitization is a behavioral therapy technique that gradually exposes individuals to their feared stimulus while teaching relaxation techniques, allowing them to build tolerance and reduce anxiety responses. This method is particularly effective for phobias and situational anxiety because it directly addresses the conditioned fear response through gradual exposure paired with relaxation. The other options are inappropriate: dopamine reduction targets different disorders like schizophrenia, defense mechanism interpretation is psychoanalytic and less effective for specific phobias, and a

q.s: To study differences in the cognitive processing of younger and older adults, Genevieve assessed a group of 30 year olds and a group of 60 year olds using the same cognitive task. She found no significant difference in cognitive processing between the two groups. Which of the following is a true statement that best explains her findings?

o.l: Researchers have not documented changes in cognitive ability over the human life span.
Genevieve’s task involved semantic memory, which does not typically show decline among people of the ages she tested.
Most decline in cognitive ability is associated with dementia, which would not yet have occurred in the participants at age 60.
Genevieve’s older participants were most likely taking memory medications that prolong the ability to be proficient in cognitive tasks.

q.ex:
Semantic memory refers to general knowledge and facts accumulated over a lifetime, such as vocabulary, concepts, and world knowledge. Research consistently shows that semantic memory remains stable or even improves through middle and older adulthood, unlike other cognitive abilities such as processing speed or working memory that may decline earlier. Since Genevieve tested 30-year-olds and 60-year-olds, both groups would be expected to perform similarly on semantic memory tasks, as significant decline in this area typically does not occur until much later in life, if at all. This explains why she found no significant difference between the two age groups.

The correct choice is i2 because semantic memory

q.s: After an electrode implanted in a cat’s brain stimulates the cat’s amygdala, the cat will most likely do which of the following?

o.l: Begin to purr and seek physical contact
