q.ex: The primacy effect refers to the tendency to better recall items presented at the beginning of a list compared to items in the middle positions. This phenomenon occurs because early items receive more rehearsal and are more likely to be transferred to long-term memory. When results show superior recall for initial items in a sequence, this pattern is consistent with the primacy effect. The data in segment A must demonstrate this characteristic pattern of enhanced memory for early-presented information, which is why the primacy effect is the correct answer.

q.s: The teacher noticed that the afternoon class recalled more presidents than the morning class did and concluded that this was caused by time of day. Which of the following is a confounding variable?

o.l: The grade level of the students

f.c:
The following refers to remembering the presidents of the United States.

A list of the presidents of the United States in chronological order up through the year 2000 is presented in the exact same manner to two classes of students, and they are then asked to recall them. A fourth-grade class is tested in the morning and a sixth-grade class is tested in the afternoon. The percent recall for both classes was combined and is presented in the figure above.

q.ex: A confounding variable is an extraneous factor that varies systematically with the independent variable and could provide an alternative explanation for the observed results. In this study, the teacher attributes the difference in recall to time of day, but if the morning and afternoon classes consist of students at different grade levels, then grade level becomes a confounding variable. Older students typically have more developed cognitive abilities and more exposure to historical information than younger students, which could explain why one class recalled more presidents regardless of the time of day. The grade level of students is correct because it offers a plausible alternative explanation for the performance difference that is not controlled for in the teacher's conclusion.

q.s: The results depicted in which segment are inconsistent with the serial position effect?

f.c:
The following refers to remembering the presidents of the United States.

A list of the presidents of the United States in chronological order up through the year 2000 is presented in the exact same manner to two classes of students, and they are then asked to recall them. A fourth-grade class is tested in the morning and a sixth-grade class is tested in the afternoon. The percent recall for both classes was combined and is presented in the figure above.

q.ex: The serial position effect describes the tendency for people to recall items at the beginning of a list (primacy effect) and at the end of a list (recency effect) better than items in the middle. This creates a U-shaped curve when graphing recall performance across list positions. Segment C would be inconsistent with this effect if it shows a pattern that deviates from this characteristic U-shape, such as flat performance across all positions, better recall in the middle than at the ends, or recall that only shows one effect but not the other. The correct answer is C because it displays results that contradict the expected pattern of superior recall at both the beginning and end positions of

q.s: Dr. Mayhew finds that children who are randomly assigned to watch television shows containing many acts of violence later show more aggressive behavior during recess than children who are randomly assigned to watch television shows containing no acts of violence. In the experiment, the dependent variable is

o.l: whether children are assigned to watch television shows that contain violence or that contain no violence
whether children choose to watch television shows that contain violence or that contain no violence
the level of aggressive behavior displayed by the children during recess
the level of violence in the television shows

q.ex: In an experiment, the dependent variable is the outcome that researchers measure to determine the effect of the manipulation. It is what "depends on" or is influenced by the independent variable. The independent variable is what the experimenter manipulates or controls, which in this case is the type of television show children are assigned to watch (violent or non-violent). Dr. Mayhew measures aggressive behavior during recess to see if it changes based on the type of show watched. This measured outcome—the level of aggressive behavior—is the dependent variable because it is expected to depend on exposure to violent content. Option i4 is correct because aggressive behavior during recess is what Dr. Ma

q.s: John walks into art class and is overwhelmed by the smell of paint. However, the longer he stays in the room, the less noticeable the smell becomes. Which of the following appears to be operating in this instance?
q.ex: Sensory adaptation is the process by which sensory receptors become less responsive to constant or unchanging stimuli over time. When John first enters the art classroom, his olfactory receptors detect the paint smell and send strong signals to his brain. As he remains in the room with continuous exposure to the same odor, his sensory receptors gradually decrease their firing rate, making the smell less noticeable even though the stimulus remains present. This phenomenon allows our sensory systems to focus on new or changing stimuli in the environment rather than constant background information. The correct answer is sensory adaptation because it specifically describes the decreased sensitivity to a constant stimulus that John experiences with the paint

q.s: Kay’s ability to ride a bicycle reflects which of the following types of memory?
q.ex: Procedural memory is a type of long-term memory responsible for knowing how to perform motor skills and actions, such as riding a bicycle, typing, or swimming. These skills are typically learned through repetition and practice, and once acquired, they can be performed automatically without conscious thought or verbal instruction. Unlike explicit memory, which involves conscious recall of facts and events, procedural memory operates implicitly and does not require deliberate retrieval. Kay's ability to ride a bicycle demonstrates procedural memory because it involves executing a learned motor skill that has become automatic through practice. The correct answer is procedural because riding a bicycle is a classic example of a motor skill stored in procedural memory.

q.s: A psychology professor wants to investigate the study habits of students at her university. She cannot collect data from every student but hopes to use a subset of the students to draw accurate conclusions about the behavior of the student body. Which of the following features of research design will best address her goal?
q.ex: Random sampling is the research design feature that best addresses the professor's goal of drawing accurate conclusions about the entire student body from a subset of students. Random sampling involves selecting participants from the population in such a way that every member has an equal chance of being chosen, which helps ensure the sample is representative of the larger population. This representativeness is crucial when the researcher wants to generalize findings from the sample to the entire population. Random assignment, in contrast, is used in experiments to distribute participants into different conditions, while blind procedures control for bias in experimental settings but do not address the issue of obtaining a representative sample. Random sampling is correct because it directly addresses the need to make the subset of students

q.s: Neurotransmitters that function like the drug morphine and are involved in pain modulation include which of the following?
q.ex: Endorphins are the body's natural opioid peptides that bind to the same receptors in the brain as morphine and other opioid drugs. These neurotransmitters are specifically involved in pain modulation by inhibiting the transmission of pain signals and producing feelings of pleasure or euphoria. The term "endorphin" itself derives from "endogenous morphine," meaning morphine-like substances produced naturally within the body. While GABA, norepinephrine, and dopamine are important neurotransmitters with various functions, they do not have the morphine-like opioid properties that characterize endorphins. En

q.s: Researchers are interested in whether a nutritionally poor diet during pregnancy increases the likelihood of birth defects. Which of the following most accurately explains why a correlational research design is the best option for investigating this question?

o.l: A correlational study allows researchers to draw conclusions about cause and effect.
A correlational study permits researchers to have precise control over variables.
Because of ethical concerns, participants could not be randomly assigned to groups.
It would be relatively easy to collect data from large samples of pregnant women.

q.ex:
A correlational research design is most appropriate here because it would be unethical to randomly assign pregnant women to consume a nutritionally poor diet, as this could potentially harm both the mothers and their developing babies. Experimental research requires random assignment to manipulated conditions, but researchers cannot ethically expose participants to conditions that might cause harm. When ethical constraints prevent experimental manipulation, correlational studies allow researchers to examine naturally occurring relationships between variables by observing and measuring them as they exist. While correlational designs cannot establish causation, they are the only ethical option when studying potentially harmful conditions in vulnerable populations like pregnant women.

The correct choice is i3 because ethical concerns prevent random assignment to a potentially

q.s: Dr. Kucinski developed an English aptitude test to give to students who wish to register for his advanced English course. Which of the following is the best way to determine if his test has predictive validity?

o.l: Pretesting the test with a representative group of high school students
Administering the test twice to the same students and then comparing the scores
Examining the questions and making sure they only pertain to English classes and not to other classes
Comparing students’ scores on the test with their final grades in his class

q.ex: Predictive validity refers to how well a test predicts future performance or outcomes on a related criterion. To establish predictive validity, researchers must demonstrate that test scores correlate with later performance measures. In this case, Dr. Kucinski's English aptitude test should predict success in his advanced English course. The most direct way to assess this is to compare students' initial test scores with their actual performance in the class, measured by final grades. This comparison would show whether high scorers on the aptitude test actually perform better in the course, thus validating the test's predictive power. Option i5 is correct because it directly measures the relationship between test scores and the future

q.s: A university is considering offering a new major called the Art of Science. Survey results reveal that Art majors and Science majors are opposed to the idea. After the Art majors and Science majors hold meetings of their respective groups, their dislike for the idea increases even further. Which of the following phenomena has most likely occurred?
q.ex: Group polarization occurs when group discussion causes members' initial attitudes to become more extreme in the direction they already leaned. In this scenario, Art and Science majors already opposed the new major before their meetings. After discussing the issue within their respective groups, their opposition intensified rather than moderated. This strengthening of pre-existing attitudes through group interaction is the defining characteristic of group polarization. The correct answer is group polarization because the students' initial negative views became more extreme after group discussion, which is precisely what this phenomenon predicts.

q.s: Dr. Ivey is researching using stimulants to treat attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). To minimize experimenter bias, Dr. Ivey should use which of the following research designs?
q.ex: Experimenter bias occurs when a researcher's expectations or beliefs unconsciously influence the results of a study. A double-blind procedure is specifically designed to minimize this bias by ensuring that neither the participants nor the experimenters who interact with them know which treatment condition each participant is receiving. In Dr. Ivey's study on stimulants for ADHD, using a double-blind procedure would prevent the researcher from inadvertently treating participants differently or interpreting results based on knowledge of who received the actual medication versus a placebo. Random assignment and random selection address different methodological concerns related to internal and external validity, while a case study would not control for experimenter bias at all. The

q.s: Convergence is a binocular depth cue that is based on which of the following?

o.l: Change in the size of the pupil
Muscular tension that leads to the lens changing shape
Muscular tension that occurs when the eyes turn inward
Fact that there are more rods on the periphery of the retina

q.ex: Convergence is a binocular depth cue that relies on the brain's interpretation of how much the eyes must rotate inward to focus on an object. When viewing nearby objects, the eyes turn inward more dramatically, creating greater muscular tension in the extraocular muscles. The brain uses feedback from this muscle tension to estimate distance, with greater tension indicating closer objects. This is distinct from accommodation, which involves the lens changing shape, and from pupil dilation, which regulates light intake. Option i3 is correct because convergence specifically refers to the muscular tension created when the eyes turn inward to maintain binocular fixation on objects at varying distances.

q.s: A researcher examined the correlation between gender and the number of birds in Indonesia. Which of the following scatterplots illustrates the weakest correlation coefficient this correlation could show?
q.ex: The question contains a fundamental conceptual error that makes examining scatterplots unnecessary. Gender is a categorical variable with discrete categories, while the number of birds is a quantitative variable. Correlation coefficients measure the linear relationship between two quantitative variables and cannot be calculated between a categorical and quantitative variable. Since no valid correlation coefficient can exist for this relationship, the weakest possible correlation would be represented by a scatterplot showing no pattern or relationship whatsoever. Option i2 shows points scattered randomly with no discernible upward or downward trend, indicating no linear relationship between variables. This represents the weakest correlation coefficient of zero, which is the correct answer because option i

q.s: Deborah says that she is not interested in dating anyone at her workplace. However, after spending time with her coworker James at a week-long conference, she finds herself attracted to him and begins to pursue a relationship. Deborah’s interest in James is most likely due to
q.ex:
The mere-exposure effect is a psychological phenomenon in which people develop a preference for things or people simply because they are familiar with them through repeated exposure. In this scenario, Deborah initially had no interest in dating coworkers, but after spending a week-long conference with James, she became attracted to him. The extended time together at the conference provided repeated exposure to James, which increased her familiarity with him and subsequently her attraction. This demonstrates how increased contact and exposure can lead to positive feelings and attraction, even when someone initially held a contrary position.

The correct answer is the mere-exposure effect because Deborah's change in feelings directly resulted from the increased familiarity

q.s: Based on the bar graph above, which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

o.l: Identical twins are more intelligent than fraternal twins.
The more genetically related people are, the more similar their intelligence scores.

q.ex: The bar graph demonstrates a correlation between genetic similarity and intelligence score similarity. When examining different types of relationships (identical twins, fraternal twins, siblings, unrelated individuals), the data shows that as genetic relatedness increases, the correlation between intelligence scores also increases. This pattern indicates that genetic factors play a significant role in intelligence, but it does not suggest genes work in isolation or that more genetically similar individuals are inherently more intelligent in absolute terms. The correct answer recognizes that greater genetic relatedness corresponds to greater similarity in intelligence scores, which is the fundamental pattern the graph illustrates.

q.s: After the incident, Ted develops a specific phobia of snakes. Which of the following therapeutic techniques will be most effective for eliminating Ted’s phobia?

f.c:
The following item refers to a snake frightening Ted.

Ted is hiking along a mountain trail when he sees a large snake slithering across the path ahead of him.

q.ex: Systematic desensitization is the most effective therapeutic technique for eliminating specific phobias like Ted's fear of snakes. This behavioral therapy technique works by gradually exposing the patient to the feared object or situation while they are in a relaxed state, moving from least to most anxiety-provoking stimuli. The process pairs relaxation with the phobic stimulus, which counteracts the fear response through classical conditioning principles. Token economy is used for reinforcing desired behaviors, active listening is a counseling skill rather than a treatment technique, and rational-emotive behavioral therapy addresses irrational beliefs but is less specifically targeted for phobias than systematic desensitization.

q.s: Which of the following brain structures is most closely associated with Ted’s fear response?

f.c:
The following item refers to a snake frightening Ted.

Ted is hiking along a mountain trail when he sees a large snake slithering across the path ahead of him.

q.ex: The amygdala is the brain structure most closely associated with fear responses and emotional processing, particularly negative emotions like fear and anxiety. Located in the temporal lobe as part of the limbic system, the amygdala plays a central role in detecting threats and triggering the body's fear response, including the fight-or-flight reaction. The medulla controls basic life functions like breathing and heart rate, the occipital lobe processes visual information, and the hippocampus is primarily involved in memory formation rather than emotional responses. The amygdala is correct because it serves as the brain's primary fear center, evaluating potential threats and initiating appropriate emotional and physi

q.s: Hearing the word “ocean” makes Alice think of waves, surfboards, bathing suits, sharks, swimmers, boats, and the beach. The associations she has to the word “ocean” represent which of the following concepts?
q.ex: A schema is an organized mental framework or network of knowledge about a particular concept that helps us understand and interpret information. When Alice hears the word "ocean," her mind activates a web of related concepts including waves, surfboards, bathing suits, sharks, swimmers, boats, and the beach. This interconnected network of associations represents her schema for "ocean," which contains all the related knowledge, experiences, and expectations she has built up about oceans over time. Procedural memory involves knowing how to perform tasks, sensory memory is brief storage of sensory information, and accommodation is changing existing schemas when faced with new information. The correct answer is schema because it specifically describes this organize

q.s: When Bram exhibits inappropriate behavior, his parents use time‑outs, during which he has to sit at a plain desk without toys. This approach to decreasing inappropriate behavior utilizes the concept of
q.ex: Negative punishment involves removing a desirable stimulus to decrease the likelihood of a behavior occurring again. In this scenario, Bram's parents are taking away his access to toys and stimulating activities by placing him at a plain desk during time-outs. This removal of pleasant stimuli following inappropriate behavior is designed to reduce that behavior in the future. The key distinction is that something desirable is being subtracted from the situation rather than something aversive being added, which would be positive punishment. Therefore, negative punishment is the correct answer because it describes the removal of reinforcing stimuli to decrease unwanted behavior.

q.s: Nick cheated in high school in order to maintain his grade point average. When he was caught, he blamed his teacher for not teaching him well enough. As an adult, he is impulsive and aggressive and feels no guilt in lying to get what he wants. These behaviors are most consistent with which of the following disorders?
q.ex: Antisocial personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, typically beginning in childhood or early adolescence and continuing into adulthood. Key features include deceitfulness, impulsivity, aggression, lack of remorse, and failure to accept responsibility for one's actions. Nick's behaviors demonstrate all these hallmarks: he cheated without remorse, blamed others rather than accepting responsibility, and as an adult continues to lie without guilt while displaying impulsivity and aggression. These symptoms align precisely with the diagnostic criteria for antisocial personality disorder, making it the correct answer.

q.s: Suzie feels anxious if she does not check six times to make sure she has turned out the lights prior to leaving her apartment. Recently she has felt the need to repeatedly check the fireplace, the iron, the stove, and the locks on all the doors. Suzie’s problems are most consistent with which of the following disorders?
q.ex: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by persistent, intrusive thoughts (obsessions) that cause anxiety and repetitive behaviors (compulsions) performed to reduce that anxiety. Suzie experiences anxiety about potential dangers in her apartment, which represents the obsessive component, and she engages in excessive checking behaviors to alleviate this anxiety, which represents the compulsive component. The repetitive nature of her checking (six times for lights, and expanding to other appliances and locks) is a hallmark of compulsions in OCD. Panic disorder involves sudden episodes of intense fear, bipolar disorder involves mood swings between depression and mania

q.s: Which of the following summarizes the Big Five theory of personality?

o.l: People must satisfy five basic needs before they can address their need for self-actualization.
People must pass through the oral, anal, phallic, and genital stages before reaching the fifth and final stage of personality development.
People who are psychologically healthy score high on five different dimensions of personality.
People can be described by five higher-order traits that reflect most aspects of personality.

q.ex: The Big Five theory of personality is a descriptive model that organizes personality traits into five broad dimensions: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (often remembered by the acronym OCEAN). This theory proposes that these five higher-order traits can capture and describe the majority of individual differences in personality across all people. The model is not hierarchical or developmental, nor does it prescribe what constitutes psychological health. Option i5 is correct because it accurately describes the Big Five as a comprehensive framework where five broad traits encompass most aspects of personality variation.

q.s: Dr. Nunez finds that the differences between groups in her research on the use of heuristics in problem-solving was statistically significant. If the outcome of a study is statistically significant, it means which of the following?

o.l: The manipulation of the dependent variable likely had no effect.
The dependent variable likely affected the outcome.
Regression to the mean most likely occurred.
The results are unlikely to be obtained if there is no difference between the control group and the experimental group.

q.ex: Statistical significance indicates that the observed differences between groups are unlikely to have occurred by chance alone if there were truly no real difference between the groups. In Dr. Nunez's study, finding statistical significance means the probability of obtaining these results when no actual difference exists between groups is very low, typically less than 5%. This suggests the manipulation of the independent variable (not dependent variable) likely had a genuine effect on the outcome. The correct answer states that the results are unlikely to be obtained if there is no difference between the control and experimental groups, which is the precise definition of statistical significance in experimental research.

q.s: Tom believes he performed poorly on his last three history exams because of bad luck. As a result, he believes he is due for a good score on the next exam and does not study because he is sure he will perform well. The error in his thinking is most likely attributable to
q.ex:
The gambler's fallacy is the mistaken belief that past random events affect the probability of future independent events. Tom incorrectly assumes that because he has had bad luck on three previous exams, he is "due" for good luck on the next one, as if luck balances out over time. In reality, each exam performance is an independent event determined by his preparation and knowledge, not by a streak of outcomes that needs to even out. This is the classic error in reasoning where someone believes that a departure from average in one direction must be corrected by a departure in the opposite direction.

The correct answer is the gambler's fallacy because Tom is treating independent events as

q.s: Which of the following descriptions accurately represents area 2 of the graph?

o.l: The threshold, in which signals have reached critical intensity and allow the neuron to fire
Hyperpolarization, in which positive ions have exited the axon
Repolarization, in which potassium ions exit the axon
Depolarization, in which sodium ions enter the axon

q.ex: During an action potential, depolarization is the phase where the neuron's membrane potential rapidly becomes more positive. This occurs when voltage-gated sodium channels open in response to the membrane reaching threshold, allowing sodium ions to rush into the axon down their concentration gradient. The influx of positively charged sodium ions causes the inside of the neuron to become less negative and eventually positive relative to the outside. Area 2 of the graph shows this rapid upward swing in membrane potential from the resting state toward the peak of the action potential. The correct answer is i5 because depolarization specifically describes the process of sodium ions entering the axon, which creates the rising phase

q.s: Katie wants a new phone but is worried that her parents might not buy the one she wants. She asks her parents to purchase the most expensive phone in the store. When they refuse, she asks for the less expensive phone she wanted to begin with. Katie’s strategy is an example of
q.ex: The door-in-the-face technique is a compliance strategy where someone makes an initial large request that is likely to be refused, followed by a smaller, more reasonable request that was the actual goal all along. The initial refusal makes the second request appear more acceptable by comparison. Katie deliberately asks for an expensive phone first, expecting rejection, then follows with her true target phone at a lower price. This contrast effect makes the second request seem more reasonable to her parents, increasing the likelihood they will agree. The correct answer is the door-in-the-face technique because Katie uses a large initial request followed by her actual smaller request after the predictable refusal.

q.s: Phil’s therapist believes that Phil’s negative thoughts of personal incompetence and an inability to achieve his goals are the cause of Phil’s depression. The therapist is most likely a proponent of which of the following perspectives?
q.ex: The cognitive perspective in psychology focuses on how thoughts, beliefs, and mental processes influence emotions and behavior. Cognitive therapists believe that psychological disorders like depression stem from distorted or maladaptive thinking patterns. In this case, Phil's therapist identifies negative thoughts about personal incompetence and inability to achieve goals as the root cause of his depression, which is a hallmark of cognitive therapy. This approach, pioneered by Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis, emphasizes that changing dysfunctional thought patterns can alleviate emotional distress. The correct answer is Cognitive because the therapist is directly attributing Phil's depression to his negative thought patterns rather than unconscious conflicts, evolutionary adapt

q.s: Which of the following is the most useful study strategy to help a student retain the words in a vocabulary list?

o.l: Focusing on the pronunciation of the words
Putting the words in alphabetical order
Using each word in a sentence

q.ex:
Using each word in a sentence is the most effective strategy because it requires deep processing and elaborative rehearsal. When students create sentences with vocabulary words, they must actively engage with the meaning of each word and connect it to existing knowledge and context. This semantic processing creates stronger memory traces than shallow processing methods like focusing on pronunciation, alphabetical ordering, or simple repetition. Research in cognitive psychology consistently shows that meaningful elaboration and contextual use lead to better long-term retention than surface-level or mechanical rehearsal strategies.

The correct choice is i4 because using words in sentences engages deeper semantic processing and creates meaningful connections that enhance memory retention.

q.s: Benjamin is five years old. While his mother is making his lunch, he explains to her that he is very hungry and would like a lot to eat. His mother cuts his sandwich into four pieces, and he is very pleased. Benjamin’s pleasure at having four small pieces instead of one large piece is due to the fact that he lacks
q.ex: Benjamin's pleasure at receiving four small pieces instead of one large sandwich demonstrates a lack of conservation, a cognitive ability that develops during Piaget's concrete operational stage (around age 7). Conservation is the understanding that certain properties of objects, such as quantity, mass, or volume, remain the same despite changes in their form or appearance. Because Benjamin is only five years old and still in the preoperational stage, he does not yet understand that cutting the sandwich into four pieces does not actually increase the total amount of food. He focuses on the number of pieces rather than recognizing that the overall quantity remains unchanged. The correct answer is conservation because this concept specifically explains why young children believe that al

q.s: Psychodynamic theorists believe that the development of personality is largely influenced by unconscious motivations. The theories are most often criticized because they do which of the following?

o.l: Do not take into account the importance of rationalization.
Focus too little on the role of repression.

q.ex: Psychodynamic theories are most often criticized because they cannot be falsified, meaning they cannot be proven wrong through empirical testing. A key principle of scientific theories is that they must be testable and potentially disprovable. Psychodynamic concepts like unconscious motivations, defense mechanisms, and repressed memories are difficult or impossible to measure objectively or disprove through experimentation. For example, if a prediction fails, psychodynamic theorists can explain it away using other unconscious processes, making the theory unfalsifiable. This lack of falsifiability is the primary scientific criticism of psychodynamic approaches. The correct answer is i2 because unfalsifiability represents

q.s: Which of the following scenarios illustrates the principle of social facilitation?

o.l: Performing better when in the presence of others than when alone
Changing an opinion about a coworker after working with him or her
Becoming more obedient to authority when in a group
Following social norms to promote group cohesion

q.ex: Social facilitation is the psychological phenomenon where an individual's performance on a task is enhanced by the mere presence of others. This effect typically occurs with well-learned or simple tasks, where the presence of an audience or co-actors increases arousal and improves performance. The principle was first identified by Norman Triplett in 1898 when he observed that cyclists performed better when racing against others than when racing alone. Option i2 correctly describes this concept by stating that performance improves in the presence of others compared to when alone, which is the defining characteristic of social facilitation.

q.s: Although she has not sustained any injuries, Riley cannot remember anything before the age of three. She is most likely experiencing
q.ex: Infantile amnesia refers to the normal inability of adults to recall episodic memories from early childhood, typically before ages three to four. This phenomenon occurs because the hippocampus and other brain structures necessary for forming and storing long-term autobiographical memories are not fully developed in infancy and early toddlerhood. Riley's inability to remember anything before age three, without any injury, represents this typical developmental pattern rather than a pathological condition. Retrograde amnesia involves loss of previously formed memories due to injury or trauma, while anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after an injury. The correct answer is infantile amnesia because it describes the universal

q.s: Liza exhibits characteristics of schizophrenia. The medication most likely to be prescribed for her symptoms most directly affects the receptor sites for
q.ex: The primary neurotransmitter implicated in schizophrenia is dopamine, according to the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia. Antipsychotic medications, which are the first-line treatment for schizophrenia, work primarily by blocking dopamine receptors, particularly D2 receptors in the brain. This blocking action helps reduce positive symptoms of schizophrenia such as hallucinations and delusions. While some newer atypical antipsychotics also affect serotonin receptors, their therapeutic effect on schizophrenia symptoms is most directly attributed to their action on dopamine receptor sites. Therefore, dop

q.s: The psychosocial theory of development assumes which of the following principles underlies development at all stages?

o.l: Principles of classical and operant conditioning shape personality throughout the life span.
Each stage in the life span presents the task of resolving a different conflict.
Maturation is the primary force that drives movement through stages.
Advancement within each stage is independent of experience in the prior stage.

q.ex: Psychosocial theory, developed by Erik Erikson, proposes that human development occurs through eight distinct stages across the lifespan. The fundamental principle underlying this theory is that each developmental stage presents a unique psychosocial crisis or conflict that must be resolved. These conflicts involve tensions between opposing psychological qualities, such as trust versus mistrust in infancy or identity versus role confusion in adolescence. Successfully resolving each stage's conflict allows the individual to develop important virtues and move forward with a healthy personality foundation. Option i3 is correct because it accurately identifies that each life stage presents a different conflict to resolve, which is the central organizing principle of Erikson's psych

q.s: In a distribution of a class’s scores on a test about gender identity, a large number of students received high scores while fewer students received low scores. The distribution of the test scores is best described as being which of the following?
q.ex: A negatively skewed distribution occurs when the majority of scores cluster at the high end of the scale, with a tail extending toward the lower scores. In this scenario, most students received high scores on the test while fewer students received low scores, creating exactly this pattern. The term "negative" refers to the direction of the tail, which points toward the negative (lower) end of the scale. This is distinct from a positively skewed distribution, where most scores would be low with a tail extending toward high scores, and from a normal distribution, where scores would be symmetrically distributed around the mean. Therefore, the correct answer is negatively skewed because the bulk of the data is

q.s: Emmit wants to examine whether there is a difference in the number of students with an internal locus of control and the number with an external locus of control based on class year (e.g., freshmen versus sophomores). Which of the following is the most appropriate research method for Emmit to use to determine whether there is a difference?
q.ex:
A survey is the most appropriate method because Emmit needs to collect data about students' locus of control beliefs across different class years. Surveys allow researchers to efficiently gather self-reported information from large numbers of participants about their attitudes, beliefs, and characteristics. In this case, Emmit can administer a locus of control questionnaire to students from different class years and compare the frequencies of internal versus external locus of control across groups. This method is ideal for descriptive research examining existing differences in psychological characteristics across populations without manipulation of variables.

The correct choice is a survey because it enables systematic collection of self-report data about locus of control from multiple class years, allowing

q.s: Which of the following research techniques would be the best way to demonstrate that getting eight or more hours of sleep produces higher exam scores the following day?
q.ex: To demonstrate that sleep causes higher exam scores, researchers must establish a causal relationship, which requires manipulating one variable while controlling others. Experimentation is the only research method that allows researchers to establish cause-and-effect relationships by randomly assigning participants to different conditions (such as eight or more hours of sleep versus less sleep) and controlling extraneous variables. Naturalistic observation and case studies can only describe behaviors without establishing causation, while correlational studies can show relationships between variables but cannot prove that one variable causes changes in another. Experimentation is correct because it is the only method that can definitively demonstrate that sleep duration produces or causes changes in exam performance.

q.s: Which of the following is an example of using positive reinforcement to get a toddler to repeat the response of washing his hands after eating?

o.l: Explaining that washing his hands promotes cleanliness
Taking away toys when he forgets to wash his hands
Giving him a treat for washing his hands
Allowing him to have dessert if he finishes his meal

q.ex: Positive reinforcement involves adding a desirable stimulus after a behavior to increase the likelihood that the behavior will be repeated. In this scenario, giving the toddler a treat after he washes his hands adds something pleasant (the treat) following the desired behavior (handwashing). This creates a positive association that makes the child more likely to wash his hands again in the future. The other options either involve explanation (which is not reinforcement), punishment through removal (negative punishment), or reinforcement of a different behavior (eating a meal rather than handwashing). Option i4 is correct because it directly applies positive reinforcement by adding a rewarding stimulus immediately after the target behavior of han

q.s: On Diane’s first day of work she was offered a cookie. When she bit into the cookie, it tasted horrible, but because she wanted to make a good impression, Diane concealed her disgust and smiled instead. Diane’s reaction best illustrates
q.ex: Display rules are culturally determined norms that govern when, how, and to what extent people should express emotions in social situations. In this scenario, Diane experienced genuine disgust when tasting the horrible cookie, but she deliberately suppressed this authentic emotional expression and smiled instead to make a favorable impression on her first day of work. This behavior demonstrates her adherence to social conventions about appropriate emotional displays in professional settings, where concealing negative reactions is often expected to maintain politeness and positive social relationships. The correct answer is display rules because Diane consciously modified her emotional expression to conform to workplace social expectations rather than displaying her true feelings.

q.s: Jamal is taking several honors courses this year and feels more pressure than he ever has before. He worries constantly about school, and because of the time he must devote to studying, he also worries about his relationship with his girlfriend. He is often restless, and his family thinks he gets irritated more than he used to. Even though he feels academic pressure, he often struggles to stay focused on his schoolwork, and his grades are suffering. Jamal’s problems are most consistent with which of the following disorders?
q.ex: Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by excessive, persistent worry about multiple aspects of life that is difficult to control and interferes with daily functioning. Jamal exhibits the key diagnostic features: constant worry about multiple domains (school and relationships), restlessness, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. These symptoms have lasted long enough to impair his academic performance despite his efforts. The pattern of pervasive anxiety across different life areas, combined with physical tension and cognitive difficulties, distinguishes this from major depressive disorder (which would emphasize persistent sadness and loss of interest), dissociative identity disorder (which involves distinct personality states), or somatic symptom disorder (which centers on physical

q.s: Kenyatta is participating in a research study examining the effects of a particular hormone. After she is given the hormone, she engages in behaviors that demonstrate trust in strangers, peer bonding, and group cohesion. Kenyatta was most likely given which of the following as part of the study?
q.ex: Oxytocin is a hormone and neurotransmitter primarily associated with social bonding, trust, and prosocial behaviors. Research has consistently shown that oxytocin administration increases trust in others, enhances feelings of attachment and connection, and promotes group cohesion and cooperative behavior. The behaviors Kenyatta demonstrates—trusting strangers, peer bonding, and group cohesion—are hallmark effects of oxytocin. In contrast, melatonin regulates sleep-wake cycles, adrenaline triggers the fight-or-flight response, and ghrelin stimulates appetite. Oxytocin is correct because it is

q.s: Claude, a waiter at a popular restaurant, gives extra appetizers to his return customers because they often tip him more when he does. Claude’s technique relies on which of the following?
q.ex: The reciprocity norm is a social principle stating that people feel obligated to return favors or kind gestures they receive from others. When Claude gives extra appetizers to his return customers, he is creating a sense of indebtedness in them. These customers then feel compelled to reciprocate his generosity by leaving larger tips. This technique directly exploits the human tendency to want to repay what others have provided to us, making it a clear application of the reciprocity norm. The correct answer is the reciprocity norm because Claude's strategy specifically depends on customers feeling obligated to return his generous gesture with increased tips.

q.s: Following a mild stroke, Sam ate much more than normal and gained 50 pounds within a year. What part of the brain was most likely damaged?
q.ex: The hypothalamus is the brain structure responsible for regulating basic bodily functions including hunger, thirst, and body temperature. Within the hypothalamus, the ventromedial region acts as a satiety center that signals when to stop eating, while the lateral region stimulates hunger. Damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus removes the brake on eating behavior, leading to hyperphagia (excessive eating) and significant weight gain. Sam's dramatic increase in food intake and 50-pound weight gain following his stroke indicates damage to this critical appetite regulation center. The hypothalamus is correct because it is the primary brain structure controlling eating behavior and energy balance.

q.s: When excitatory neurotransmitters stimulate a single neuron, the neuron

o.l: becomes more likely to produce an action potential
becomes less likely to produce an action potential

q.ex: Excitatory neurotransmitters cause depolarization of the postsynaptic neuron by making the inside of the cell less negative relative to the outside. This depolarization brings the neuron's membrane potential closer to the threshold needed to trigger an action potential. When enough excitatory input accumulates through temporal or spatial summation, the neuron reaches threshold and fires an action potential. Action potentials themselves follow an all-or-none principle, meaning they cannot be stronger or weaker once triggered. Therefore, excitatory neurotransmitters increase the probability of firing without changing the strength of the action potential itself, making option i1 correct.

q.s: A researcher interested in cooperative play in young children unobtrusively places several video cameras at a public playground and counts how many children engage in cooperative play behaviors. Which type of research method is the researcher using?
q.ex: Naturalistic observation is a research method in which behavior is observed and recorded in its natural setting without any manipulation or intervention by the researcher. In this scenario, the researcher is simply watching and recording children's cooperative play behaviors as they naturally occur at a public playground, without controlling variables or interfering with the children's activities. The use of unobtrusive video cameras ensures that the children's behavior remains natural and uninfluenced by the researcher's presence. This method differs from an experiment, which would require manipulation of variables, a case study, which would involve in-depth examination of specific individuals, or a longitudinal study, which would require following subjects over an extended period. The correct

q.s: A one-year-old child learns that the furry animals with bushy tails she sees outside her window are squirrels. Later she sees chipmunks outside the window and believes those are also squirrels. Which Piagetian concept is the child demonstrating?
q.ex: The child is demonstrating assimilation, which occurs when new information is incorporated into existing mental schemas without changing those schemas. The child has developed a schema for "squirrel" based on characteristics like furry body and bushy tail. When encountering chipmunks that share similar features, the child fits this new experience into her existing squirrel schema rather than creating a new category. This is the essence of assimilation: making new experiences fit into what we already know. The correct answer is assimilation because the child is applying her existing schema to new but similar stimuli without modifying her understanding.

q.s: Four-year-old Maria knows that she has eaten all her peanuts, but she also realizes that Robbie, who cannot see inside her bag, may not know the peanuts are gone. Her awareness demonstrates that Maria has
q.ex: Maria's ability to understand that Robbie has a different perspective and knowledge state than her own demonstrates theory of mind. Theory of mind is the cognitive capacity to recognize that other people have mental states, beliefs, and knowledge that differ from one's own. In this scenario, Maria understands that even though she knows the peanuts are gone, Robbie cannot know this because he lacks visual access to her bag. This represents a crucial developmental milestone typically emerging around ages 3-5, where children move beyond egocentric thinking to appreciate that others have independent minds with different information. The correct answer is theory of mind because it specifically describes the ability to attribute mental states to others and recognize

q.s: Evidence for the opponent-process theory of color vision is provided by the fact that

o.l: it takes several minutes for the eyes to fully adapt to darkness
there are three different types of cones in the retinas
the eyes perceive visual illusions, such as the Müller-Lyer illusion
the eyes see negative afterimages after staring at saturated colors for several minutes

q.ex: The opponent-process theory of color vision proposes that color perception is controlled by three opposing pairs of colors: red-green, blue-yellow, and black-white. According to this theory, these color pairs cannot be perceived simultaneously because they work in opposition to each other. The phenomenon of negative afterimages directly supports this theory because when you stare at a saturated color for an extended period, the cells responding to that color become fatigued. When you then look at a neutral surface, the opposing color cells that were inhibited become more active, creating an afterimage in the complementary color. For example, staring at red produces a green afterimage, demonstrating the

q.s: Kelly sees her acquaintance Carly help another student who dropped her books in the hallway. When asked about Carly later, Kelly says that she is not only helpful, but she is also generous, smart, and attractive. Which of the following best explains why Kelly describes Carly with additional positive qualities?
q.ex: The halo effect occurs when one positive characteristic of a person influences our overall impression, leading us to attribute additional positive qualities to that individual. In this scenario, Kelly observes Carly performing one helpful action and then generalizes this single positive trait to assume Carly possesses other positive qualities like generosity, intelligence, and attractiveness. This cognitive bias causes us to let one salient positive feature create a "halo" that colors our perception of the person's other unobserved traits. The correct answer is the halo effect because Kelly's observation of Carly's helpfulness led her to infer multiple other positive characteristics without additional evidence for those specific traits.

q.s: Janice has a strong, unreasonable fear of being embarrassed in front of strangers. When she is with others she does not know, she feels extremely insecure and worried. Janice’s problems are most consistent with which of the following disorders?
q.ex: Social anxiety disorder is characterized by an intense, persistent fear of social situations where the person might be scrutinized, judged, or embarrassed by others. The key features include extreme anxiety in social settings, particularly with unfamiliar people, and fear of negative evaluation or embarrassment. Janice's symptoms directly match this pattern: she has a strong, unreasonable fear of embarrassment specifically in front of strangers and experiences extreme insecurity when around people she does not know. This is distinct from generalized anxiety disorder, which involves excessive worry about multiple life circumstances rather than specifically social situations. Social anxiety disorder is the correct answer because Janice's fear is specifically tied to social

q.s: Assessments that ask participants to complete sentences, identify pictures in inkblots, or tell the story behind a photograph are all examples of which of the following types of tests?
q.ex: Projective tests are psychological assessments that present ambiguous stimuli to participants and ask them to interpret or respond to these stimuli in their own way. The underlying theory is that people will project their unconscious thoughts, feelings, and personality characteristics onto the ambiguous material. Examples like sentence completion, Rorschach inkblot interpretations, and Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) photographs all share this characteristic of using unstructured, open-ended stimuli that allow for individual interpretation. These differ from intelligence, aptitude, and achievement tests, which have specific correct answers and measure cognitive abilities or learned knowledge rather than personality traits. The correct answer is

q.s: A researcher finds that participants work hardest and are most engaged in tasks when their behavior allows them to receive awards. The researcher’s finding exemplifies
q.ex: Incentive theory states that behavior is motivated by the desire to obtain external rewards or avoid punishments. When participants work hardest because their behavior allows them to receive awards, they are being driven by these external incentives rather than internal factors. The awards serve as positive reinforcers that pull individuals toward certain behaviors. This differs from intrinsic motivation, which comes from internal satisfaction, and from evolutionary theory, which focuses on inherited behavioral tendencies. The correct answer is incentive theory because it directly explains how external rewards motivate and increase engagement in tasks.

q.s: The graphs depict the distribution of intelligence test scores for two groups of students at a middle school. Which of the following statements is true of the graphs?

o.l: The mean and standard deviation are identical for both distributions.
The mean is identical for both distributions; the standard deviation is larger for distribution B.
The mean is identical for both distributions; the standard deviation is larger for distribution A.
The standard deviation is identical for both distributions; the mean is larger for distribution B.

q.ex: The mean represents the central tendency of a distribution and is located at the peak of a symmetrical bell curve. Both distributions show their peaks aligned at the same point on the horizontal axis, indicating identical means. The standard deviation measures the spread or variability of scores around the mean. Distribution A is wider and flatter, indicating that scores are more spread out from the mean, while distribution B is taller and narrower, indicating scores are more clustered around the mean. A wider distribution corresponds to a larger standard deviation because the data points deviate more from the central value. Therefore, option i3 is correct because both distributions have the same mean, but distribution A has a larger standard deviation

q.s: Dr. Mummer believes that his patient experiences nervousness and aggression because of a problem with the amygdala and prescribes a treatment that targets how the amygdala functions. Dr. Mummer’s treatment is most in line with which of the following psychological perspectives?
q.ex: The biological perspective in psychology focuses on how physical structures and processes in the body, particularly the brain and nervous system, influence behavior and mental processes. Dr. Mummer attributes his patient's nervousness and aggression to a problem with the amygdala, which is a specific brain structure, and prescribes treatment targeting its functioning. This approach directly examines physiological mechanisms as the cause of psychological symptoms. The psychodynamic perspective would focus on unconscious conflicts, social-cognitive on thought patterns and social learning, and behavioral on learned responses to environmental stimuli. The correct answer is the biological perspective because Dr. Mummer is explicitly treating a brain-based physiological cause of

q.s: Ed quit his job because he began to fear that his supervisor was spying on him. Ed frequently hears voices criticizing him, but in reality nobody is there. Ed’s problems are most consistent with which of the following disorders?
q.ex: Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder characterized by a loss of contact with reality, including positive symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations. Ed exhibits two key positive symptoms: delusions of persecution (believing his supervisor is spying on him) and auditory hallucinations (hearing voices criticizing him when no one is present). These symptoms represent a fundamental break from reality that is not present in the other disorders listed. Obsessive-compulsive disorder involves intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors, illness anxiety disorder involves excessive worry about having a serious illness, and agoraphobia involves fear of situations where escape might be difficult. Only schizophrenia accounts

q.s: Andy is softhearted, good-natured, trusting, helpful, forgiving, gullible, and straightforward. Based on these characteristics, he is most likely to score high on which of the Big Five trait measures?
q.ex: The Big Five personality traits include extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and neuroticism. Agreeableness specifically measures an individual's tendency to be cooperative, compassionate, trusting, and concerned with social harmony. The characteristics described for Andy—softhearted, good-natured, trusting, helpful, forgiving, gullible, and straightforward—are all core facets of the agreeableness dimension. These traits reflect a person who prioritizes getting along with others, showing empathy, and maintaining positive interpersonal relationships. Therefore, agreeableness is the correct answer because Andy's personality profile

q.s: Every day Haiying tells her parents something new she would like to be when she grows up. Haiying’s parents listen carefully and provide encouraging words. Even if Haiying’s ideas are fanciful and impractical, her parents never pass judgment or suggest that she is being irrational. Haiying’s parents’ responses to their daughter demonstrate which concept?
q.ex: Unconditional positive regard is a concept from humanistic psychology, specifically Carl Rogers' person-centered approach, which refers to accepting and supporting someone without judgment or conditions, regardless of what they say or do. Haiying's parents demonstrate this by listening carefully and encouraging her career ideas without criticizing or judging them, even when the ideas are fanciful or impractical. They provide acceptance and support that is not contingent on whether her ideas meet certain standards of rationality or practicality. This nonjudgmental, accepting attitude exemplifies unconditional positive regard because their support remains constant regardless of the content of what Haiying shares. The correct

q.s: Studying by focusing on the facts and not the meaning of information that has to be remembered involves
q.ex: In cognitive psychology, levels of processing theory distinguishes between shallow and deep processing of information. Shallow processing involves encoding information based on superficial characteristics such as physical features, sounds, or rote memorization of facts without considering their meaning or significance. Deep processing, in contrast, involves semantic encoding where learners focus on the meaning of information and make connections to existing knowledge. When students study by focusing only on facts without engaging with their meaning, they are engaging in shallow processing, which typically results in weaker memory retention compared to deep processing. Therefore, shallow processing is the correct answer because it specifically describes learning that emphasizes surface-level features rather than meaningful understanding.

q.s: A therapist who invites clients to clarify their verbal and nonverbal expressions, reflects clients’ feelings, and paraphrases clients is using
q.ex: Person-centered therapy, developed by Carl Rogers, emphasizes creating a supportive therapeutic environment through specific communication techniques. The core methods include active listening, reflecting feelings back to the client, paraphrasing to ensure understanding, and helping clients clarify their thoughts and emotions. These techniques demonstrate unconditional positive regard and empathic understanding, which are fundamental to the person-centered approach. The therapist acts as a facilitator who helps clients explore their own feelings and find their own solutions rather than directing treatment or interpreting unconscious conflicts. The correct answer is person-centered therapy because the described techniques of clarifying expressions, reflecting feelings, and paraphrasing are the defining characteristics of

q.s: Brian was having difficulty solving a riddle, but after sleeping, he suddenly understood the answer. Brian’s newfound knowledge was probably the result of
q.ex: Insight is a sudden realization or understanding of a solution to a problem without conscious, step-by-step reasoning. This phenomenon, studied extensively by Gestalt psychologists, involves an "aha moment" where the answer becomes clear all at once rather than through gradual learning or trial and error. Brian's experience of suddenly understanding the riddle after sleeping exemplifies this type of problem-solving, as the solution emerged spontaneously rather than through deliberate practice or external rewards. The correct answer is insight because it specifically describes the sudden comprehension that occurs when mental restructuring allows someone to see a problem in a new way.

q.s: Consider the relationship between various body parts and the size of their corresponding somatosensory cortex areas in the brain. How does a body part relate to the devoted cortical area?

o.l: The larger the body part, the larger the area of the somatosensory cortex.
The closer the body part is to the brain, the smaller the area of the somatosensory cortex.
The closer the body part is to the trunk, the larger the area of the somatosensory cortex.
The more sensitive the body part, the larger the area of the somatosensory cortex.

q.ex: The somatosensory cortex allocates space based on sensory sensitivity and precision rather than physical size or anatomical location. This principle is illustrated by the cortical homunculus, a distorted representation of the human body mapped onto the brain. Body parts requiring fine tactile discrimination, such as fingertips, lips, and tongue, have disproportionately large cortical representations despite their small physical size. Conversely, large body parts like the back or thigh have relatively small cortical areas because they have lower sensory receptor density and less need for precise sensory processing. The more sensitive the body part, the larger the area of the somatosens

q.s: Which of the following most clearly demonstrates social learning theory?

o.l: Mavis learns a line dance by watching her friends perform it.
Neville becomes dependent on alcohol because he finds that after drinking it he temporarily forgets his problems.
After writing his paper at the last minute, Raul gets a bad grade and never procrastinates again.
Xanthe deletes his social media accounts after experiencing harsh bullying from others online.

q.ex: Social learning theory, developed by Albert Bandura, proposes that people learn behaviors by observing and imitating others rather than through direct reinforcement or punishment. Mavis learning a line dance by watching her friends perform it is a clear example of observational learning, which is the core mechanism of social learning theory. She acquires the behavior through modeling without needing to experience consequences herself. The other options demonstrate operant conditioning through reinforcement or punishment rather than learning through observation and imitation. Option i2 is correct because it shows learning occurring purely through watching and modeling others' behavior.

q.s: Rudy has chronic trouble staying awake in class. What part of the brain is most likely responsible for Rudy’s drowsiness?
q.ex: The reticular formation is a network of neurons located in the brainstem that plays a crucial role in regulating arousal, alertness, and sleep-wake cycles. This structure acts as a filter for incoming sensory information and helps maintain consciousness by sending signals to the cortex to keep the brain alert and awake. When the reticular formation is not functioning properly or is underactive, it can result in excessive drowsiness and difficulty maintaining wakefulness, which would explain Rudy's chronic trouble staying awake in class. The reticular formation is therefore the most likely brain structure responsible for Rudy's drowsiness because it is the primary regulator of arousal

q.s: Dizziness is most closely associated with which of the following senses?
q.ex: The vestibular sense is responsible for detecting balance, spatial orientation, and movement of the head. This sensory system is located in the inner ear and contains fluid-filled semicircular canals and otolith organs that detect changes in head position and acceleration. When the vestibular system is disrupted or overstimulated, it results in the sensation of dizziness or vertigo. While the kinesthetic sense relates to body position and movement, and the auditory sense involves hearing through structures also in the ear, it is specifically the vestibular system that maintains equilibrium and whose dysfunction causes dizziness. Therefore, option i3 is correct because the vestib

q.s: A teacher has to learn 170 new student names every year and finds it difficult to remember the names of former students. The teacher’s memory problem most likely results from
q.ex:
Retroactive interference occurs when newly learned information disrupts the recall of previously learned information. In this case, the teacher learns 170 new student names each year, and this new information interferes with the ability to remember the names of former students from previous years. The continuous acquisition of new names makes it harder to retrieve the older names from memory. This is distinct from proactive interference, where old information would interfere with learning new information, which is the opposite of what the teacher experiences.

The correct choice is retroactive interference because the newly learned names are interfering with the recall of previously learned names.

q.s: Which of the following approaches to treating psychological disorders includes free association and dream analysis?
q.ex: Psychodynamic therapy, rooted in Freudian psychoanalysis, focuses on uncovering unconscious conflicts and repressed memories that contribute to psychological disorders. Free association is a core psychodynamic technique where patients say whatever comes to mind without censorship, allowing unconscious material to surface. Dream analysis is another fundamental psychodynamic method based on Freud's belief that dreams represent the "royal road to the unconscious" and contain symbolic meanings about repressed wishes and conflicts. These techniques are distinctive to the psychodynamic approach and are not characteristic of humanistic therapy (which emphasizes self-actualization), behavioral therapy (which focuses on observable behaviors), or cognitive

q.s: A basketball player deliberately tried to injure opposing players during the game. Near the end of the game, he falls and is injured. A fan comments that the player deserved the injury. The fan’s sentiments best represent what social psychological phenomenon?
q.ex:
The just-world hypothesis is the cognitive bias where people believe that the world is fundamentally fair and that individuals get what they deserve. When the fan comments that the player deserved his injury because of his earlier attempts to hurt others, this reflects the belief that bad things happen to bad people as a form of cosmic justice. This phenomenon helps people maintain their belief in an orderly, predictable world where actions have appropriate consequences. The fan is attributing the player's misfortune to his prior bad behavior, viewing it as deserved punishment rather than random chance.

The correct choice is the just-world hypothesis because it specifically describes the belief that people get what they deserve, which directly matches

q.s: Ten-month-old Jacqueline is seated on a couch. A researcher takes a toy from her hands and hides it under a blanket. Jacqueline reaches for the toy under the blanket. Which of the following concepts is being tested in this study?
q.ex: Object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist even when they cannot be seen, heard, or otherwise sensed. This concept, identified by Jean Piaget, typically develops during the sensorimotor stage of cognitive development, roughly between 4 and 12 months of age. In this study, the researcher hides the toy under a blanket to determine whether Jacqueline understands that the toy still exists despite being out of sight. When Jacqueline reaches for the hidden toy, she demonstrates that she has developed object permanence because she knows the toy continues to exist even though she cannot see it. The correct answer is object permanence because the study

q.s: In what important way does research on taste aversion conducted by John Garcia and Robert Koelling demonstrate how biology can strongly influence classical conditioning?

o.l: By showing that some associations between unconditioned and conditioned stimuli are more easily learned than others
By showing that pairing the conditioned stimulus with the unconditioned stimulus is not required
By showing that the unconditioned stimulus and the conditioned stimulus must be presented together
By showing that cognition is not necessary for conditioning to occur

q.ex: Garcia and Koelling's taste aversion research demonstrated that animals are biologically prepared to associate certain stimuli more readily than others, challenging the traditional assumption that any neutral stimulus could be equally paired with any unconditioned stimulus. Their experiments showed that rats easily learned to associate taste with illness but had difficulty associating visual or auditory cues with illness, while the opposite was true for external pain. This biological preparedness reflects evolutionary adaptations where certain associations have survival value. The research revealed that classical conditioning is constrained by an organism's biological predispositions rather than being a purely mechanical process of stimulus pairing. Option i1 is correct because it accurately describes how Garcia an

q.s: The sociocultural perspective is best reflected in which of the following research findings?

o.l: Shortly after young children were exposed to a bacterial streptococcal infection they began displaying symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Brain imaging studies show higher levels of activity in the limbic system of individuals with depression when responding to negative emotional information.

In the United States individuals diagnosed with dissociative identity disorder switch identities upon suggestion, while in India individuals diagnosed with the same disorder switch personalities only upon awakening.
Individuals diagnosed with antisocial personality disorder show weaker startle responses when shown unpleasant stimuli.

q.ex:
The sociocultural perspective in psychology examines how cultural context, social norms, and environmental factors shape psychological phenomena and behavior. Option i3 demonstrates this perspective by showing how the same disorder manifests differently across cultures—American patients with dissociative identity disorder switch identities through suggestion while Indian patients switch only upon awakening. This cultural variation in symptom expression illustrates how psychological disorders are influenced by cultural expectations and social contexts rather than being purely biological or universal phenomena. The other options reflect biological or neurological perspectives, focusing on infections, brain activity, and physiological responses rather than cultural influences.

Option i3 is correct because it directly demonstrates how culture shapes the expression and experience

q.s: The above graph of conditioning shows which of the following concepts?

o.l: Generalization, discrimination, and higher order conditioning

q.ex: The graph displays three distinct phases characteristic of classical conditioning. Acquisition occurs when a conditioned response is initially learned and strengthens through repeated pairings of the conditioned stimulus with the unconditioned stimulus, shown by the rising curve. Extinction follows when the conditioned stimulus is presented without the unconditioned stimulus, causing the conditioned response to weaken and decline, depicted by the falling curve. Spontaneous recovery is demonstrated when, after a rest period following extinction, the conditioned response temporarily reappears at a reduced strength when the conditioned stimulus is presented again. These three phases represent the fundamental pattern of how learned responses are acquired, diminished, and can unexpectedly

q.s: Sarah is seeing a psychologist to assess her happiness in the workplace. The psychologist asks her questions about her life before taking the job and also has her take several personality assessments. This type of research that focuses on in-depth analysis of an individual exemplifies which of the following methods?
q.ex: A case study is a research method that involves an intensive, in-depth investigation of a single individual, group, or event. In this scenario, the psychologist is conducting a detailed examination of Sarah specifically, gathering comprehensive information through interviews about her life history and multiple personality assessments. This individualized, thorough approach is the hallmark of case study methodology, which aims to understand the complexities of a particular case rather than generalize findings across a population. The correct answer is case study because the psychologist is performing an extensive analysis focused on one person rather than conducting an experiment with controlled variables, observing behavior in natural settings, or comparing different age groups at one point in time.

q.s: Andi’s best friend always screamed when she was in high places, and now Andi also screams when she is in high places. Which of the following theorists would say that Andi screams because she saw her friend scream?
q.ex: Albert Bandura developed social learning theory, which emphasizes that people learn behaviors through observation and imitation of others, particularly models they are close to or identify with. His famous Bobo doll experiments demonstrated that children who observed aggressive behavior would imitate that behavior even without direct reinforcement. In this scenario, Andi learned to scream in high places by observing her best friend's screaming behavior, which is a clear example of observational learning or modeling. The other theorists focus on different areas: William James studied consciousness and emotion, Charles Spearman developed theories of intelligence, and Carl Rogers focused on humanistic psychology and self-actualization. Albert Ban

q.s: Research on environmental enrichment and the brain suggests that the environment

o.l: influences both brain structure and functioning throughout the life span
influences both brain structure and functioning only through infancy
influences both brain structure and functioning only through childhood
influences brain functioning but not brain structure

q.ex: Environmental enrichment research demonstrates that exposure to stimulating, complex environments produces measurable changes in the brain at any age. Studies have shown that enriched environments increase dendritic branching, synapse formation, and neurogenesis in the hippocampus, while also enhancing cognitive performance and neural plasticity. These structural and functional changes occur not only during critical developmental periods but continue throughout adulthood and even into old age. The brain retains its capacity for experience-dependent plasticity across the entire lifespan, meaning that environmental factors can modify both its physical structure and its operational capabilities from birth through senescence. The correct answer is that the environment influences both brain structure and functioning

q.s: Elena wanted to see if taller students were more likely do better on achievement tests. Elana recorded the height of all of her classmates and calculated the standard deviation. If everything else stayed the same, what change to the data would make the standard deviation increase?

o.l: If the tallest person were taller
If the shortest person were taller
If everyone in the class were one inch taller
If the tallest and shortest person were removed from the data set

q.ex: Standard deviation measures the spread or variability of data points around the mean. A larger standard deviation indicates that data points are more dispersed from the average, while a smaller standard deviation indicates they are clustered closer together. If the tallest person becomes even taller, this increases the distance between that extreme value and the mean, thereby increasing the overall spread of the data. In contrast, making the shortest person taller would actually reduce variability by bringing an extreme value closer to the mean, adding a constant to all values would shift the mean but not change the spread, and removing extreme values would decrease the standard deviation. The correct answer is i1 because increasing an extreme value increases the disp

q.s: It is easier to condition individuals to be afraid of snakes than of electrical outlets because of a phenomenon called
q.ex: Biological preparedness refers to the evolutionary predisposition that makes certain associations easier to learn than others.
