Source 1

Introduction

Electronic devices are used widely across many cultures. Media screens include televisions, computers, tablets, and smartphones. Parents and caregivers may wonder about the relationship between their children paying attention to media screens and the cognitive changes that are described in developmental theories. This research study examined when infants first experienced media screens, how often they were exposed to media screens, and their later cognitive development. The researchers also considered mothers’ education levels and verbal interactions with their infants.

Participants

The researchers tracked 274 mothers and their infant participants when the infants were at 6, 12, 18, 24, 36, and 48 months of age. The infants were healthy in terms of length of gestation, birth weight, growth patterns, and the presence of diseases or disorders.

Method

At each session, the researchers asked the mothers how much time their infants were exposed to media screens while awake during an average weekday. The mothers reported their own level of education and the age when their infants were first exposed to media screens. Research participants completed an assessment when the infants were 24 months, 36 months, and 48 months of age. The assessment measures infant motor skills, visual reception, comprehension of spoken words, and language formation.

Results and Discussion

On average, mothers reported that their infants’ first exposure to media screens occurred at one month of age. Screen exposure was primarily to televisions, followed by tablets and smartphones, and computers. The data showed that when mothers had more years of education, their infants were first exposed to media screens later than were infants whose mothers had fewer years of education. Mothers with more years of education also exposed their children to fewer media screens (correlation coefficient = -.20), and they verbally interacted more with their children during media screen exposure (correlation coefficient = .17). Participants who were exposed to 6.5 hours of screen time per day, which was considered a high level, scored lower for some motor skills and visual reception scales administered at 24 months (correlation coefficient = -.41), 36 months (correlation coefficient = -.26), and 48 months (correlation coefficient = -.28). The relationships between high levels of screen time and cognitive development were especially strong among participants who were first exposed to screen media at an early age or when mothers did not verbally interact with the participants during media screen exposure.

Supanitayanon, S., Trairatvorakul, P., & Chonchaiya, W. (2020). Screen media exposure in the first 2 years of life and preschool cognitive development: A longitudinal study. Pediatric Research, 88, 894-902. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41390-020-0831-8 

Source 2

Introduction

In the research study, participants completed mental imagery, working memory, and vocabulary tasks. Their parents reported on when the participants were first exposed to media screens, how often exposure occurs, and the kinds of screen devices used.

Participants

Two hundred sixty-six children between the ages of 3 and 10 years who attended pre- or primary school in Germany participated in this study. For the majority (56.4%), one or both parents had a university degree. Most of the participants spoke German at home, but 26.3% of them spoke a language other than German at home.

Method

Parents of the children completed surveys to provide information about their children’s screen time and use across different times of the day. Parents reported on different kinds of devices their children used and the age when children first began using devices.

The children completed three cognitive tasks: a mental imagery task, a working memory task, and a vocabulary task.

  • For the mental imagery task, the children were prompted to think about two objects and decide which of the two objects better fit into a category provided by the researchers (e.g., “Which is shinier, [a] trumpet or [a] violin?”). The researchers recorded the children’s responses on 34 trials and how quickly they responded on each trial, and the task was repeated at a later time

  • For the working memory task, the children were read nine strings of numbers that varied in length from two, three, or four digits. After each string, the children were asked to recall the string of numbers, but in the reverse order of how the researchers presented it.

  • For the vocabulary task, the children were shown 39 pictures of objects and were asked to name each one.

Results and Discussion

The researchers found the most common type of media screen exposure was to television. On average, the children were first exposed to screen media at almost 2 years of age. Working memory, vocabulary, and mental imagery were positively correlated to each other. On the mental imagery task, the researchers found a negative correlation between the amount of screen time at Time 1 and how accurate the children were on the task at Time 2.

Suggate, S. P., & Martzog, P. (2020). Screen-time influences children’s mental imagery performance. Developmental Science, 2020;23:e12978. https://doi.org/10.111/desc.12978

Introduction

The researchers studied pregnant women who lived in Brazil, assessing their infants’ cognitive development over time. The mothers also reported their own levels of education and how much time their children were exposed to media screens.

Participants

The researchers studied a randomly selected group of 470 women who were up to 24-weeks pregnant and lived in Brazil. The women gave informed consent to for their own and their children’s participation in the study, and the study was approved by an ethics committee to ensure the participants’ welfare and well-being.

Method

The mothers completed assessments at four points during pregnancy and after birth. When the children were at 18 months of age, they completed an assessment that measures cognitive, language, motor, socio-emotional, and behavioral components. Mothers reported their own level of education and how many hours their children were exposed to media screens during a typical day.

Results and Discussion

The children’s performance on the cognitive tasks was better when their mothers had more education. Their mean performance and standard deviation on the cognitive tasks as a function screen media exposure are:

Introduction

In the 1950s and 1960s, Stanley Milgram, a psychologist at Yale University, led a series of studies that tested whether people would obey the commands of a researcher in a lab. The study presented is a replication of one of Milgram’s original studies.

Participants

Individuals who responded to advertisements and flyers went through a series of screening procedures to eliminate people who had taken more than two psychology courses in college; been diagnosed with, or had therapy for, a psychological disorder; abused alcohol or drugs; had medical conditions affected by stress; or experienced severe trauma. The final sample had 29 men and 41 women. The participants ranged in age from 20 to 81 (mean age = 42.9 years, standard deviation = 15.67, median age = 41). Participant education and race/ethnicity demographics are presented in the table.

Education and Ethnicity Number of Participants Percentage of Participants
Education    
High school or less 12 17.1
Some college 16 22.9
Bachelor’s degree 28 40.0
Master’s degree 14 20.0
Ethnicity    
White 38 54.3
 Asian 19 26.7
Latino/a/Hispanic 9 12.9
African American 3 4.3
Did not state 1 1.4

A committee of professionals reviewed the study to ensure the appropriateness of the study before researchers began.
 

Method

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: the “base” condition and the “modeled refusal” condition. The participants agreed to be in the study and knew they could withdraw at any time and keep the $50 they were paid to participate.

In the base condition, the participant was paired with a “learner,” who was a research confederate. The participant read 25 different word-pairs (e.g., strong–arm) that the “learner” had to recall. If the “learner” gave an incorrect answer, the participant administered an electric shock using a “shock generator” that had switches ranging from 15 to 450 volts in 15-volt increments. The shock was fake, but the participant did not know this. The. The participant moved up one switch on the shock generator for each incorrect answer.

While the participants watched, the researcher strapped the “learners” into a chair with electrodes. The participant then went to another room for the remainder of the study. The “learners” gave correct and incorrect responses according to a predetermined schedule. After participants pressed the 75-volt switch, they heard a small grunt from the “learner.” The grunts got louder after each successive shock. When a participant pressed the 150-volt switch, the “learner” yelled, “Ugh. Get me out of here. I told you I had heart trouble. My heart’s starting to bother me now. I refuse to go on. Let me out.”

If the participant expressed reluctance or hesitation at any time, the researcher gave one of four directions, in this order: “Please continue”; “The research requires that you continue”; “It is absolutely essential that you continue”; and “You have no other choice, you must continue.” The researcher assessed whether the participants continued to administer shocks after receiving each direction. The base condition ended when the participant refused to continue or agreed to continue at the shock level just past 150 volts.

In the modeled refusal condition, the procedures were the same as the base condition except for an additional confederate who was paired with each participant. The men were paired with a White man in his 50s. Women were paired with a White woman in her late 20s. The researcher pretended to randomly choose the participant to be Teacher 2 and the additional confederate to be Teacher 1. Teacher 1 administered shocks to the “learner” according to the procedures as the participant watched. At the 90-volt shock level, Teacher 1 said to the researcher, “I don’t know about this.” The researcher responded with “Please continue.” Teacher 1 paused and then said, “I don’t think I can do this,” and pushed their chair from the table. The researcher then asked Teacher 2 (the participant) to continue the test, picking up where Teacher 1 left off.

As with the base condition, if the participant (Teacher 2) expressed reluctance or hesitation, the researcher gave one of the four directions as described. The researcher assessed whether the participants continued to administer shocks after receiving each direction. The modeled refusal condition also ended when the participant refused to continue or agreed to continue at the shock level just past 150 volts.

When the study was over, the researcher explained informed participants of the true purpose of the study after the study was complete, specifically that the “learner” was not receiving electric shocks. The “learner” entered the lab room at that point to assure the participant that they were fine.

As Bellah was moving away from home and starting college, she experienced some difficulties with adjusting to her new environment and schedule. Which of the following best describes why Bellah would describe her difficulties as eustress instead of distress?

o.l: Bellah’s genetic heritage would make her more predisposed to interpreting stress as eustress instead of distressed.
Bellah’s family taught her norms about stress that lead to her have positive expectations about stress as a young adult.
Bellah’s in a developmental stage that causes her to view stress with a positive attitude.
Bellah is experiencing delusional thinking about stress.

The stimulus explicitly states that Bellah's family taught her that maintaining a positive attitude about stress is always better, establishing a learned framework for interpreting challenges. This socialization process created norms and expectations that would lead Bellah to view her college adjustment difficulties as opportunities for growth rather than threats. Kendall learned in AP Psychology class about the tend-and-befriend theory, in which some people react to stress by tending to their own needs and/or the needs of others and seeking connection with others. Upon hearing that this theory seems mostly to describe the behavior of women instead of men, Kendall remarked to the class that he knew that would be the case all along.

Which of the following cognitive biases is Kendall demonstrating?
q.ex: Hindsight bias is the tendency to believe, after learning an outcome, that one would have predicted or known it all along. In this scenario, Kendall claims he "knew that would be the case all along" only after being told that the tend-and-befriend theory primarily describes women's behavior. This is a classic example of hindsight bias because Kendall is retrospectively claiming he predicted this gender difference, even though he had no way of knowing it before the information was presented. q.s: Which of the following best describes a situation where an individual’s perceptions influence their experience of stress?

o.l: Rutger experiences the physical and emotional symptoms associated with generalized anxiety disorder.
Jamie interprets experiences like getting stuck in traffic or her phone battery getting low as bothersome daily hassles.
Bane learned that women experience stress differently than men.
Micah copes with stress by focusing on how to manage their emotional reactions.

q.ex: The question asks about how individual perceptions influence the experience of stress. Stress is fundamentally a subjective experience that depends on how a person interprets and appraises events rather than the objective nature of the events themselves. Jamie's situation demonstrates this cognitive appraisal process, where she personally interprets relatively minor inconveniences like traffic or low phone battery as bothersome hassles. These events are not inherently stressful; they become stressful through Jamie's perception and interpretation of them. Option i2 is correct because it directly illustrates how an individual's subjective perception transforms neutral or minor events into stress-inducing experiences.

q.ex: Stress and anxiety are distinct psychological states that share overlapping symptoms but differ in their nature and duration. According to the table, both conditions can produce the same physical symptoms (headaches, body pain, high blood pressure, sleep loss) and cognitive symptoms (excessive worry, uneasiness, tension). However, stress is situational and resolves when the triggering situation ends, while anxiety is persistent and continues even without an immediate threat. The key distinction is that stress is tied to specific circumstances and can be positive or negative, whereas anxiety involves constant apprehension that interferes with daily life regardless of external stressors. Dr. Taneesha is interested in water intake as an indication of healthy behaviors. She randomly selected ten individuals at a mall and asked, “On average, how many glasses of water do you drink each day?” The data set her interviews produced are as follows: 6, 5, 2, 0, 0, 3, 0, 8, 4, 1.

What is the mode of the data set?
q.ex: The mode is the value that appears most frequently in a data set. In the given data set (6, 5, 2, 0, 0, 3, 0, 8, 4, 1), the value 0 appears three times, which is more than any other value. The value 2.9 represents the mean (average), and 3.5 would be the median (middle value when ordered), but neither of these is the mode. The value 8 is simply the maximum value in the set. Therefore, 0 is correct because it is the most frequently occurring value in the data set.

q.s: Which of the following may explain why some people experience growth after a traumatic experience?

o.l: Some people are genetically predisposed to interpret stress as eustress instead of distress.
Some cultures may encourage people to interpret stress as a challenge rather than an obstacle.
Some people have evolved to interpret trauma as opportunities for growth.
Some people will comply with authority figures who demand they view trauma as a growth opportunity.

q.ex: Post-traumatic growth refers to positive psychological change that can occur following highly stressful or traumatic events. Cultural factors play a significant role in how individuals interpret and respond to traumatic experiences. Cultures that emphasize resilience, meaning-making, and viewing challenges as opportunities for personal development can shape how their members cognitively appraise and process trauma. This cultural framing provides individuals with interpretive frameworks and coping strategies that facilitate finding meaning and growth in adversity. The correct answer is that some cultures may encourage people to interpret stress as a challenge rather than an obstacle because cultural values and beliefs directly influence cognitive appraisal processes and coping mechanisms following trauma.

During his Psychology of Well-Being course in college, Jacob learns about research that suggests regularly expressing gratitude toward others can increase subjective well-being. Based on this life experience, Jacob believes the outcome of this research is obvious, and everyone would intuitively recognize the value of gratitude.

Which cognitive bias does Jacob’s thinking represent?
q.ex: Jacob's thinking demonstrates hindsight bias, which occurs when people believe an outcome was predictable or obvious after learning about it, even though they would not have predicted it beforehand. After learning the research findings about gratitude and well-being, Jacob now thinks the results are obvious and that everyone would intuitively recognize this connection. This is the classic "I knew it all along" phenomenon where knowledge of an outcome makes it seem inevitable or self-evident in retrospect. Jacob is failing to recognize that before learning about this research, the relationship between gratitude and well-being might not have been obvious at all. q.s: Dr. Tonya surveyed 100 people, measured their height in inches, and asked whether they practiced gratitude. After analyzing the data, she claims that height causes people to be less grateful. Which of the following is a limitation of the study?

o.l: The dependent variable was not manipulated.
The independent variable was not manipulated.
The results are correlational, not causational.
The laboratory setting of the situation does not reflect the “real world.”

q.ex: Dr. Tonya conducted a survey study where she measured existing characteristics (height and gratitude practices) without manipulating any variables. In correlational research, researchers observe relationships between variables as they naturally occur, but cannot establish causation because there is no experimental manipulation or control over confounding variables. Since Dr. Tonya simply measured height and gratitude without randomly assigning participants to different conditions or manipulating either variable, she can only identify a correlation between height and gratitude. Making a causal claim that "height causes people to be less grateful" exceeds what the correlational data can support. q.s:
A team of psychologists created two well-being training programs for the U.S. military to help soldiers with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Soldiers were given two surveys before and after the well-being training programs were implemented that measured a variety of variables, including demographics, feelings of gratitude, and thoughts of suicide.

What variable relationships would researchers examine to determine if these well-being training programs were successful?

o.l: A positive correlation between gratitude and rates of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
How much rates of PTSD and suicide declined among those in the military.
Soldiers in well-being training were less likely to be promoted to higher ranks.
Self-harm rates would increase only for those with PTSD.

q.ex: To determine if the well-being training programs were successful, researchers would need to examine whether the targeted negative outcomes decreased after the intervention was implemented. The study used a pre-post design, measuring variables before and after the training programs, which allows researchers to assess changes over time. Since the programs were designed to help soldiers with PTSD, success would be indicated by reductions in PTSD symptoms and related harmful outcomes like suicidal thoughts. Option i2 correctly identifies that researchers would examine declines in PTSD rates and suicide among military personnel, which directly measures whether the intervention achieved its intended therapeutic goals.

q.s: A classmate reading Dr. Kebede’s study disregards the results and states “this really isn’t even an experiment.” Which of the following supports the fact that Dr. Kebede’s study is an experiment?

o.l: There are two variables in the study; the gratitude and the thankfulness.
The study would be published in a peer-reviewed journal.
Dr. Kebede included random assignment to groups in the study.
The study was conducted over three months.

f.c:
Dr. Kebede believes that as people express gratitude more frequently, their subjective well-being will increase. To test this, Dr. Kebede conducts a study in which participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. In both groups, participants are asked to record their sense of well-being by keeping a weekly journal and responding to the prompt: “All things considered, how satisfied are you with your life as a whole these days?”

In the first group, the participants were required to set a goal to express gratitude and thankfulness through daily affirmations or to others throughout the day. The participants in the second group are not tasked with expressing gratitude but are still asked to keep the weekly journal. After three months, Dr. Kebede collects the journals and reads the responses.

q.ex:
An experiment is defined by the researcher's manipulation of an independent variable and random assignment of participants to conditions. Random assignment is the key feature that distinguishes a true experiment from other research designs like correlational studies or quasi-experiments. It allows researchers to control for confounding variables and establish cause-and-effect relationships between variables. The presence of random assignment to groups is what makes Dr. Kebede's study a true experiment rather than another type of research design.

The correct choice is i3 because random assignment to groups is the defining characteristic of experimental research that separates it from non-experimental designs.

q.s: In this study, what is the independent variable?

o.l: The participant response to the journal prompt
The wording of the journal prompt

f.c:
Dr. Kebede believes that as people express gratitude more frequently, their subjective well-being will increase. To test this, Dr. Kebede conducts a study in which participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. In both groups, participants are asked to record their sense of well-being by keeping a weekly journal and responding to the prompt: “All things considered, how satisfied are you with your life as a whole these days?”

In the first group, the participants were required to set a goal to express gratitude and thankfulness through daily affirmations or to others throughout the day. The participants in the second group are not tasked with expressing gratitude but are still asked to keep the weekly journal. After three months, Dr. Kebede collects the journals and reads the responses.

q.ex: The independent variable is the factor that researchers deliberately manipulate or control in an experiment to observe its effect on the dependent variable. In this study, researchers are manipulating whether participants express gratitude or not, making this the independent variable. The expression of gratitude is what the experimenters are changing between conditions to measure its impact on outcomes like well-being. The wording of the journal prompt is merely the method used to manipulate gratitude expression, while participant responses and well-being scores are measured outcomes, not manipulated factors. The correct answer is the expression of gratitude because it is what researchers are systematically varying to test its effects.

q.s: Dr. Kebede read through all of the journal responses submitted by the participants in both groups and concluded that expressing gratitude does indeed increase subjective well-being. Which of the following cognitive biases is most likely to affect Dr. Kebede’s interpretation of the journals?

f.c:
Dr. Kebede believes that as people express gratitude more frequently, their subjective well-being will increase. To test this, Dr. Kebede conducts a study in which participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. In both groups, participants are asked to record their sense of well-being by keeping a weekly journal and responding to the prompt: “All things considered, how satisfied are you with your life as a whole these days?”

In the first group, the participants were required to set a goal to express gratitude and thankfulness through daily affirmations or to others throughout the day. The participants in the second group are not tasked with expressing gratitude but are still asked to keep the weekly journal. After three months, Dr. Kebede collects the journals and reads the responses.

q.ex: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in a way that confirms one's preexisting beliefs or hypotheses. In this scenario, Dr. Kebede appears to have already formed a conclusion that expressing gratitude increases subjective well-being before systematically analyzing the data. When reading through journal responses, this preexisting belief could lead Dr. Kebede to selectively notice and emphasize entries that support the hypothesis while overlooking or downplaying contradictory evidence. This bias is particularly problematic in qualitative research where interpretation of written responses involves subjective judgment. Confirmation bias is the correct answer because it directly describes the cognitive

q.s:
Dr. Ake developed a measure that asked people about how much they agreed with several statements about their subjective well-being. The participants had to choose a number between 1 and 5, with 1 meaning they strongly disagreed and 5 meaning they strongly agreed. Those who chose the number 3 were indicating that they were neutral about the statement.

Which of the following identifies the type of measurement tool Dr. Ake used?
q.ex: A Likert scale is a psychometric measurement tool that asks respondents to indicate their level of agreement or disagreement with statements using a fixed range of response options, typically numbered from 1 to 5 or 1 to 7. In this scenario, Dr. Ake's measure uses a 1-5 scale where participants rate their agreement with statements about subjective well-being, with 1 representing strong disagreement, 5 representing strong agreement, and 3 representing neutrality. This structure precisely matches the definition of a Likert scale, which is commonly used in psychological research to measure attitudes, opinions, and perceptions. The

q.s:
Liu is a Chinese exchange student studying in the United States. She is feeling lonely and may have depression. She goes to a psychologist to report her symptoms. The major symptom Liu reports to the psychologist is that she has been feeling much back pain lately, a common symptom of depression in China. Because the psychologist does not see this as a symptom of depression, he refers her to a physical therapist.

Which of the following may influence the decision of the psychiatrist?
q.ex: The psychologist's decision was likely influenced by confirmation bias, which is the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information in a way that confirms one's preexisting beliefs or hypotheses. The psychologist held a preexisting belief about what constitutes depression symptoms based on Western clinical presentations, which typically emphasize psychological and emotional symptoms rather than physical ones like back pain. When Liu presented with back pain as her primary complaint, the psychologist interpreted this information through his existing framework and dismissed it as unrelated to depression, confirming his belief that depression does not manifest as back pain. This led him to refer her to a physical therapist rather than recognizing that depression can manifest differently

q.s:
Several different employers were sent resumes of potential employees. The resumes were sent to the employers in pairs. Both candidates were equally qualified, but in each pair, one applicant described mental health problems as an explanation for the reason they left their previous job. The results showed that applicants reporting mental health problems had a 27% lower probability of getting an interview.

Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the results of this study?

o.l: Employers overuse the availability heuristic in the hiring process.
There is cultural stigma around mental health problems that make employers less likely to hire those afflicted.
Ageism persists in the workplace and often leads to discriminatory hiring practices.
Employers tend to make decisions based on the central route to persuasion, and the information provided was more aligned to the peripheral route to persuasion.

q.ex: Cultural stigma refers to negative attitudes, beliefs, and stereotypes that society holds about certain groups or conditions, leading to discrimination and prejudice. In this study, the only difference between paired resumes was the disclosure of mental health problems, yet those candidates had significantly lower interview rates. This demonstrates that employers held biased attitudes specifically against applicants with mental health histories, regardless of equal qualifications. The availability heuristic, ageism, and persuasion routes do not explain why mental health disclosure alone would reduce interview probability by 27%. The correct answer is option i2 because the systematic discrimination against equally qualified candidates based solely on mental health disclosure directly demonstrates the existence and impact of

q.s: When describing how psychological problems evolve, which of the following is a strength of the biopsychosocial model?

o.l: The model emphasizes the belief that psychological problems are caused by genetics.
The model supports the humanistic view that disorders stem from a lack of unconditional positive regard.
The model adheres to the behaviorist view that psychological problems result exclusively from classical and operant conditioning.
The model considers, in addition to other factors, the role that cultural norms and expectations play in the development of psychological problems.

q.ex: The biopsychosocial model is a comprehensive framework that integrates biological, psychological, and social factors in understanding health and illness. Unlike reductionist approaches that focus on single causes, this model recognizes that psychological problems arise from complex interactions among genetic predispositions, individual psychological processes, and social-cultural contexts. The strength of this model lies in its holistic perspective, which includes consideration of cultural norms, social support systems, environmental stressors, and societal expectations alongside biological and psychological factors. Options i1, i2, and i3 each describe single-factor explanations that contradict the integrative nature of the biopsychosocial approach

q.s: Dr. Brennan is interested in investigating the negative and positive consequences of diagnosing his female patients with bipolar disorder. To ensure that ethical procedures are followed, what must Dr. Brennan do prior to beginning the research study?

o.l: Ensure that a random sample of subjects is selected
Receive informed consent from each of the participants
Assign subjects randomly to control and experimental groups

q.ex: Ethical research procedures require that participants understand what they are agreeing to participate in and voluntarily consent to take part in the study. Before beginning any research involving human subjects, researchers must obtain informed consent, which means participants must be told about the nature of the study, potential risks and benefits, and their right to withdraw at any time. This ethical requirement protects participants' autonomy and ensures they are not subjected to research procedures without their knowledge and agreement. While random sampling, controlling confounding variables, and random assignment are important methodological considerations for research design, they are not ethical requirements that must be completed before beginning a study. Receiving informed consent from each participant is the correct answer because it

q.s: Dr. Neal is conducting research on the impact of genetics on anxiety disorders. Which of the following reflects appropriate attention to ethical procedures?

o.l: Dr. Neal publishes the results of the research and although names of the subjects are included in the article, the address and phone number are not printed.

Dr. Neal meets with each of the subjects individually after the conclusion of the study to share and explain the results, answer questions, and make certain the subjects feel positive about participation in the study.

If Dr. Neal tells the subjects that he is researching genetic physical properties such as hair and eye color to not make subjects anxious about being included in an anxiety study, he would not have to debrief them.
Dr. Neal tries to minimize the paperwork and hassle for each participant by not requiring informed consent prior to the beginning of the study.

q.ex: Ethical research procedures require informed consent, confidentiality, and debriefing. Option i2 demonstrates proper debriefing, where the researcher meets with participants after the study to explain results, answer questions, and ensure their well-being. Option i1 violates confidentiality by publishing participants' names. Option i3 involves deception without proper debriefing, which is unethical. Option i4 eliminates informed consent, a fundamental ethical requirement that ensures participants understand and voluntarily agree to participate in research. Option i2 is correct because debriefing is an essential ethical procedure that helps participants understand the study's purpose and ensures they

q.s:
A psychologist is devising a research study to test the diathesis-stress model. She gathers a list of interested subjects who have one or more members of their family who have been diagnosed with schizophrenia. She randomly assigns the subjects to one of two groups and identifies them with a code number to maintain confidentiality. The experimental group will be subjected to a series of stress-inducing situations while the control group will be allowed to read books, engage in quiet conversation, and relax. The psychologist then proposes to follow the subjects for six years.

Which of the following is most likely of concern for an IRB to consider whether the psychologist followed appropriate ethical procedures?

o.l: By proposing to follow the subjects for six years, the psychologist is violating their privacy and confidentiality.
By gathering a list of participants that share a family diagnosis of schizophrenia, the psychologist is disregarding the research procedure of random sampling.
By subjecting participants in the experimental group to stress-inducing situations, this study may not protect participants from harm.
By only taking interested subjects into the experiment, the sample may reflect a bias that confound the results.

q.ex: The primary ethical concern for an Institutional Review Board (IRB) is the protection of research participants from physical and psychological harm. In this study, the experimental group is deliberately exposed to stress-inducing situations, which could potentially trigger or exacerbate mental health issues, particularly given that participants have a genetic predisposition to schizophrenia. The diathesis-stress model itself suggests that stress can activate underlying vulnerabilities, making this intervention especially risky for this population. While the other options raise methodological concerns or misunderstand research procedures, only option i3 addresses a fundamental ethical principle that IRBs are charged with evaluating: whether the potential harm to

q.s: Dr. Jamal is designing research to study narcissistic personality disorder. Which of the following should Dr. Jamal make certain to do to adhere to ethical research guidelines?

o.l: Read the existing research to make sure no other researcher has conducted this type of study.
Discuss the study with other researchers in the field.
Obtain informed consent from the participants prior to conducting the study.
Locate and reserve lab space, hire assistants and order any necessary equipment.

q.ex:
Ethical research guidelines in psychology require that researchers protect the rights and welfare of participants. The most fundamental ethical requirement is obtaining informed consent, which means participants must be fully informed about the nature of the study, any potential risks, and their right to withdraw at any time before agreeing to participate. This principle is codified in professional ethics codes such as the APA Ethics Code and is required by institutional review boards. While reading existing research, discussing with colleagues, and preparing lab resources are important aspects of good research practice, they are not ethical requirements in the same way that informed consent is mandatory for protecting human subjects.

The correct choice is i3 because obtaining informed consent is a non-negoti

q.s:
Dr. Mizrahi is designing a study to test whether antidepressants are more effective than placebos. Using electronic medical records, Dr. Mizrahi gathers a random sample of his patients who display a set of symptoms typically associated with major depressive disorder. He randomly assigns participants to receive an antidepressant medication or a placebo as a substitute for their daily multivitamin. Neither the participants nor Dr. Mizrahi know who is in which group.

Which of the following should be of concern when trying to evaluate whether Dr. Mizrahi adhered to established ethical research guidelines?

o.l: Dr. Mizrahi did not get informed consent from his patients.
Since a double-blind procedure was used, it is of ethical concern that Dr. Mizrahi does not know which group is getting the placebo.
Although there is debate about the use of deception in placebo studies, it is an ethical concern that deception was used in this case.
By limiting his sample to only diagnosed patients, Dr. Mizrahi will be unable to generalize the results of the study.

q.ex: The most critical ethical violation in this study is the absence of informed consent. Established ethical research guidelines, such as those outlined in the Belmont Report and enforced by institutional review boards, require that participants voluntarily agree to participate in research after being fully informed about the study's procedures, risks, and benefits. Dr. Mizrahi substituted participants' daily multivitamins with either antidepressants or placebos without their knowledge or permission, which constitutes a serious breach of autonomy and informed consent requirements. While the study involves deception through placebo use, such deception can be ethically justified in certain research contexts if participants provide informed consent an

q.s: Which of the following disorders is the infographic describing?

f.c:
Signs & Symptoms

q.ex: The infographic describes schizophrenia spectrum disorders, which are characterized by disturbances in thought processes, perceptions, emotional responsiveness, and social interactions. Key diagnostic features include positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, negative symptoms like flat affect and social withdrawal, and cognitive impairments affecting memory and executive function. These disorders typically involve a break from reality and disorganized thinking that distinguishes them from mood disorders like depression, fear-based anxiety disorders, or dissociative disorders that primarily involve disruptions in consciousness and identity. The correct answer is schizophrenia spectrum disorders because the infographic evidently presents symptoms and characteristics that align with psychotic features

q.s: How might a psychologist using the sociocultural perspective differ from a psychologist of the biological perspective in explaining the causes of the symptoms listed in the infographic above?

o.l: A sociocultural psychologist would look to environmental factors while a biological psychologist would consider genetics and chemical imbalances in the brain.

A sociocultural psychologist would look to unconscious thoughts and experiences developed during childhood while a biological psychologist would look to physical characteristics such as eye color, height and weight.
A sociocultural psychologist would investigate where individuals showing symptoms fall on the introversion/extroversion scale, while a biological psychologist would use projective tests.

A sociocultural psychologist would evaluate which maladaptive thoughts, beliefs, attitudes, or emotions are present in the individual and the biological psychologist would focus on maladaptive learned associations between stimuli.

f.c:
Signs & Symptoms

NOTE: Anhedonia is the inability to enjoy oneself. Avolition is lack of motivation.

q.ex: The sociocultural perspective in psychology examines how social and cultural environments, including factors like family dynamics, socioeconomic status, cultural norms, and social relationships, influence behavior and mental processes. In contrast, the biological perspective focuses on physiological and genetic factors, such as brain chemistry, neurotransmitter levels, hormones, and inherited genetic predispositions. When explaining psychological symptoms, a sociocultural psychologist would investigate environmental and social influences on the individual, while a biological psychologist would examine physical and genetic causes like chemical imbalances or hereditary factors. Option i1 is correct because it accurately distinguishes between these two perspectives: sociocultural psych

q.s: If a researcher wanted to do an experiment to examine if a biological treatment was successful for addressing the positive symptoms, which of the following might be an important ethical consideration?

o.l: The control group would lead the debriefing after the study.
Individuals in the study would be randomly assigned to the control group.
The control group would receive the biological treatment.
The participants might not be able to give consent.

f.c:
Signs & Symptoms

NOTE: Anhedonia is the inability to enjoy oneself. Avolition is lack of motivation.

q.ex: The most important ethical consideration when studying biological treatments for positive symptoms (typically referring to symptoms like hallucinations and delusions in schizophrenia) is whether participants can provide informed consent. Positive symptoms often involve severe disruptions in thinking, perception, and reality testing that may impair a person's cognitive capacity to understand the nature, risks, and benefits of participating in research. Ethical research requires that participants have the mental capacity to comprehend what they are consenting to and can make voluntary, informed decisions about their participation. When working with populations experiencing severe psychiatric symptoms, researchers must carefully assess decision-making capacity and may need to involve legal guardians or use additional safeguards to

q.s: Dr. Castro is interested in investigating the effectiveness of behavioral therapy on the fear of spiders. Without telling the participants, she puts each of them in a room filled with cages of spiders. Which ethical guideline did Dr. Castro violate?
q.ex: Informed consent requires researchers to inform participants about the nature of the study, including any procedures, risks, and discomforts they may experience, before they agree to participate. Dr. Castro violated this principle by placing participants in a room with spiders without telling them beforehand. Participants have the right to know what they are agreeing to in a study, especially when it involves exposure to potentially distressing stimuli like their phobic object. By not disclosing this information in advance, Dr. Castro denied participants the opportunity to make an informed decision about whether to participate. Informed consent is the correct answer because it specifically addresses the requirement that participants must be fully informed about study procedures

q.s: Which of the following ethical principles for therapists is most like the research ethical principle of “do no harm”?
q.ex:
Nonmaleficence is the ethical principle that directly corresponds to "do no harm" in both therapeutic and research contexts. The term nonmaleficence literally means "not doing harm" and requires professionals to avoid actions that cause injury or damage to clients or research participants. This principle obligates therapists to refrain from practices that could physically or psychologically harm their clients, just as researchers must ensure their studies do not harm participants. While fidelity relates to trustworthiness, integrity to honesty, and respect for dignity to autonomy, only nonmaleficence explicitly embodies the core mandate to prevent harm.

The correct choice is nonmaleficence

q.s: Sports psychologists are studying the use of rational-emotive behavior therapy on the understanding and promotion of mental health in athletes. Once they have received informed consent, the researchers split the athletes into two groups. The experimental group was shown a series of videos in which athletes were injured and then were given rational-emotive behavior therapy to discuss what they viewed. The control group did not watch any videos and received conventional positive thinking training. Which of the following would most likely be of most concern for the IRB reviewing this study?

o.l: The researchers should have made the participants in the control group watch the injury videos.
The researchers are likely exposing the participants to harm by showing videos of injuries.
The researchers deceived the participants by not telling the control group about the videos.
The researchers should have randomly assigned participants to groups.

q.ex: An Institutional Review Board (IRB) is primarily concerned with protecting research participants from physical and psychological harm. In this study, showing athletes videos of injuries could cause psychological distress, anxiety, or trauma, particularly since athletes may identify strongly with the injured individuals in the videos. The IRB would need to evaluate whether the potential benefits of the research justify exposing participants to potentially disturbing content and whether adequate safeguards are in place to minimize harm. While random assignment and other methodological concerns are important for research quality, the IRB's primary mandate is participant safety, making potential exposure to harm through injury videos the most pressing ethical concern. The correct choice is i2 because protecting participants

Having a patient create a hierarchy like the one presented above is most consistent with which therapeutic technique?
q.ex: Systematic desensitization is a behavioral therapy technique developed by Joseph Wolpe that treats anxiety disorders by gradually exposing patients to feared stimuli while they remain relaxed. A core component of this technique is creating an anxiety hierarchy, which is a ranked list of anxiety-provoking situations ordered from least to most distressing, typically using a scale like SUDS (Subjective Units of Distress Scale). The hierarchy shown in the stimulus is exactly this type of tool, with situations ranked from 40 to 95 based on their distress level. This allows the therapist to systematically work through the hierarchy with the patient, starting with lower-anxiety situations

q.s: Which of the following concepts does this conversation illustrate?

f.c:
Four-year-old Ethan and his mother have the following conversation:

MOTHER: Ethan, do you have a brother?
ETHAN: Yes.
MOTHER: What’s his name?
ETHAN: My brother’s name is Anthony.
MOTHER: Does Anthony have a brother?
ETHAN: No.

q.ex: Egocentrism is the inability to distinguish between one's own perspective and someone else's perspective, a characteristic of Piaget's preoperational stage of cognitive development. In this developmental phase, children assume that others see, hear, and feel exactly the same way they do. The conversation demonstrates egocentrism because the child is unable to take another person's point of view or understand that others may have different thoughts or perceptions than their own. This differs from conservation (understanding quantity remains constant despite changes in appearance), animism (attributing life to inanimate objects), and object permanence (knowing objects exist even when not visible). The correct answer is ego

q.s: Betty was just diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Which of the following effects is she most likely to experience?

o.l: The neurons in her body will not be able to reach threshold, leading to fatigue.
Depolarization in her neurons will not occur, causing sensory impairment.
Neurotransmitters will remain in the synapse for an extended period, causing memory loss.
Neural messages will travel slowly down the axon, leading to motor impairment.

q.ex: Multiple sclerosis is a disease that damages the myelin sheath, the fatty insulation that surrounds and protects axons in the nervous system. The myelin sheath is essential for saltatory conduction, which allows action potentials to jump quickly between nodes of Ranvier along the axon. When myelin is damaged or destroyed, neural signals must travel more slowly down the axon because they can no longer jump efficiently from node to node. This slowed neural transmission particularly affects motor function, leading to symptoms like muscle weakness, coordination problems, and difficulty with movement. Option D is correct because it accurately describes how demyelination in multiple sclerosis causes slowed neural

q.s: Which of the following best describes the type of measurement instrument that Dr. Maryam is using?

f.c: Dr. Maryam is investigating the ability of patients to recover brain function after a stroke. Dr. Maryam asks patients who had a stroke and volunteered for this study a series of specific open-ended questions and records their responses.

q.ex: Without the full context of what Dr. Maryam is measuring, the correct answer indicates she is using a qualitative measurement instrument. Qualitative measurement involves collecting non-numerical data such as observations, interviews, open-ended responses, or descriptive information to understand experiences, behaviors, or phenomena in depth. This contrasts with quantitative measurement, which involves numerical data and statistical analysis. Personality inventories and fMRI are specific types of instruments that typically produce quantitative data through numerical scores or brain imaging measurements. The correct answer is qualitative because Dr. Maryam's instrument collects descriptive, non-numerical data rather than numerical measurements.

q.s: Dr. Sperry records a video of Jim, a participant in split-brain research, and then plays it in class to teach students about hemispheric differences. Which of the following procedures should Dr. Sperry use to show the video in class?

o.l: Obtain Jim’s permission to use the video.
Debrief Jim after the research session.
Demonstrate the educational value of the video to Jim.

q.ex: Dr. Sperry must obtain Jim's permission to use the video in class because informed consent is a fundamental ethical principle in psychological research and practice. While Jim likely consented to participate in the research study itself, using his video for educational purposes beyond the original research constitutes a separate use that requires additional explicit consent. The American Psychological Association's ethical guidelines require psychologists to obtain informed consent before using identifiable information or recordings for purposes not originally agreed upon. Simply using a first name, debriefing, or explaining educational value does not satisfy the ethical requirement for explicit permission to share identifiable recordings with students.

q.s: Which of the following principles underlies Simon’s strategy?

f.c: When Simon opens a new coffee shop, he offers to give each customer a free cup of coffee on their birthday. He hopes this will make people more likely to buy coffee at his shop in the future.

q.ex: The social reciprocity norm is a fundamental principle of social psychology stating that people feel obligated to return favors or concessions made by others. When someone does something for us or makes a concession, we experience psychological pressure to reciprocate with a similar gesture. Simon's strategy likely involves making an initial concession or offer that creates a sense of obligation in the other person to respond in kind. This differs from door-in-the-face, which specifically involves making an extreme request first to make a smaller request seem reasonable, and from groupthink or conformity, which involve group dynamics rather than reciprocal exchanges. The correct answer is the social reciprocity norm because

q.s: Markum reads online articles to assess the advantages and disadvantages of several universities and uses this information to decide where to attend. Which of the following brain regions is Markum primarily using as he decides which university to attend?
q.ex: The frontal lobe, particularly the prefrontal cortex, is responsible for higher-order cognitive functions including decision-making, planning, reasoning, and weighing consequences. When Markum evaluates information about different universities by assessing advantages and disadvantages, he is engaging in executive functions that require deliberate analysis and judgment. The temporal lobe is primarily involved in memory and auditory processing, the parasympathetic nervous system controls rest and digest responses, and the medulla regulates automatic functions like breathing and heart rate. The frontal lobe is correct because it is the brain region specifically responsible for the complex decision-making process Markum is undertaking.

q.s: Which of the following principles best explains the assumption of Justine’s new classmates?

f.c: Justine transferred to a new school where she does not know anyone. She does not talk to others and sits by herself at lunch. Her classmates assume she is arrogant and rude.

q.ex: The fundamental attribution error occurs when people overemphasize personality-based explanations for others' behaviors while underestimating the influence of situational factors. When Justine's new classmates make assumptions about her, they are likely attributing her behavior to her internal characteristics or personality rather than considering external circumstances that might be affecting her actions. This tendency to judge others based on dispositional factors while ignoring contextual influences is the defining feature of the fundamental attribution error. The correct answer is fundamental attribution error because it specifically describes how people make incorrect assumptions about others by focusing on personality traits rather than situational factors.

q.s:
Using the source provided, respond to all parts of the question.

 
 

Your response to the question should be provided in six parts: A, B, C, D, E, and F. Write the response to each part of the question in complete sentences. Use appropriate psychological terminology in your response.

A. Identify the research method used in the study.

f.c:
Introduction

Researchers performed a study to determine if cell phone calls that interrupt in-person interactions between a mother and her child affect how well the child learns vocabulary words.

Participants

This study comprised 38 pairs of participants. Each pair comprised a mother and her two-year-old child. The average age of the mothers was 35.26 years (age range = 29.53 to 47.10 years; 19 mothers did not report their age). All the two-year-old children were developing along standard physical, social, and emotional timelines. The average age of the children was 27.05 months (2.25 years), and an equal number of boys and girls participated. All mother-child pairs lived in suburban communities surrounding the same major East Coast United States city; 90.9% of families self-identified as white while the remaining 9.10% self-identified as Hispanic, Pacific Islander, African American, or multiethnic.1 Mothers agreed to be in the study and knew they could withdraw from participation at any time. Researchers ensured that the individual participants could not be identified from the data collected.

Method

At the beginning of the study, mothers and their children were placed in separate rooms. The children played in a supervised, child-friendly room. Meanwhile, in a separate room, the researchers trained the mothers regarding the meaning of two completely new words: blicking (meaning a type of bouncing) and frepping (meaning a type of shaking). The researchers made up these words and their meanings for the purpose of this study. To demonstrate blicking to their child, each mother was provided an 18-inch gender-neutral2 doll. To demonstrate frepping to their child, each mother could shake a 6-inch rattle. 

After providing each mother with a phone, which had been set to vibrate mode, the researchers trained each mother on how to answer the phone. The researchers told each mother to expect occasional phone calls during the study. During each call, the researchers provided one of three directions to the mother: 1) begin teaching the new word (teaching phase), 2) move to the next word (transition phase), or 3) engage in a conversation with the researcher as if talking with a friend (interruption phase). 

To initiate the teaching phase, the researchers called each mother and told her to teach the designated word to her child. Half of the mothers were told to teach blicking first while the other half were told to teach frepping first. The researchers interrupted half of the mothers while the mothers taught their first word and then interrupted the second half of the mothers while the mothers taught their second word. For the uninterrupted teaching phase, each mother received a transition call from a researcher that instructed her to start teaching the identified word. The mother then had 60 seconds to teach the word to her child. 

Figure 1 and Figure 2 depict the research design for the teaching phase, the transition phase, and the interruption phase. 

Figure 1: Teaching Sequence in Interruption-First Condition

  • The teaching time for Word 1 and Word 2 and interruption call times are shown as follows:
    • Word 1 (30 seconds)
    • Interruption Call (30 seconds)
    • Word 1 (30 seconds)
    • Transition Call (5–7 seconds)
    • Word 2 (60 seconds)

 

Figure 2: Teaching Sequence in Interruption-Second Condition

  • The teaching time for Word 1 and Word 2 and interruption call times are shown as follows:
    • Word 1 (60 seconds)
    • Transition Call (5–7 seconds)
    • Word 2 (30 seconds)
    • Interruption Call (30 seconds)
    • Word 2 (30 seconds)

For each interrupted teaching phase, the mother received a call after 30 seconds of teaching her child. During the interrupted teaching phase, the researchers and the mother talked about morning coffee routines for about 30 seconds. After about 30 seconds, the researchers instructed the mother to continue teaching her child the assigned word. Each mother had an additional 30 seconds to teach the word.

The researchers counted how many times the mothers used the words blicking or frepping during the instruction sessions.

After receiving instruction on blicking and frepping, each child sat in their mother’s lap and watched a video. The video began with an attention-getting image in the center of the screen (an image of a laughing baby) followed by the instruction to “Find [blicking or frepping].” The video then transitioned to a scene in which a puppet demonstrated the appropriate action for each word (bouncing for blicking and shaking for frepping) or demonstrated an unrelated action (twisting side to side or putting a hand on a box while standing up). Researchers measured how long the children paid attention to the action in the video to determine whether the children learned blicking or frepping. The mothers closed their eyes during the video to avoid accidentally cueing the children to pay attention to the correct action in the video. Researchers informed participants of the true purpose of the study after the study was complete.

Results and Discussion

On average, the mothers repeated the word approximately 24 times in the interrupted teaching phase and approximately 20 times in the uninterrupted teaching phase. The difference was not statistically significant. 

The children paid attention to the word they learned in the uninterrupted session for an average of 0.63 seconds and in the interrupted session for an average of 0.50 seconds. The difference in means was statistically significant, suggesting that in-person interruptions between parent and child can affect how well young children learn vocabulary words.

Reed. J., Hirsh-Pasek, K., & Golinkoff, R.M. (2017). Learning on hold: Cell phones sidetrack parent-child interactions. Developmental Psychology, 53(8): 1438–1436.

When someone forms a positive or negative general impression, that impression "radiates" to color perceptions of unrelated qualities. For example, if Harold possesses one notably positive trait that Hiroshi observes, Hiroshi may assume Harold has other positive qualities as well, or vice versa with negative traits. This cognitive bias causes people to make sweeping judgments about someone's character based on limited information or a single salient feature. The halo effect is the correct answer because it specifically explains how one aspect of a person shapes overall opinions about

It specifically tracks the rate at which information is forgotten as time passes from the moment of encoding. Option C directly tests this temporal decay by comparing memory retention at two different time intervals (15 minutes versus 60 minutes) after the same learning event. The other options examine different memory phenomena: elaborative versus maintenance rehearsal (encoding strategies), serial position effects (primacy and recency), and context-dependent memory. q.s: Which of the following concepts relates to Rowan’s schema in this scenario?

f.c:
When Rowan was six years old, his father took him to see a tennis match. Rowan enjoyed learning the rules of the game and watching the players hit the ball back and forth across the net with their tennis racquets. 

Five months later, Rowan’s aunt took him to a park to play pickleball, a game similar to tennis. He had a great afternoon learning to hit the ball back and forth with the pickleball paddle instead of a tennis racquet. That night, Rowan told his parents that he had a great time playing “tennis” with his aunt.

q.ex: In Piagetian cognitive development theory, assimilation refers to the process of incorporating new information into existing mental schemas without changing those schemas. When an individual encounters new experiences or information that fits within their current understanding, they assimilate that information by interpreting it through their existing cognitive framework. This contrasts with accommodation, where schemas must be modified to incorporate information that does not fit existing mental structures. Assimilation is the correct answer because it directly relates to how schemas process and integrate compatible new information while maintaining their current structure.

q.s: Which of the following concepts is most likely responsible for Declan’s change in opinion?

f.c: When Declan first meets his civics teacher, he thinks she is too loud and demanding. Over the following weeks, he grows to like that she is funny and sets high standards.

q.ex: The mere exposure effect is a psychological phenomenon where people develop a preference for things simply because they are familiar with them. Through repeated exposure to something or someone, individuals tend to develop increasingly positive attitudes toward that stimulus, even without any additional positive interactions or information. This effect explains why Declan's opinion changed over time as he became more familiar with whatever he was initially neutral or negative about. The mere exposure effect is distinct from other biases because it requires only repeated contact or exposure, not personal involvement in events (actor/observer bias), self-protective reasoning (self-serving bias), or beliefs about fairness and deservingness (just-world phenomenon). The correct answer is the mere exposure effect

q.s: Which of the following processes accounts for this change?

f.c: Moriah is in favor of community programs that encourage recycling. She joins an online social media group that supports recycling, and the members frequently discuss the importance of recycling. After Moriah is in the group for several months, her views have become even more favorable toward recycling than they were when she joined the group. Moriah also notes that the views of the rest of the group have become more strongly favorable toward recycling as well.

q.ex: Group polarization occurs when group discussion strengthens the initial inclinations of individual group members, causing the group's average position to become more extreme in the direction it was already leaning. When people with similar views discuss an issue, they tend to reinforce each other's opinions through shared arguments and social comparison, leading to more polarized positions than individuals held before the discussion. This process explains why a group's collective decision or attitude often becomes more extreme than the average of individual members' initial positions. The correct answer is group polarization because it specifically describes the phenomenon where group interaction intensifies and shifts attitudes in the direction the group was already inclined toward.

q.s: Keenan’s thinking is most clearly an example of which of the following concepts?

f.c: In his psychology class, Keenan was learning about the various ways people respond to and cope with stressful life events. While he believed that both men and women dealt with stress in the same way, his teacher explained that women are much more likely than men to reach out to friends to both give and receive support. Upon learning this, Keenan told a classmate this finding was totally predictable and obvious because women are typically more nurturing than men.

q.ex: Hindsight bias occurs when people believe, after learning an outcome, that they would have predicted or expected that outcome beforehand. This cognitive bias makes past events seem more predictable than they actually were at the time. Keenan's thinking demonstrates this pattern by claiming he "knew it all along" or could have foreseen something after it already happened. This is distinct from overconfidence, which involves excessive certainty in one's abilities or predictions before an outcome occurs, and from confirmation bias, which involves seeking information that supports existing beliefs. The correct answer is hindsight bias because Keenan is retrospectively claiming predictability after the fact.

The doctor's assessments specifically test the patient's ability to perform coordinated movements without visual guidance—touching the nose and walking with eyes closed both require awareness of body position and movement. While touch receptors play a role in kinesthesis, the doctor is primarily evaluating the patient's ability to sense body position and coordinate movement, which is the defining function of kinesthesis. Therefore, option C is correct because kinesthesis is the sensory system responsible for body awareness

Items in the middle of the list are most likely to be forgotten because they benefit from neither effect. q.ex: Defense mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies that operate according to Freud's psychodynamic theory to protect the ego from anxiety caused by conflicts between the id's impulses and the superego's moral standards. The ego serves as the mediator between these opposing forces and reality, and when threatened by unacceptable thoughts or feelings, it employs defense mechanisms like repression, denial, or projection to reduce psychological distress. Self-actualization relates to humanistic psychology, not psychodynamic theory, while latent learning is a cognitive concept and moratorium is an identity development term. q.s: After accidentally touching a hot pan with his hand, Benedict immediately withdraws his hand without thinking. Which of the following processes best describes this example of a spinal reflex arc?

o.l: The sensation of heat is sent to Benedict’s brain for processing. The brain then sends a message to the peripheral nervous system, causing him to remove his hand from the hot pan.
Benedict’s peripheral nervous system immediately detects the heat, processes the response, and causes Benedict to remove his hand from the hot pan. The central nervous system is not involved.
Benedict’s peripheral and central nervous systems work independently in this situation, with the peripheral nervous system moving his hand and the central nervous system perceiving the heat.
Sensory neurons in Benedict’s peripheral nervous system detect the heat and send a rapid signal to an interneuron in the spinal cord, which then directs a motor neuron to move his hand.

q.ex: A spinal reflex arc is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that bypasses the brain by processing the signal at the spinal cord level. In this pathway, sensory neurons detect the stimulus and transmit the signal to interneurons located in the spinal cord. The interneurons then immediately relay the signal to motor neurons, which trigger the muscle response. This three-neuron pathway allows for an extremely fast protective response because the signal does not need to travel to the brain for processing before action is taken. Option D correctly describes this sequence: sensory neurons detect heat, interneurons in the spinal cord process the signal, and motor neurons execute the withdrawal response.

q.s: Which of the following concepts was at work?

f.c: Josie was given a password by her teacher. To remember the password, she repeated it in her mind multiple times until she typed it into her login screen a few moments later.

q.ex: The phonological loop is a component of working memory that temporarily stores and rehearses verbal and acoustic information. It consists of two parts: a phonological store that holds sound-based information for a few seconds, and an articulatory rehearsal process that allows us to repeat information to keep it active in memory. This system is crucial for tasks involving verbal information, such as remembering phone numbers, following spoken instructions, or maintaining a conversation. The phonological loop was the concept at work because the scenario involved processing and temporarily holding verbal or sound-based information in working memory.

q.s: After years of watching their mother drive a car, Rowan knows how to start the car when sitting in the driver’s seat for the first time. Which of the following types of learning best explains how Rowan acquired this new behavior?
q.ex: Observational learning, also known as social learning or modeling, occurs when an individual acquires new behaviors by watching others perform them without direct reinforcement or practice. In this scenario, Rowan learned how to start a car simply by observing their mother drive over many years, not through personal trial and error or receiving rewards and punishments. This demonstrates the key principle of observational learning where knowledge is gained vicariously through observation rather than direct experience. The correct answer is observational learning because Rowan acquired the behavior of starting a car by watching their mother's actions repeatedly, which is the defining characteristic of this learning type.

q.s: Which of the following statements most accurately describes why this study is an experiment?

o.l: The researchers operationally defined the variables.
The participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups.
The sample was representative of the population being observed.

f.c:
Researchers at an advertising agency conducted a study to determine whether classical conditioning principles could influence consumers' preferences for a particular product. They randomly assigned 100 college students from a nearby university to one of two groups. 

Both groups watched a commercial for the same brand of shoes. One group watched a commercial that did not feature a celebrity endorsement, while the second group watched a commercial that featured a celebrity endorsement from a physically attractive celebrity. The participants were exposed to these ads multiple times a day for two weeks. 

At the end of the two weeks, the participants were asked to rate, on a scale of 1 to 10, how likely they were to purchase the brand of shoes advertised in the commercial they watched.

q.ex: An experiment is defined by the researcher's ability to manipulate an independent variable and control for extraneous variables, with random assignment being a key feature that distinguishes true experiments from other research methods. Random assignment means participants have an equal chance of being placed in any condition, which helps ensure that groups are equivalent at the start and that any differences in outcomes can be attributed to the manipulation rather than pre-existing differences. While operational definitions, representative samples, and hypotheses are important elements of research, they are not unique to experiments and can be found in correlational studies, observational research, and other methodologies. Random assignment to groups is the defining characteristic that makes a study a true experiment rather

q.s: Which of the following best describes the experimental group in this research design?

o.l: All 100 participants in the study were part of the experimental group.
The group that watched a commercial for the shoes that did not include a celebrity endorsement was the experimental group.
The group that watched a commercial for the shoes featuring a physically attractive celebrity was the experimental group.
This research did not involve an experimental group because there was no independent variable.

f.c:
Researchers at an advertising agency conducted a study to determine whether classical conditioning principles could influence consumers' preferences for a particular product. They randomly assigned 100 college students from a nearby university to one of two groups. 

Both groups watched a commercial for the same brand of shoes. One group watched a commercial that did not feature a celebrity endorsement, while the second group watched a commercial that featured a celebrity endorsement from a physically attractive celebrity. The participants were exposed to these ads multiple times a day for two weeks. 

At the end of the two weeks, the participants were asked to rate, on a scale of 1 to 10, how likely they were to purchase the brand of shoes advertised in the commercial they watched.

q.ex: In experimental research design, the experimental group is the group that receives the treatment or manipulation being tested, which involves the independent variable. The control group receives either no treatment or a standard condition for comparison purposes. In this study, the independent variable is the presence of a celebrity endorsement in the commercial. The group that watched the commercial featuring a physically attractive celebrity represents the experimental condition because they received the treatment being investigated. The group that watched the commercial without celebrity endorsement would be the control group, serving as the baseline for comparison. Therefore, option C correctly identifies the experimental group as those exposed to the celebrity-endorsed commercial.
